title: Telling which nouns English counts and which it measures

pays_in.note: The abstract nouns an essay runs on are almost all measured ones.
pays_in.model: There is little evidence that longer hours produce better work.

pays_in.note: Chart language needs the measured and counted words kept apart.
pays_in.model: Less energy was used in 2020, although the number of households rose.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers are full of these words and the errors are audible.
pays_in.model: There's so much conflicting advice about it that people give up.

pays_in.note: A summary-completion answer is wrong if it pluralises a word the passage measures.
pays_in.model: The study found no evidence of long-term damage to the reed beds.

teach.can_do: I can tell whether a noun is one English counts or one it measures, and choose everything around it accordingly.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost every article and quantity mistake starts here. Get this judgement right and half the noun problems downstream never happen.
teach.meaning: English splits nouns in two. Some it counts one by one: a report, two reports, several reports. Others it treats as a quantity you measure rather than count: research, advice, equipment, evidence, traffic. Those never take an s and never take a in front of them. The split is not about the world, it is about the way English happens to package things, which is why furniture is measured and chairs are counted in the same room.

form.pattern: counted: a report, two reports  ·  measured: research, some research, a great deal of research
notes: a measured noun takes a singular verb: the evidence is clear, the equipment was delivered
to count a measured noun, count its container: a piece of advice, an item of equipment, two pieces of research
the common measured nouns learners pluralise: information, advice, research, equipment, knowledge, evidence, progress, feedback, traffic, furniture, luggage
a few nouns sit on both sides with two meanings: experience, time, paper, work
form.negative: there is not much evidence for it yet
form.question: How much evidence is there?

left.text: a report, two reports, several reports

right.text: evidence, some evidence, plenty of evidence

spec.caption: The line runs through the words, not through the world. Chairs are counted and furniture is measured, and they are the same room.

worked_example.sentence: Her supervisor sent over two pieces of feedback before the deadline.
worked_example.why_this_form: Feedback is measured, so a number cannot sit next to it. English counts the pieces instead, and the number goes there.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two feedbacks is not a smaller slip than a wrong word. It is a shape English has no room for at all, and a reader stops dead at it.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor gave me three pieces of advice about the essay.
notice_set.question: How many separate things did the tutor say?
notice_set.why: The number has moved onto the pieces, because it could not sit next to the word it belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: We need more equipment before the field trip.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you how many items are needed?
notice_set.why: More measures a quantity. If you want a number, you have to name the units it comes in.

notice_set.sentence: The department has ordered four new microscopes.
notice_set.question: Can you count what was ordered?
notice_set.why: They arrive one at a time and English counts them one at a time, which is what the s at the end is doing.

notice_set.sentence: There is not much research on the Verdon estuary.
notice_set.question: Is this about a small number of studies or a small amount of work?
options: They are the same thing here
notice_set.why: Research is a body of work, so English measures it. Studies is the word to use when you want a number.

notice_set.sentence: She has a lot of experience of teaching large groups.
notice_set.question: Is this about events she remembers or about skill built up over years?
notice_set.why: One word, two meanings, and English marks the difference: the skill is measured and the events are counted.

notice_set.sentence: She had two odd experiences on her first day.
notice_set.question: Is she talking about things that happened, or about what she is good at?
notice_set.why: The s does the work. With it, the word means separate happenings you could list.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether English counts this word or measures it, then choose.
teach.false_rule: That anything you can see and touch must be countable. Furniture, luggage and equipment are all things you can carry, and English measures every one of them.

errors.wrong: The report gives useful informations about rural schools.
errors.right: The report gives useful information about rural schools.
errors.why_it_happens: In most other languages this word behaves like an ordinary countable noun, so the plural is produced automatically before any rule about English can fire.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on informations.
errors.l1_note: Nearly universal; the word is countable in French, Spanish, Arabic and many others.

errors.wrong: I would like to give you an advice about the interview.
errors.right: I would like to give you a piece of advice about the interview.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows that a lone singular noun usually needs a small word in front of it and supplies one. The rule is right; this is simply not the kind of noun it applies to.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: an becomes a piece of.

errors.wrong: The evidence from both surveys are difficult to read.
errors.right: The evidence from both surveys is difficult to read.
errors.why_it_happens: Surveys sits right next to the verb and pulls it into the plural. The word the sentence is actually about is four words earlier and is measured, not counted.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: There is fewer traffic on the coast road since the charge came in.
errors.right: There is less traffic on the coast road since the charge came in.
errors.why_it_happens: Fewer sounds more careful than less, so it gets used as the polite version of it. They are not two levels of politeness; they belong to the two different halves of the noun system.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: fewer becomes less.

used_in.quote: Information, evidence, coverage and access all appear in the first paragraph, and every one of them is measured.

payload.sentence: My tutor gave me three pieces of advice before the interview.
payload.question: How many separate suggestions were there?

feedback.why_key: The number has been moved onto the word that can carry it, and it still tells you exactly how many there were.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the number on the container word.

items.decision_cue: a student's summary of a study

payload.context: From a student's summary of a study.
payload.sentence: The paper gives many evidences for the same conclusion.
reasons: this word is measured, not counted
the paper cannot give anything
the conclusion is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A reader who meets this word with an s on it stops, and the sentence has cost you a moment of attention it needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the noun before you add the s.

payload.context: From a note on a river survey.
payload.stem: There is ___ (little / few) evidence that the reed beds have recovered.

expected: little

feedback.why_key: Evidence is measured, and the measuring word is the one that goes with it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the quantity word to the half the noun belongs to.

payload.context: From a chart description covering energy use by household.
payload.stem: ___ (Less / Fewer) households were on the old tariff by 2019.

expected: fewer

feedback.why_key: Households can be counted, so the counting word is the right one even though the sentence sounds formal.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the noun in your head before you choose.

payload.given: The handbook contains many useful informations for new students.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the noun is treated the way English treats it.

expected: a great deal of useful information for new students
a lot of useful information for new students
much useful information for new students

feedback.why_key: Once the s goes, the quantity word in front has to change too, because the two always travel together.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the noun first and let the quantity word follow.

payload.audio_text: There's a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked.

expected: there's a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked
there is a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked
theres a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked

feedback.why_key: Hearing that a fluent speaker never puts an s on this word is worth more than being told twice that it has none.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of the noun, not just the start.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a trial of two treatments.
payload.sentence: The evidence from both trials are difficult to compare.
reasons: the verb has followed the wrong noun
the trials cannot be compared
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The word the sentence is about is at the front and is measured. The plural next to the verb belongs to a phrase that is only describing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the noun the sentence is about, then set the verb.

payload.sentence: She has had many experiences of managing teams, and two experience of running a whole site.

expected: two experiences

feedback.why_key: The same word is used correctly twice and wrongly once, which is what makes this the hardest kind of mistake to catch in your own writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread every use of a word you got right once.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about how much of what people read online is checked before it is published. Use at least two nouns that English measures rather than counts.

feedback.why_key: Two of these words in one sentence is where the quantity words in front of them start being chosen rather than guessed.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the noun, then choose the word in front of it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the first body paragraph of your social media news answer. Circle every noun you have measured rather than counted and check the verb that follows each one. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure this is the judgement that slips first, so a real paragraph is the only honest test of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every verb that follows a measured noun.

title: Saying how much or how many without giving a number

point_json.grammar_name: some, any, much, many, a lot of

pays_in.note: Questions about your day, your town and your food need these constantly.
pays_in.model: There aren't many decent cafes round here, to be honest.

pays_in.note: General statements about society run on them.
pays_in.model: A lot of people cook less than their parents did.

pays_in.note: A short-answer item can hang on whether you heard much or many.
pays_in.model: There isn't much space in the storeroom at the moment.

teach.can_do: I can say how much or how many there is without counting anything.
teach.why_it_matters: These are among the most frequent words in spoken English, and the wrong one is heard immediately even when everything else in the sentence is right.
teach.meaning: Most of the time you do not know a number and do not need one. English has a small set of words for saying roughly how much there is, and each of them belongs on one side of the counted and measured split. Two of them, some and any, split a different way: some goes with a plain statement, and any goes with a negative or a question. Once you have those two pairs, you can say how much of anything there is.

form.pattern: some / any + counted or measured  ·  many + counted  ·  much + measured  ·  a lot of + either
notes: some in a plain statement: there are some seats left, there is some bread left
any in a negative or a question: there aren't any seats, is there any bread?
some also appears in an offer or a request, where the answer is expected to be yes: would you like some tea?
much and many sit most comfortably in negatives and questions; plain statements normally take a lot of
form.negative: there isn't much time and there aren't many people
form.question: Is there much time? Are there many people?

left.text: many, a few, several, a lot of

right.text: much, a little, a great deal of, a lot of

spec.caption: A lot of appears in both boxes, which is why it is the safest thing to say when you are not sure.

worked_example.sentence: There isn't much time before the market closes, and there aren't many stalls left open.
worked_example.why_this_form: Time is measured and stalls are counted, so the two halves of the sentence take the two different words even though they are making the same complaint.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swapping them does not change the meaning at all, which is precisely why it is worth learning: the mistake is audible and it costs you nothing to avoid.

notice_set.sentence: There isn't much bread left.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about loaves or about an amount?
notice_set.why: Bread is measured here, so the word in front of it is the measuring one.

notice_set.sentence: There aren't many rolls left.
notice_set.question: Could you count what is left?
notice_set.why: Rolls come one at a time, so the counting word goes in front of them.

notice_set.sentence: Is there any milk in the fridge?
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already know the answer?
notice_set.why: This word turns up when the speaker does not know, which is why it lives in questions and negatives.

notice_set.sentence: There's some milk in the fridge.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking or telling?
notice_set.why: A plain statement takes the other word of the pair, and the two almost never swap.

notice_set.sentence: Would you like some more soup?
notice_set.question: What is the speaker expecting you to say?
notice_set.why: An offer expects a yes, so it takes the statement word even though it has a question mark on the end.

teach.rule_line: Some for telling and offering, any for asking and denying.
teach.false_rule: That any is just the question version of some. It marks an open, unknown quantity, which is why an offer, whose answer is half agreed already, takes some.

errors.wrong: There were much people waiting outside the hall.
errors.right: There were a lot of people waiting outside the hall.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is learned first and used as the general word for a large amount, without the counted and measured split being attached to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes a lot of.

errors.wrong: We do not have many time before the coach leaves.
errors.right: We do not have much time before the coach leaves.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is reaching for the more formal-sounding word rather than checking what kind of noun follows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: many becomes much.

errors.wrong: I did not take any photo of the harbour.
errors.right: I did not take any photos of the harbour.
errors.why_it_happens: Any looks like a singular word because it has no s of its own, so the noun after it is left singular too.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the s on photo.

used_in.quote: Almost every answer about what you eat and where you buy it needs one of these words.

payload.sentence: There isn't much bread left.
payload.question: Is the speaker thinking about loaves or about an amount?

feedback.why_key: The word in front tells you which way the speaker is thinking about it, before the noun even arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the quantity word as a clue to the noun.

payload.context: A shopkeeper explaining why the shelves are empty.
payload.sentence: There were much people in this morning.
reasons: the quantity word does not go with this noun
the time is wrong
the shop cannot be empty
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: People come one at a time, so the word in front has to be one of the counting ones.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the noun can be counted, then choose.

payload.context: Two people looking in a nearly empty fridge.
payload.stem: Is there ___ (some / any) milk left?

expected: any

feedback.why_key: Nobody knows the answer yet, and that is the situation this word belongs to.
feedback.feed_forward: Use any when you genuinely do not know.

payload.context: A host at the table with a full pan in front of them.
payload.stem: Would you like ___ (some / any) more soup?

expected: some

feedback.why_key: It has a question mark and it is not really a question. The host expects a yes, and that is what decides the word.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether an answer is already half expected.

payload.given: There is a lot of work to do before Friday.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it as a negative statement with the same meaning reversed.

expected: much work to do before friday
there isn't much work to do before friday
there isnt much work to do before friday
there is not much work to do before friday

feedback.why_key: A lot of is what a plain statement takes, and much is what a negative takes, so both words change when the sentence flips.
feedback.feed_forward: Switch to much or many as soon as you go negative.

payload.audio_text: There aren't many places to eat near the office.

expected: there aren't many places to eat near the office
there arent many places to eat near the office
there are not many places to eat near the office

feedback.why_key: Two short words run together at the start and they carry both halves of the meaning: the negative and the counting.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the two small words before you write the rest.

payload.context: Someone describing a market they visited on holiday.

expected: i didn't take any photos of the fish stalls
i didnt take any photos of the fish stalls

feedback.why_key: Any leaves the number open, and an open number in English is a plural unless you mean not even one.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the s on the noun after any.

payload.sentence: There are many evidence for this and not many time to look at all of it.

expected: much evidence
a great deal of evidence
a lot of evidence

feedback.why_key: Both halves are wrong in the same way, and finding the first one usually shows you the second.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix one, then look for the same mistake again.

payload.prompt_text: Write two short sentences about what is in your kitchen at the moment: one about something you can count and one about something you can only measure.

feedback.why_key: Putting the two kinds of noun side by side is the fastest way to feel the difference the words are marking.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the counted one first, then the measured one.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked about food and cooking at home. Speak for forty seconds and use at least three of these words, with the noun each one needs.

feedback.why_key: At speaking speed there is no time to check, so this is where the pairing either has become automatic or has not.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the noun in your head before the word in front of it.

title: Saying whether a small amount is enough or is a shortage

point_json.grammar_name: a few and few, a little and little, and the language of proportion

pays_in.note: Proportion language is most of what a chart answer needs above the numbers themselves.
pays_in.model: The majority of journeys were made on foot, and a significant proportion by bicycle.

pays_in.note: The difference between conceding a point and dismissing it is one word.
pays_in.model: A few schemes have worked, but little of that success has been repeated elsewhere.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers need a way to grant part of a case without granting all of it.
pays_in.model: A few people manage it, but not many, and that's the whole problem.

pays_in.note: A true or false stem often turns on whether the passage said few or a few.
pays_in.model: Few of the original buildings survived the redevelopment.

teach.can_do: I can say that a small amount is enough, or that it is a shortage, and be understood the way I meant.
teach.why_it_matters: One missing word turns good news into a complaint. It is the cheapest meaning reversal in English and nobody warns learners about it.
teach.meaning: A few and few describe the same quantity and take opposite views of it. A few looks at what there is: some, enough to work with. Few looks at what there is not: hardly any, and the sentence is a complaint. A little and little do the same job for measured nouns. Nothing else in the sentence changes, so the only thing telling the reader which way you meant it is one small word at the front.

form.pattern: a few / few + counted noun  ·  a little / little + measured noun
notes: with the a, the sentence is positive: a few stalls stayed open, a little time is left
without it, the sentence is negative: few stalls stayed open, little time is left
the bare versions are formal and belong in writing rather than in conversation
for a large share without a number: the majority of, a significant proportion of, plenty of
the majority of takes its verb from the noun after of: the majority of households were, the majority of the money was
form.negative: few of the stalls stayed open, and little of the money was spent locally
form.question: How many of the stalls stayed open?

ends: there is enough to work with

marks.label: a few stalls stayed open
some stalls stayed open
few stalls stayed open

worked_example.sentence: A few of the older traders are still there, so the market has kept some of its character.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second half of the sentence is positive, so the first half has to be too. The a is what makes the two halves agree.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the a away and the opening becomes a complaint, and the sentence then argues with itself halfway through.

notice_set.sentence: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
notice_set.question: Did the market keep going?
notice_set.why: The speaker is pointing at what survived, which is why the sentence feels like good news.

notice_set.sentence: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
notice_set.question: Did the market keep going?
notice_set.why: The same number, and the speaker is pointing at the shortage instead.

notice_set.sentence: There is a little time left before the tender closes.
notice_set.question: Can the bid still go in?
notice_set.why: Enough is left to act on, which is the whole message of this version.

notice_set.sentence: There is little time left before the tender closes.
notice_set.question: Can the bid still go in?
notice_set.why: The same clock, and this version is telling you to give up on it.

notice_set.sentence: The majority of the households in the district were on the old tariff.
notice_set.question: Roughly what share of households is being described?
notice_set.why: It is the useful way to report a large share when the exact number is not worth giving.

teach.rule_line: The a turns a shortage into a supply. Nothing else in the sentence changes.
teach.false_rule: That few and a few are one word with an optional article. They point in opposite directions, and a reader follows whichever one you wrote.

contrast.question: Am I saying there is some, or am I saying there is almost none?

fork.answer: Some, enough to work with, and I am pleased about it
Almost none, and I am pointing at the shortage
A large share, and I do not want to give a number
fork.selects: the majority of, a significant proportion of

a.text: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
a.means: Some stayed open. The market kept going and the sentence is pleased about it.

b.text: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
b.means: Almost all of them shut. The market emptied and the sentence is reporting a loss.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Writing few when you meant a few does not read as a slip. It reads as a complaint, and the rest of your paragraph then argues against a shortage you never intended to report.

edge_case.text: Without the a, both words are formal and suit writing. In conversation people reach for hardly any or not many, and that is the right choice there, not a lesser one.

contrast.stronger_test: Put but on the end and see which way the sentence wants to go. A few stayed open, but... expects a problem. Few stayed open, but... expects a consolation.

worked_pairs.a: A few of the older traders are still there.
worked_pairs.b: Few of the older traders are still there.
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence is about survival and the other is about loss, and the difference between them is two letters and a space.

worked_pairs.a: There is a little money left in the maintenance budget.
worked_pairs.b: There is little money left in the maintenance budget.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first sentence lets you order the repair. The second tells you to write the letter explaining why you cannot.

worked_pairs.a: The majority of the households were on the old tariff.
worked_pairs.b: The majority of the money was spent on the old tariff.
worked_pairs.gloss: The verb follows the noun after of, not the word majority, which is why the two sentences take different verbs.

errors.wrong: Few of the funding reached the smaller schools.
errors.right: Little of the funding reached the smaller schools.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored few as the negative word and reaches for it whatever kind of noun follows. The positive and negative pair exists twice, once on each side of the noun system.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: few becomes little.

errors.wrong: Few people came to the meeting, which was a good turnout for a wet evening.
errors.right: A few people came to the meeting, which was a good turnout for a wet evening.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the number was small and picks the word for a small number, without noticing that the second half of their own sentence is pleased about it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: a.

errors.wrong: The majority of the households in the district was on the old tariff.
errors.right: The majority of the households in the district were on the old tariff.
errors.why_it_happens: Majority looks singular and it is five words from the verb, so it wins the argument over the plural noun that actually decides the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was becomes were.

used_in.quote: Reporting six modes without repeating a number six times is exactly what this proportion language is for.

payload.sentence: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
payload.question: Did the market keep going?

feedback.why_key: The speaker is counting what survived, and that is what makes the sentence sound like good news.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the small word at the front before the number.

payload.sentence: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
payload.question: Did the market keep going through to the spring?

feedback.why_key: Exactly the same number of stalls, and this version is counting the ones that shut.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice which side of the number the writer is standing on.

payload.context: An email to a team who still have time to finish the bid.

payload.context: From a paragraph describing a chart of household tariffs.
payload.stem: The majority of households in the district ___ (be) on the fixed tariff by 2020.

expected: were

feedback.why_key: The verb takes its instruction from households, not from majority, however far away it has ended up.

payload.context: A short note from a manager who is relieved the deadline can still be met.
payload.stem: There is still ___ (a little / little) time before the deadline, so the bid can go in.

expected: a little

feedback.why_key: Relieved is the clue. The version with the article is the one that lets the sentence finish the way it started.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the small word to the mood of the sentence.

payload.given: Only a small number of the older shops are still trading.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the opening so that a single word carries the shortage.
payload.starter: ___ of the older shops are still trading.

expected: few
few of the older shops are still trading

feedback.why_key: Five words become one and the complaint survives the cut, which is what makes the short version worth having.
feedback.feed_forward: Use one word where you were about to use five.

payload.audio_text: There's a little time left, so we can still send it.

expected: there's a little time left so we can still send it
there is a little time left so we can still send it
theres a little time left so we can still send it

feedback.why_key: The whole difference is one unstressed vowel, and it is the difference between sending the bid and not sending it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small sound before the quantity word.

payload.context: From a piece in the local paper welcoming the market's survival.
payload.stem: ___ of the original traders are still there.

options.why_this_means: That some have hung on, and the writer is pointing at what survived.
That almost all have gone, and the writer is pointing at what was lost.

expected: a few

feedback.why_key: A piece that has already told you it is celebrating cannot open its next sentence with a complaint.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the whole piece's mood, then pick the word.

payload.context: From a piece in the local paper explaining why the market has emptied out.
payload.stem: ___ of the original traders are still there.

options.why_this_means: That some have hung on, and the writer is pointing at what survived.
That almost all have gone, and the writer is pointing at what was lost.

expected: few

feedback.why_key: The same eight traders. What has changed is which half of the story the writer is telling.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the argument, not the number, choose the word.

payload.context: An email to a caretaker approving a small repair.
payload.stem: There is ___ money left in the maintenance budget, so go ahead and order the part.

options.why_this_means: That some is left and it can be spent.
That almost none is left and nothing more should be spent.

expected: a little

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence gives permission, so the first half cannot be refusing it.

payload.context: An email to a caretaker refusing a small repair.
payload.stem: There is ___ money left in the maintenance budget, so the part will have to wait.

options.why_this_means: That some is left and it can be spent.
That almost none is left and nothing more should be spent.

expected: little

feedback.why_key: Same budget, same balance, opposite instruction, and one word carries all of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the ending of your sentence first if you are unsure.

payload.context: Two sentences from different drafts of a report on a high street.
sentences: A few of the older shops have survived.
Few of the older shops have survived.

title: Using the when my reader can already tell which one I mean

point_json.grammar_name: the: second mention, unique things, and defining phrases

pays_in.note: A paragraph that introduces an example and then refers back to it needs both halves of this.
pays_in.model: A charge was introduced in Marlow in 2018. The charge has since been raised twice.

pays_in.note: A letter about a problem is one long chain of first and second mentions.
pays_in.model: There is a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom, and the crack has widened since March.

pays_in.note: Telling a story means bringing things in and then pointing back at them.
pays_in.model: We found a small café near the station, and the café turned out to be run by his cousin.

pays_in.note: Following what a passage refers back to is largely a matter of following these words.
pays_in.model: The proposal described above was withdrawn before the deadline.

teach.can_do: I can use the when my reader can pick out which one I mean, and a when they cannot.
teach.why_it_matters: This is one decision, taken dozens of times in every answer you write. Getting it right costs nothing once the question is the right one.
teach.meaning: The is not about how important a thing is or how much you like it. It is a signal to your reader that they can already pick out which one you mean. There are only a few ways they can: you mentioned it a moment ago, there is only one of it in the situation you are both in, or the words straight after it narrow it down to one. If none of those is true, your reader cannot pick it out, and you need a instead.

form.pattern: the + any noun, counted or measured, singular or plural
notes: second mention: a lift was fitted last year, and the lift broke in June
only one in the situation: the roof, the kitchen, the manager, the sun
narrowed by what follows: the lift in the north block, the report you sent me
the never changes shape, whatever noun comes after it
form.negative: the lift has not worked since June
form.question: Which lift do you mean?

left.role: reader cannot pick it out yet
left.text: a lift, a report, a manager

right.text: the lift, the report you sent, the manager

spec.caption: Things usually travel left to right in a paragraph: you bring something in with a, and from then on it takes the.

worked_example.sentence: A notice went up in the lobby in March, and the notice is still there in October.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first mention brings the notice into the paragraph and the second points back at it, so the reader knows without asking which piece of paper is meant.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with the notice would assume the reader already has one in mind, and a reader who does not will stop and look back for it.

notice_set.why: The second sentence brings in a new one, so a reader assumes the building has more than one.

notice_set.why: Both things are being brought in for the first time, which is what a is for.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether your reader can already tell which one is meant.
teach.false_rule: That the goes in front of anything important, or anything you have ever mentioned. It is about what your reader can identify right now, from what they already have.

contrast.question: Can my reader already pick out which one I mean?

fork.answer: Yes: I mentioned it, or there is only one here, or the words after it narrow it down
No: it is one of several and I am bringing it in for the first time

a.text: A lift was fitted last year.
a.means: There may be several lifts, and this is the first time you are hearing about this one.

b.text: The lift was fitted last year.
b.means: We both know which lift. Either there is only one, or we have already been talking about it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Opening a paragraph with the lift when your reader has never heard of it does not look like an article mistake. It reads as though you have skipped a sentence, and the reader goes back to look for the one they think they missed.

edge_case.text: Some things take the because there is only one in the world rather than one in the room: the sun, the government, the environment. Treat them as the same rule with a very large room.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask yourself whether a reader could answer the question which one? from what they have already read. If they can, write the. If they would have to ask you, write a.

worked_pairs.gloss: The first sentence introduces both. The second assumes you already have both, which only works if somebody has introduced them first.

title: Leaving the out when I mean the whole category

pays_in.note: Every essay opens with a general claim, and every general claim needs this.
pays_in.model: Online courses have made higher education reachable for people who work full time.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers are general claims almost from beginning to end.
pays_in.model: Young people read differently now, not less.

pays_in.note: Telling a general claim from a specific one is often what a true, false or not given item is testing.
pays_in.model: Tidal schemes have never produced electricity at a competitive price.

teach.can_do: I can make a statement about a whole category without putting a word in front of it.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the single most common noun mistake in essay writing, and it happens in the first sentence of the first paragraph, where it does the most damage.
teach.meaning: When you are talking about a whole category rather than about particular members of it, English puts nothing in front of the noun at all. No small word, no signal, nothing. That is why an essay about all computers everywhere starts with computers and not with the computers. Most languages mark a general statement in some way, and English marks it by leaving the space empty, which is exactly what makes it hard to remember.

form.pattern: nothing + plural counted noun  ·  nothing + measured noun
notes: the whole category, plural: computers have changed how offices work
the whole category, measured: pollution is a serious problem in older cities
an abstract idea in general: education, poverty, technology, freedom, research
a singular counted noun still needs a small word, even in a general statement: a computer is now cheaper than a bicycle
form.negative: computers have not made offices quieter
form.question: Have computers changed how offices work?

left.text: computers, pollution, education

right.text: the computers in this room, the pollution in the estuary

spec.caption: The left box has nothing in front of it, and the empty space is the signal.

worked_example.sentence: Solar panels have become cheap enough to fit on an ordinary house.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim is about panels as a category, not about a set a reader could walk over and look at, so the space in front stays empty.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Adding the would point at particular panels on a particular roof, and the reader would look back through the page to find out which ones.

notice_set.sentence: Cameras have changed what counts as evidence in a courtroom.
notice_set.question: Is this about particular machines you could point at?
options: No, it is about all of them
notice_set.why: The claim covers the whole category, and the empty space in front is what says so.

notice_set.sentence: The cameras in the market square were replaced last year.
notice_set.question: Is this about particular machines you could point at?
options: No, it is about all of them
notice_set.why: The words after the noun narrow it down to a set in one room, which is when the small word comes back.

notice_set.sentence: Pollution is a serious problem in most older cities.
notice_set.question: Which pollution is meant?
notice_set.why: A measured noun works the same way: a general claim leaves the space in front empty.

notice_set.sentence: A computer now costs less than a good bicycle.
notice_set.question: Is this a general statement or about one machine?
notice_set.why: A general statement can also be made with a singular noun, and then the small word is back, because a singular counted noun always needs one.

notice_set.sentence: In modern society, people expect an answer within minutes.
notice_set.question: Which society is meant?
notice_set.why: This is a general claim, so nothing goes in front, however formal the phrase sounds.

teach.rule_line: A whole category takes nothing in front of it. Leave the space empty.
teach.false_rule: That an important abstract noun deserves the in front of it. It does not sound more serious, it sounds more specific, which is the opposite of general.

contrast.question: Am I talking about the whole category, or about particular ones?

fork.answer: The category as a whole, using a plural noun or a measured one
Particular ones my reader can pick out
One of several, mentioned for the first time

a.text: Computers have changed the way offices are run.
a.means: All computers, everywhere. This is a claim about the category as a whole.

b.text: The computers have changed the way offices are run.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Opening an essay with the computers does not read as an article slip. It reads as though you are pointing at machines the reader cannot see, and they spend the next line looking for them instead of following your argument.

edge_case.text: Most place names take nothing, and a few take the: rivers, ranges and groups of islands keep it. Learn those as words rather than as a rule, because there is no rule to learn.

contrast.stronger_test: Try putting all of them in front of the noun. If all computers still says what you meant, the space in front stays empty.

title: Running one three-question check in front of every noun I write

point_json.grammar_name: The article decision: a, the, or nothing

pays_in.note: You will run this check forty or fifty times in one answer.
pays_in.model: A degree taught in a second language costs students time before it saves them any.

pays_in.note: Chart language moves constantly between categories and particular figures.
pays_in.model: Cycling accounted for a small share of journeys, and the share fell after 2018.

pays_in.note: General claims in a discussion need the empty space, and examples need the pointer.
pays_in.model: People generally trust a doctor more than they trust the health service as a whole.

pays_in.note: A passage signals whether a claim is general or particular with these words alone.
pays_in.model: The scheme described in the previous section was never repeated.

teach.can_do: I can run one short check in front of any noun and come out with the right word every time.
teach.why_it_matters: Articles are among the last things any learner gets reliable, so what you need is not a feeling but a procedure you can run in three seconds under pressure.
teach.meaning: You have met the three choices separately. Putting them together is one question asked in a fixed order, and the order matters, because the first question that gets a yes ends the check. Ask whether you mean the category as a whole. If not, ask whether your reader can pick out which one you mean. If not, you are introducing one of several, and what happens then depends only on whether the noun is one English counts.

form.pattern: Q1 category? nothing.  Q2 identifiable? the.  Q3 otherwise: a with a singular counted noun, nothing with a plural or a measured one
notes: question one: renewable energy is expensive to store
question two: the storage problem described above is the reason
question three, singular counted: a battery lasts about ten years
question three, plural or measured: batteries lose capacity, storage costs money
a singular counted noun can never stand alone: not battery lasts ten years
form.negative: a battery does not last for ever
form.question: How long does a battery last?

rungs.text: Q1  Do I mean the whole category?  ->  nothing
Q2  Can my reader pick out which one?  ->  the
Q3  Neither: singular counted  ->  a, otherwise nothing

worked_example.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store, and a battery big enough for a house still costs more than the roof it sits under.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first noun is a whole category, so nothing goes in front. The second is one of many, so it takes a. The third is narrowed by the words after it, so it takes the.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The renewable energy would point at one particular supply, which is not a claim anybody could check, and battery on its own is a shape English does not have.

notice_set.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
notice_set.question: Is this about one supply or about the whole idea?
notice_set.why: The first question gets a yes, so the check stops there and the space stays empty.

notice_set.sentence: The storage problem described above is the main obstacle.
notice_set.question: Can a reader tell which problem is meant?
options: Only if they know the subject
notice_set.why: The words after the noun narrow it to one, which is the second question answered yes.

notice_set.sentence: A battery large enough for a house costs about as much as a small car.
notice_set.question: Is one particular battery meant?
options: No, any one of that kind
notice_set.why: Neither of the first two questions gets a yes, the noun is singular and counted, so it takes the third answer.

notice_set.sentence: Batteries lose capacity as they age.
notice_set.question: How many batteries are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The first question again, and a plural noun making a general claim takes nothing in front.

notice_set.sentence: Battery lasts about ten years.
notice_set.question: Does this sound like something an English speaker would write?
notice_set.why: A singular counted noun cannot stand on its own, whichever of the three answers you were aiming at.

teach.rule_line: Category, then identifiable, then one of several. Stop at the first yes.
teach.false_rule: That articles are a feel you pick up by reading. Reading helps and is not enough: the decision is taken faster than noticing works, so you need a check.

contrast.question: Whole category, one my reader can pick out, or one of several?

fork.answer: The whole category, with a plural or a measured noun
One my reader can pick out from what they already have
One of several, singular and counted

a.text: Buses in Marlow run every ten minutes.
a.means: This is what bus travel in Marlow is like, as a general fact about the town.

b.text: The buses in Marlow run every ten minutes.
b.means: The particular service we have been discussing, which the reader already has in mind.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Both versions are correct English and they answer different questions. If your paragraph is about what the town is like, the pointer narrows a general claim into a timetable, and your reader takes away a smaller point than you made.

edge_case.text: Two places where the check does not help: fixed phrases like at home, by car, in bed and at school, and names, which have to be learned one at a time. Neither is worth arguing with. Learn them as words.

contrast.stronger_test: If the noun is singular and counted, something has to go in front of it, whatever the rest of the check said. That one fact catches more mistakes than the whole of the rest of the procedure.

worked_pairs.a: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
worked_pairs.b: The renewable energy generated at Verdon is stored in an old mine shaft.
worked_pairs.gloss: Question one is yes for the first sentence and no for the second, because the words after the noun have pinned it to one place.

worked_pairs.a: A battery lasts about ten years.
worked_pairs.b: The battery in the loft was replaced in March.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both nouns are singular and counted, so both need something. Which word depends only on whether the reader can pick it out.

worked_pairs.a: Students who commute pay more for housing.
worked_pairs.b: The students who commute pay more for housing.
worked_pairs.gloss: Words after the noun do not automatically call for the pointer. The first sentence is about all commuting students anywhere; the second is about a group already under discussion.

errors.wrong: The renewable energy is expensive to store.
errors.right: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
errors.why_it_happens: Question two is answered before question one, so a general claim gets treated as though the reader could pick out which supply is meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: The.

errors.wrong: Storage problem described above is the main obstacle to any of this.
errors.right: The storage problem described above is the main obstacle to any of this.
errors.why_it_happens: The words after the noun already identify it, so the pointer at the front feels redundant. It is the pointer, not the description, that English requires.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: The.

errors.wrong: A research into tidal power has been going on for thirty years.
errors.right: Research into tidal power has been going on for thirty years.
errors.why_it_happens: Question three has been reached and answered as though the noun were one English counts. The check is only as good as the countability judgement it sits on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: A.

used_in.quote: Every sentence of this answer contains at least two nouns, and every one of them needs the check run on it.

the time is wrong

title: Pointing at things nearby, far off, and back up the page

pays_in.note: It is how a second sentence picks up a first without repeating it.
pays_in.model: Two schemes were withdrawn in the same year. This pattern was not a coincidence.

pays_in.note: A chart answer keeps pointing back at figures it has just given.
pays_in.model: These three headings between them took two thirds of the total.

pays_in.note: Telling a story means pointing at times and places as you move through it.
pays_in.model: That summer was the last one before everything changed.

pays_in.note: Working out what a pointing word refers back to is a question type on its own.
pays_in.model: This finding was not repeated in any of the later studies.

teach.can_do: I can point at something near me, something further off, and something I wrote two lines ago.
teach.why_it_matters: Pointing back at your own last sentence is how a paragraph holds together, and pointing back vaguely is how one falls apart.
teach.meaning: These four words point. Two of them point at what is near, in space, in time or in the conversation, and two point at what is further off. Each pair has one word for a single thing or a measured noun and one for several. In writing, they do something more useful: they point back at what you have just said, which lets your next sentence pick it up without repeating it.

form.pattern: this / that + one thing or a measured noun  ·  these / those + more than one
notes: near, in space or in the conversation: this shelf, these figures, this evidence
further off, or already finished: that summer, those figures, that argument
they can stand alone without a noun: this is the problem, those were the good years
pointing back in writing, the safe version puts a noun after the word: this shift, these findings, this problem
form.negative: these figures do not support the claim
form.question: What do these figures show?

marks.label: this shelf, these figures
that summer, those figures

worked_example.sentence: Fares rose and two services were cut. These two changes together pushed people back into cars.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second sentence points back at both things at once and names what they are, so the reader knows exactly what has been picked up.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: This pushed people back into cars would point back at something without saying what, and a reader has to choose between the fares, the cuts, or both.

notice_set.sentence: These figures were collected before the charge came in.
notice_set.question: How many sets of numbers are being pointed at?
notice_set.why: The word chosen tells you the count before the noun even arrives.

notice_set.sentence: This evidence was collected before the charge came in.
notice_set.question: How much is being pointed at?
notice_set.why: A measured noun takes the single-thing word, because there is nothing to count.

notice_set.sentence: That summer, nobody expected the mill to close.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about the summer just gone?
notice_set.why: The far word puts distance in, and here the distance is in time rather than in space.

notice_set.sentence: Fares rose and services were cut. This has made people angry.
notice_set.question: What exactly has made people angry?
notice_set.why: The word points back at something and does not say what, so the reader has to guess between two things.

notice_set.sentence: Fares rose and services were cut. These two changes have made people angry.
notice_set.question: What exactly has made people angry?
notice_set.why: Adding a noun after the pointing word closes the gap, and the reader has nothing left to guess.

teach.rule_line: When you point back at your own writing, put a noun after the word.
teach.false_rule: That this on its own is fine because the reader will work it out. They often can, and the moment they cannot the paragraph stops with you not there.

errors.wrong: These evidence suggests that the scheme worked.
errors.right: This evidence suggests that the scheme worked.
errors.why_it_happens: Evidence feels plural because it is made of many pieces, so the plural pointing word is chosen for it. English measures the noun and takes the single-thing word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: These becomes This.

errors.wrong: This figures show a steady rise from 2015 onwards.
errors.right: These figures show a steady rise from 2015 onwards.
errors.why_it_happens: The pointing word is chosen before the noun is settled, and once it is written it is not looked at again.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: This becomes These.

errors.wrong: Fares rose and two services were cut. This has made people angry.
errors.right: Fares rose and two services were cut. These two changes have made people angry.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows what they are pointing at, so the sentence reads perfectly to them. The reader has two candidates and no way of choosing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one noun: put a noun after This.

used_in.quote: A pie chart answer groups slices and then points back at the group, which is this point doing all the work.

payload.sentence: These figures were collected before the charge came in.
payload.question: How many sets of numbers are being pointed at?

feedback.why_key: The pointing word settles the count before the noun arrives, which is why the two have to agree.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the pointing word as a count.

payload.context: From a summary of a study on air quality.
payload.sentence: These evidence suggests that the filters made no difference.
reasons: the pointing word does not match the noun
the filters cannot be measured
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The noun is one English measures, so it takes the single-thing pointer even though the evidence is made of many pieces.
feedback.feed_forward: Settle the noun kind, then pick the pointer.

payload.stem: ___ (this / these) two categories together accounted for over half of the budget.

feedback.why_key: Two of anything takes the plural pointer, and the number is sitting there in the sentence to remind you.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a number in front of the noun.

payload.context: From a summary of a trial.
payload.stem: ___ (this / these) evidence was gathered over eighteen months.

expected: this

feedback.why_key: A measured noun has nothing to count, so the single-thing pointer is the only one it can take.
feedback.feed_forward: Use this with a noun English measures.

payload.given: Ticket prices went up and the late bus was withdrawn. This has annoyed a lot of commuters.

these changes have annoyed a lot of commuters
these two decisions have annoyed a lot of commuters
these decisions have annoyed a lot of commuters

feedback.why_key: One noun added and the reader stops having to choose between the fare rise and the withdrawn bus.
feedback.feed_forward: Name what you are pointing at.

payload.context: Someone talking about a year that changed things for their family.

expected: that summer nobody expected the mill to close

feedback.feed_forward: Keep the pointer next to the noun it points at.

expected: these two changes together made a real difference

feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of the pointing word.

expected: these three changes changed
this shift changed
these changes changed

feedback.feed_forward: Put a noun after every pointing word you write.
