title: Describing a process from the first stage to the last in one steady voice

point_json.grammar_name: The process chain: present simple passive and its links

pays_in.note: A diagram answer is this point from the first line to the last.
pays_in.model: Used cans are sorted by weight before they are crushed into blocks.

pays_in.note: Technical passages describe how things are made in exactly this chain.
pays_in.model: The sheets are trimmed to size before they are stacked for delivery.

pays_in.note: A tour or a lecture describing how something works uses this shape throughout.
pays_in.model: The samples are sealed on site and sent to the laboratory the same day.

teach.can_do: I can describe a whole process, stage by stage, without changing voice or losing track of the material.
teach.why_it_matters: A diagram answer is not a set of separate sentences. It is one chain, and the marks come from the chain holding together across all of it.
teach.meaning: A process description has no story and no characters. It has a material that goes in at one end and comes out changed at the other, and every stage is something done to that material. So the whole answer stays in one time, the present, and every sentence reports a thing done rather than a person doing. The links between stages carry the sequence, and the material stays in the subject slot from beginning to end.

form.pattern: the material + is / are + past participle, repeated for every stage
notes: the present is used even for a process that happened yesterday or will happen tomorrow
sequence words open the stage: at this stage, once the sheets have dried, the mixture is then
a stage that follows a finished one takes once or after plus have been: once the pulp has been screened
a relative link keeps two stages in one sentence: a tank, where the water is held for two days
form.negative: the mixture is not heated again after this stage
form.question: Is the pulp screened before it is pressed?

left.text: waste paper, in bales

right.text: new board, in rolls

spec.caption: Everything between the two boxes is something done to the material. Nobody appears in the middle.

worked_example.sentence: Once the pulp has been screened, it is pressed into sheets and left to dry.
worked_example.why_this_form: One sentence carries two stages and a boundary between them, and the pulp holds the subject slot right through, so a reader never loses what is being tracked.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Once workers have screened the pulp, they press it into sheets would put two people into a diagram that has none, and the reader would start wondering how many there are.

notice_set.sentence: The cans are crushed into blocks and loaded onto a lorry.
notice_set.question: How many separate things happen to the cans here?
notice_set.why: Two stages share one subject, so the sentence covers more ground without repeating the noun.

notice_set.sentence: Once the blocks have been weighed, they are sent to the smelter.
notice_set.question: Which of the two things happens first?
notice_set.why: Once marks the boundary and the finished form on the left tells you that stage is over before the next begins.

notice_set.sentence: The molten metal is poured into a mould, where it cools for several hours.
notice_set.question: What is the word where pointing at?
notice_set.why: A link like this fastens a stage to the place it happens in, so a second sentence is not needed.

notice_set.sentence: The water evaporates and leaves a crust of salt behind.
notice_set.question: Is anybody making the water evaporate?
options: No, it happens on its own
notice_set.why: A natural step in a made process keeps its ordinary shape, because nothing is being done to the water at that moment.

notice_set.sentence: At this stage the sheets are trimmed to size.
notice_set.question: Where in the process are you standing when you read this?
notice_set.why: The opening phrase is doing the work of a signpost, which is what stops six stages from reading as six unrelated facts.

teach.rule_line: One time, one voice, one material followed from the first stage to the last.
teach.false_rule: That every verb in a process takes this shape. Steps that happen on their own, such as cooling and drying, keep their ordinary form, and forcing them breaks the sentence.

errors.wrong: The cans are crushed into blocks. Then the blocks were loaded onto a lorry.
errors.right: The cans are crushed into blocks. The blocks are then loaded onto a lorry.
errors.why_it_happens: A diagram feels like a report of something already seen, so the past creeps in as soon as the writer stops concentrating on the shape.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were becomes are.

errors.wrong: The metal is cooled for several hours and then the mould is removed.
errors.right: The metal cools for several hours and then the mould is removed.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has decided that everything in a process takes the same shape and applies it to a stage where nothing is being done at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is cooled becomes cools.
errors.l1_note: Only where the stage genuinely happens on its own; a cooling tower does cool the metal.

errors.wrong: Once the pulp screened, it is pressed into sheets.
errors.right: Once the pulp has been screened, it is pressed into sheets.
errors.why_it_happens: Once feels like it has already marked the stage as finished, so the writer sees no work left for anything else to do.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one pair: has been.

used_in.quote: Six stages, one material, no people: the answer is a single chain built out of this point.
The tutorial walks through how the samples are handled, and every step arrives in this shape.

payload.sentence: The bales are broken open and the paper is fed into a shredder.
payload.question: Is the writer describing something happening this minute?

feedback.why_key: A process description reports a routine, not an occasion, which is why the present holds for the whole answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat every stage as something that happens each time.

payload.context: From a description of how metal parts are cast.
payload.sentence: The metal is cooled for several hours before the mould is opened.
reasons: nothing is doing the cooling here
the time is wrong
the mould cannot be opened
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Metal in a mould cools because it is left alone. Give the stage this shape and you have invented a machine that is not in the diagram.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anything is acting before you reach for be.

payload.context: From a description of how aluminium cans are recycled.
payload.stem: The cans ___ (crush) into blocks before they leave the yard.

expected: are crushed

feedback.why_key: Cans crush nothing. They are what the machine flattens, and the plural subject picks are.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the subject is plural before you write are.

payload.context: From a description of how dried pasta is made.
payload.stem: Once the dough ___ (mix), it is pushed through a shaped die.

expected: has been mixed

feedback.why_key: Once opens a stage that has to be over before the next one starts, and only the finished form closes it.
feedback.feed_forward: After once, close the stage with has been.

payload.given: Workers weighed the blocks. Then they sent them to the smelter.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the two stages as one sentence with no people in it, in the time a diagram uses.

expected: have been weighed they are sent to the smelter
once the blocks have been weighed they are sent to the smelter

feedback.why_key: Two stages, one boundary, one sentence, and the blocks never leave the subject slot.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two stages with once rather than with then.

payload.context: One stage from a description of how sea water is turned into drinking water.

expected: the water is held in a tank for two days
the water is held for two days in a tank

feedback.why_key: Where and how long can trade places, and neither of them can come between is and the word after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the pair together and move the rest around it.

payload.audio_text: Once the salt has been removed the water is safe to drink.

expected: once the salt has been removed the water is safe to drink

feedback.why_key: Three weak syllables run together in the middle and they are the whole of the stage boundary.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow the replay and write the small words first.

payload.sentence: The panels are dried in a warm room, and then they were stacked ready for cutting.

expected: they are stacked

feedback.why_key: Two stages of one process cannot sit in two different times, and the reader notices the jolt even without knowing why.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your stages in a row and check they share one time.

payload.prompt_text: In a bottling plant, glass bottles are washed and then filled. Write one sentence covering both stages, keeping the bottles as the thing the sentence follows.

feedback.why_key: Two stages in one sentence with one subject is the sentence a process answer is made of.
feedback.feed_forward: Write one subject and hang both stages off it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the full body of the aluminium can recycling answer: every stage, one time throughout, and at least one sentence joined with once. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: Six stages is where a chain either holds or comes apart, and no shorter task can show you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Read only your verbs at the end, in order, and check them.

title: Knowing where this shape is the wrong tool and using the ordinary one

pays_in.note: Every chart answer is full of verbs that have nothing on the receiving end.
pays_in.model: Household numbers grew steadily until 2018 and then levelled off.

pays_in.note: An argument about responsibility needs people at the front of sentences.
pays_in.model: Councils cut the maintenance budget three years before the wall failed.

pays_in.note: Talking about your own life needs ordinary shapes, not report grammar.
pays_in.model: The whole thing got called off about an hour before we set out.

pays_in.note: Noticing that a passage says rose rather than was raised is often the whole answer.
pays_in.model: Water levels in the lower valley rose for three consecutive winters.

teach.can_do: I can tell when a sentence has nothing for this shape to move, and write it the ordinary way instead.
teach.why_it_matters: A module that only teaches when to reach for the passive produces writers who reach for it everywhere. Half of learning it is learning where it does not go.
teach.meaning: This shape works by taking the thing on the receiving end and moving it to the front. That only works if there is something on the receiving end. A great many verbs describe what something does rather than what is done to it: rise, fall, happen, occur, appear, evaporate, arrive. Nothing is receiving anything, so there is nothing to move, and the sentence has no version of this kind at all.

form.pattern: no be, no participle: the level rose, the meeting happened, the numbers fell
notes: test the verb by asking what comes after it: if nothing can, there is no version of this kind
a few verbs work both ways with two different meanings: the level rose, the level was raised
get instead of be belongs in speech, not in an essay: it got cancelled, it was cancelled
form.negative: the numbers did not fall after the charge came in
form.question: Did the numbers fall after the charge came in?

left.text: raise, cut, build, collect, monitor

right.text: rise, fall, happen, arrive, evaporate

spec.caption: Only the left box has anything to move to the front. The right box has no version of this kind, and forcing one produces a sentence with a hole in it.

worked_example.sentence: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
worked_example.why_this_form: Rain fell and the level went up on its own. There is no one at the sluice, so the sentence has nothing to put on the receiving end.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Was raised would report a decision: someone at the sluice opened a gate and put the level up, which turns a weather event into an act.

notice_set.sentence: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
notice_set.question: Did anyone make this happen?
options: No, it happened on its own
notice_set.why: Rain does this without anybody's help, and the sentence is shaped to say so.

notice_set.sentence: The water level was raised by half a metre overnight.
notice_set.question: Did anyone make this happen?
options: No, it happened on its own
notice_set.why: This one reports a decision. Somebody at the sluice did it, even though the sentence does not name them.

notice_set.sentence: The accident happened just after six in the morning.
notice_set.question: Could this sentence be built round somebody who caused it?
options: No, this verb takes nothing after it
notice_set.why: Happen has nothing after it to move anywhere, so there is no other version of the sentence to build.

notice_set.sentence: The committee chose the cheaper of the two designs.
notice_set.question: Who is this sentence about?
notice_set.why: The news is that these people made a choice, so they belong at the front where the reader can see them.

notice_set.sentence: The concert got cancelled about an hour before it was due to start.
notice_set.question: Where would you expect to hear this?
notice_set.why: Got instead of was is ordinary spoken English and reads as careless in an essay, which is a register problem rather than a mistake.

teach.rule_line: Ask what the verb does to something. If the answer is nothing, stop.
teach.false_rule: That processes take this shape, so every step in one does. Steps that happen on their own keep the ordinary form, and forcing them invents machinery.

contrast.question: Is there anything in this event on the receiving end?

fork.answer: Nothing at all: the subject acts and nothing is acted on
Yes, but the doer is the news of the sentence
Yes, and the doer is unknown, obvious or beside the point

a.text: The water level rose by half a metre overnight.
a.means: It went up on its own after rain. Nobody was involved.

b.text: The water level was raised by half a metre overnight.
b.means: Somebody at the sluice put it up. A decision was taken.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Writing was risen where you mean rose is not a small slip. It hands the reader a sentence with a hole where the doer should be, and readers stop to look for the person who raised it before they can carry on.

edge_case.text: A handful of verbs work both ways with different meanings, and rise and raise are the pair you will meet most: things rise on their own, and people raise them. Grow, sink, increase and improve behave the same way.

contrast.stronger_test: Put the word something straight after the verb and read it aloud. Raise something works. Rise something does not, and that is your answer.

worked_pairs.a: Rainfall in the catchment fell sharply after 2016.
worked_pairs.b: Rainfall in the catchment was reduced sharply after 2016.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first reports weather. The second says somebody managed to reduce the rain, which is a claim no report would make.

worked_pairs.a: The committee chose the cheaper of the two designs.
worked_pairs.b: It was decided that the cheaper of the two designs would be used.
worked_pairs.gloss: The second version is not wrong and it is not neutral either. It removes the only people who could be asked why.

worked_pairs.a: The concert got cancelled an hour before the doors opened.
worked_pairs.b: The concert was cancelled an hour before the doors opened.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct English. The first belongs in a conversation and the second belongs in a report, and swapping them is what makes a script sound out of place.

errors.wrong: The number of visitors was increased sharply between 2015 and 2019.
errors.right: The number of visitors increased sharply between 2015 and 2019.
errors.why_it_happens: Data description feels formal, and this shape has been learned as the formal one, so it is applied to a verb that has nothing to act on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.

errors.wrong: The accident was happened just after six in the morning.
errors.right: The accident happened just after six in the morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads the accident as a victim, because in the world it is one. The grammar does not agree: happen never takes anything after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.
errors.l1_note: Common where the first language marks events as things that befall people.

errors.wrong: The second reading of the bill got postponed until the following month.
errors.right: The second reading of the bill was postponed until the following month.
errors.why_it_happens: Get is the version the learner hears constantly and it feels more natural than be, because in speech it is. In an essay it drops the register by a whole level.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: got becomes was.

errors.wrong: Three sentences in a row: The samples are collected. They are labelled. They are stored.
errors.right: The samples are collected, labelled and stored, and the labels are checked twice.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the shape is learned it becomes the only shape, and a paragraph of it reads as flat because nothing in it ever changes.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one subject: join the three into one clause with a single subject.

used_in.quote: Almost every verb the line graph needs is one that has nothing on the receiving end.

payload.sentence: The reservoir level rose by nearly a metre overnight.
payload.question: Was anybody involved in this?

feedback.why_key: This is weather. The sentence is built to report something that happened without anybody's help.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a person could have caused it before you decide.

payload.sentence: The reservoir level was raised by nearly a metre overnight.
payload.question: Was anybody involved in this one?

feedback.why_key: Somebody opened a gate. The sentence does not name them and it still tells you they exist.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the shape as a claim about whether anyone acted.

items.decision_cue: a line graph of rail passenger numbers

payload.context: From a paragraph describing a line graph of rail passenger numbers.
payload.sentence: The figure for weekday journeys was increased sharply after the line reopened.
reasons: nothing in the picture is doing this to it
the two halves are the wrong way round
the word after was is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A graph reports what a figure did, not what somebody did to it. The extra word invents a hand nobody claimed.
feedback.feed_forward: Describe a trend with the plain verb and nothing else.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a chart of household spending.
payload.stem: Spending on transport ___ (fall) every year after the fuel duty came in.

expected: fell

feedback.why_key: Nothing is falling the spending. It went down, and the plain form is the only one the verb has.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain form for a trend with no one behind it.

payload.context: From a note about how a reservoir is managed.
payload.stem: In dry summers the level ___ (lower) deliberately to protect the dam wall.

expected: is lowered

feedback.why_key: Deliberately puts a person in the sentence whether they are named or not, so here the shape is right.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a word like deliberately before you rule the passive out.

payload.given: It was decided by the committee that the cheaper design would be used.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the people who took the decision are at the front.

expected: chose the cheaper design
decided to use the cheaper design
the committee chose the cheaper design

feedback.why_key: Five words come out and nothing is lost, which tells you what those five words were doing.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the decider in front when a decision is the news.

payload.audio_text: The whole thing got cancelled an hour before the doors opened.

expected: the whole thing got cancelled an hour before the doors opened

feedback.why_key: What you hear in conversation is got, not was, and hearing the difference is the first step to keeping them apart on paper.
feedback.feed_forward: Note which of the two you heard, then decide where it belongs.

items.decision_cue: three days of heavy rain in the hills

payload.context: From a report on a river after three days of heavy rain in the hills.
payload.stem: The level ___ by half a metre overnight.

options.why_this_means: That it went up with nothing acting on it.
That somebody at the sluice put it up on purpose.

expected: rose

feedback.why_key: Rain in the hills is the cause the sentence has already given you, and rain is not a person.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the cause in the context before you choose the verb.

items.decision_cue: a controlled test of the new sluice gates

payload.context: From a report on a river during a controlled test of the new sluice gates.
payload.stem: The level ___ by half a metre overnight.

options.why_this_means: That it went up with nothing acting on it.
That somebody at the sluice put it up on purpose.

expected: was raised

feedback.why_key: A controlled test has operators in it, and the same half metre now reports what they did rather than what the weather did.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the situation, not the verb, decide whether anybody acted.

payload.context: Two friends on the phone about a festival that has fallen through.
payload.stem: Apparently the whole thing ___ at the last minute.

options.why_this_means: That the speaker is talking, not writing, and the news is the disappointment.
That the speaker is reporting for the record, in the register of a written notice.

expected: got called off

feedback.why_key: Both are correct. On the phone the shorter one is what a speaker reaches for, and using the other sounds like reading from a card.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the shape to whether you are speaking or writing.

items.decision_cue: the opening paragraph of a written report

payload.context: From the opening paragraph of a written report on the same festival.
payload.stem: Apparently the whole thing ___ at the last minute.

options.why_this_means: That the speaker is talking, not writing, and the news is the disappointment.
That the speaker is reporting for the record, in the register of a written notice.

expected: was called off

feedback.why_key: A report has no voice of its own, so the version that carries a speaking voice is the one that stands out for the wrong reason.
feedback.feed_forward: Write was in a report and save got for speech.

payload.context: Two lines taken from separate parts of one report on a national park.
sentences: Visitor numbers grew by a third over the decade.
Visitor numbers were capped at eight hundred a day.
meanings: Something happened and nobody arranged it.
Somebody made a decision and put a limit in place.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences about the same numbers, and only one of them has a person behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a decision is being reported or a trend.

items.decision_cue: rainfall has also been unusually high

payload.context: A note on a stretch of moorland where a drainage scheme has been running for two years and rainfall has also been unusually high.
payload.stem: Water levels in the peat ___ since the work began.

options.why_this_means: That the levels came up, and the sentence takes no view on whether the scheme or the weather did it.
That the scheme did it, and the sentence is giving the engineers the credit.

follow_up.question: Which one would you write if you did not want to claim the scheme caused it?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and they make different claims. One reports a measurement, the other awards a result.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the version whose claim you can actually defend.

items.decision_cue: a change in hospital waiting times

payload.context: From a paragraph about a change in hospital waiting times.
payload.sentence: The waiting time was fallen by nearly two weeks after the new clinic opened.
reasons: this verb has nothing on the receiving end
the time is wrong
the clinic cannot open
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing falls a waiting time. The word was is looking for a doer that this verb has no room for.
feedback.feed_forward: Test the verb with something after it before you add was.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows household energy use dropping every year from 2016, with no policy behind it. Write one sentence reporting the drop. Do not put anybody into the sentence who is not there.

feedback.why_key: The hard part is resisting the shape you have just spent two lessons learning, which is exactly what this asks you to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the plain verb and leave the sentence short.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences of your renewable electricity answer. At least one must report a trend with a plain verb, and at least one must report a decision with the passive. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Mixing the two inside one paragraph is what a chart answer actually needs, and it is the only way to show you can tell them apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark which sentence is a trend and which is a decision.

title: Saying that I arranged something rather than did it myself

pays_in.note: Questions about your home, your health or your things need it constantly.
pays_in.model: I had the kitchen done just before I moved in.

pays_in.note: A story about a problem usually involves somebody else fixing it.
pays_in.model: We got the whole thing looked at by someone in the village.

pays_in.note: It lets you write about what households arrange without inventing tradespeople.
pays_in.model: Owners are now required to have their properties assessed for insulation.

teach.can_do: I can say that I paid or asked somebody else to do a job, without naming them.
teach.why_it_matters: Without it, learners either claim they rewired their own flat or spend a clause naming a workman nobody asked about.
teach.meaning: There is a gap between doing a job yourself and having no connection to it at all, and most of adult life sits in that gap. This structure fills it. It says the job was arranged by you and carried out by somebody else, and it does that without naming the somebody else at all. The order matters and it is unusual: you, then the thing, then what happened to the thing.

form.pattern: have / get + the thing + past participle
notes: the thing comes between the two verbs, which is the part that feels wrong at first
have is neutral in speech and in writing; get is warmer and belongs in speech
the tense sits on have or get, never on the word at the end: I had the roof repaired, I am having it repaired
form.negative: we did not have the roof repaired until the spring
form.question: Where did you have the roof repaired?

left.text: we

right.text: the roof repaired

spec.caption: The person who did the work is nowhere in the sentence, and that is the whole reason the structure exists.

worked_example.sentence: They had the whole ground floor rewired before the tenants moved in.
worked_example.why_this_form: The owners paid for the work and did none of it, and the electrician's name is not part of the story anybody here is telling.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: They rewired the whole ground floor would claim the owners did the job themselves, which is a different weekend and a different set of skills.

notice_set.sentence: We had the roof repaired the week after the storm.
notice_set.question: Did these people climb onto the roof themselves?
notice_set.why: The structure says the job happened and somebody else did it, without ever introducing that somebody.

notice_set.sentence: We repaired the roof the week after the storm.
notice_set.question: Did these people climb onto the roof themselves?
notice_set.why: Nothing sits between the two parts, so the people at the front are the people on the ladder.

notice_set.sentence: I am getting my eyes tested on Friday.
notice_set.question: Who will do the testing?
notice_set.why: The speaker has made the appointment and will sit in the chair. The tester is not in the sentence and does not need to be.

notice_set.sentence: She had her bag stolen on the way home.
notice_set.question: Did she arrange this?
notice_set.why: The same shape also reports something bad that happened to you, which is the one use that has nothing to do with arranging anything.

notice_set.sentence: They are having the whole ground floor rewired this month.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
options: No, it is going on now
notice_set.why: The time sits on the first word of the pair, exactly as it does in any other sentence.

teach.rule_line: Put the thing in the middle: had the roof repaired, not had repaired the roof.
teach.false_rule: That have here means own or possess. It carries no meaning of its own in this structure. It is doing a job, and the job is arranging.

errors.wrong: We had repaired the roof the week after the storm.
errors.right: We had the roof repaired the week after the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other structure the learner knows keeps the two verb parts together, so the thing gets pushed out to where it usually goes and the sentence quietly changes meaning.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: the roof goes between had and repaired.

errors.wrong: I am getting my eyes test on Friday.
errors.right: I am getting my eyes tested on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The last word is a long way from the verb that governs it, so the ending is dropped when attention runs out at the end of the clause.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: test becomes tested.

errors.wrong: Residents got their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.
errors.right: Residents had their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.
errors.why_it_happens: Get is the version everybody hears and it arrives first. In a report it reads as chatty next to the formal vocabulary around it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: got becomes had.

used_in.quote: Almost any honest answer about work done to a flat needs this structure twice.

payload.sentence: We had the chimney repointed the week after the storm.
payload.question: Who went up the ladder?

feedback.why_key: The thing sitting in the middle is what tells you the speaker arranged the job rather than doing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a noun between the two verbs.

payload.context: Marta is telling a colleague about an appointment she has booked.
payload.sentence: I am getting tested my eyes on Friday.
reasons: the thing is in the wrong place
the day is wrong
getting cannot be used here
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Everything in the sentence is a word this structure uses, and they are in an order it does not allow.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the thing before the last word, every time.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a flat that has just been sold.
payload.stem: They had the whole ground floor ___ (rewire) before it went on the market.

expected: rewired

feedback.why_key: The ending is the only thing marking the floor as the thing the electrician worked on.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the last word its ending even when the sentence is long.

payload.context: A student explaining why their laptop has been away for a week.
payload.stem: I am ___ (have) the screen replaced under the warranty.

expected: having

feedback.why_key: The time sits on the first word of the pair, so the -ing goes there and nowhere else.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the tense on have or get, never on the last word.

payload.given: A builder from the village repaired our chimney last autumn.
payload.instruction: Rewrite so that we are the ones arranging the work, and no builder appears.

expected: had our chimney repaired last autumn
we had our chimney repaired last autumn
had the chimney repaired last autumn

feedback.why_key: The builder disappears, the chimney moves into the middle, and the sentence is now about the household.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the thing into the middle when the doer leaves.

payload.context: Someone explaining what they are doing on Friday morning.

expected: i am getting my eyes tested on friday
on friday i am getting my eyes tested

feedback.why_key: The day can move to the front and the middle three words cannot move at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the middle first, then place the time phrase.

payload.audio_text: We had the kitchen done just before we moved in.

expected: we had the kitchen done just before we moved in

feedback.why_key: Spoken at speed, had the runs together into a single sound, and it is the sound that carries the whole meaning.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a noun sitting between two verbs.

payload.sentence: Residents got their meters replaced under a scheme funded by the council.

expected: had their meters replaced

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is ungrammatical. One word is a level below everything around it, and that is what a reader hears.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had in a report and keep got for conversation.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one job in your home that somebody else did for you. Write one sentence about it that does not name the person who did it.

feedback.why_key: The person you would normally name is exactly the person this structure exists to leave out.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what was done, not who did it.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked about your home and what you have changed in it. Speak for forty-five seconds and use this structure at least twice, once about the past and once about something arranged for the near future.

feedback.why_key: Using it twice in one answer, in two different times, is where the word order stops needing thought.
feedback.feed_forward: Plan the two things first, then start the clock.

title: Reporting what people generally think without saying who thinks it

pays_in.note: It opens the paragraph where you set out a view before disagreeing with it.
pays_in.model: It is often argued that longer school days improve results, though the evidence is thin.

pays_in.note: It is how you report a general view in a discussion without claiming it as yours.
pays_in.model: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

pays_in.note: Passages mark their own hedged claims this way, and questions test whether you saw the hedge.
pays_in.model: The settlement is believed to have been abandoned within a generation.

teach.can_do: I can put a claim into an essay without owning it and without inventing somebody to blame for it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between an essay that asserts and an essay that positions. It buys credit for the argument as well as for the grammar.
teach.meaning: Sometimes you need a claim in your paragraph that you are not prepared to sign your name to. This structure puts the claim on the page and leaves the believing to people in general. Nobody is named, no source is invented, and the sentence is honest about where it stands. It also lets you introduce a view in order to disagree with it in the next line, which is what most argument paragraphs are made of.

form.pattern: It is thought that + a full clause  —  or  —  X is thought to + verb
notes: the two carry the same meaning: It is thought that the scheme works, and The scheme is thought to work
an adverb in the middle sharpens it: widely accepted, generally assumed, commonly held
for something already over, the second pattern takes to have: the wall is thought to have failed in the storm
the verbs that fit are the reporting ones: think, believe, say, argue, assume, accept, suggest, know
form.negative: it is not generally accepted that the scheme has worked
form.question: Is it generally accepted that the scheme has worked?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this claim?

steps.gloss: I am saying it, and you can hold me to it

steps.text: It is widely accepted that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: other people say it and I am not arguing with them

steps.text: It has been suggested that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: somebody has said it once, and I am about to look at whether it holds

worked_example.sentence: It is generally accepted that class size matters less than the quality of teaching.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim needs to be in the paragraph so the next sentence can qualify it, and the writer has no study to point at and should not pretend to.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stated flat, it would put the writer's own name on a finding they have not defended, which is a bigger promise than the paragraph can keep.

notice_set.sentence: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is their own view?
options: No, they are reporting what people hold
notice_set.why: The claim is in the paragraph and the writer is standing beside it rather than behind it.

notice_set.sentence: Early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Who is answerable for this claim?
notice_set.why: With nothing in front of it, a claim belongs to whoever wrote it down.

notice_set.sentence: The sea wall is thought to have failed during the November storm.
notice_set.question: Is the failure certain?
options: No, it is what people believe
notice_set.why: The structure reports a belief about the past, which is exactly what you need when the cause is still being argued over.

notice_set.sentence: It has been suggested that the charge simply moved the traffic elsewhere.
notice_set.question: How many people hold this view, on the evidence of the sentence?
options: At least one, and possibly few
notice_set.why: Suggested is the weakest verb in the set, and it is the one to use before you take a claim apart.

notice_set.sentence: It is generally assumed that new roads reduce congestion, but the evidence is mixed.
notice_set.question: What is the second half of the sentence doing?
options: Pushing back against the first half
notice_set.why: Introducing a view in order to argue with it is the commonest reason to reach for this structure at all.

teach.rule_line: Report the claim, name nobody, then say what you think of it.
teach.false_rule: That this is a way of sounding academic. It shows where you stand, and a paragraph that uses it and never comes off the fence has used it wrongly.

errors.wrong: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion.
errors.right: The scheme is thought to reduce congestion.
errors.why_it_happens: The two patterns are learned as one and then blended. Once the subject is at the front, the clause has nowhere to attach and the sentence carries the claim twice.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one join: that it reduces becomes to reduce.

errors.wrong: It widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.right: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.why_it_happens: The adverb sits where the small word belongs and fills the gap to the eye, so the sentence looks complete while it is being written.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: is.

errors.wrong: Everyone knows that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.right: It is widely argued that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants weight behind the claim and reaches for the biggest available number of believers, which a reader immediately doubts.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one opening: Everyone knows that becomes It is widely argued that.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer needs both views on the page before either can be judged, and this is how the first one arrives.
Answers about what people generally do need a way to report a view without pretending to have counted.

payload.sentence: It is widely assumed that reading at home lifts later results.
payload.question: Whose view is this?

feedback.why_key: The writer has put the claim on the page without signing it, which leaves them free to qualify it next.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opening words to see who is answerable.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about road building.
payload.sentence: It is obvious to everyone that widening a motorway never eases congestion for long.
reasons: it claims more agreement than anybody can show
the verb form is wrong
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A reader who has not met this claim immediately becomes the exception, and the sentence has lost them in seven words.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a claim as widely held rather than as beyond argument.

payload.context: From the opening of a report on a coastal collapse.
payload.stem: It ___ (think) that the wall failed during the November storm.

expected: is thought

feedback.why_key: The small word before the participle is the whole structure, and it is the one most often left out.
feedback.feed_forward: Write is before the reporting word, always.

payload.context: From a summary of research into sleep.
payload.stem: Short sleep is believed ___ (increase) the risk of several long-term conditions.

expected: to increase

feedback.why_key: This pattern hands the claim to the subject and then needs an infinitive to carry the rest. Nothing else fits after believed here.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the second pattern with to, not with that.

payload.given: It is thought that the market improves footfall in the surrounding streets.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the market is the subject, keeping the same meaning.

expected: is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets
the market is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets

feedback.why_key: The claim does not change. Only the way in changes, and the two ways are worth having because paragraphs need both.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the subject forward and turn that into to.

payload.context: One sentence from a report on an abandoned settlement.

expected: the site is believed to have been abandoned within a generation

feedback.why_key: Four small words run in a fixed order in the middle, and none of them can be dropped or swapped.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the middle from the left, one word at a time.

payload.audio_text: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

expected: it's generally thought that people read less than they used to
it is generally thought that people read less than they used to
its generally thought that people read less than they used to

feedback.why_key: In speech the opening shrinks to a single syllable, and that syllable is the entire hedge.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the short opening even when you barely hear it.

payload.sentence: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion in the centre.

expected: to reduce

feedback.why_key: Two ways in have been used at once, so the sentence announces its claim twice and finishes neither.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick one of the two patterns and finish it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the opening sentence of a paragraph that sets out the popular view that online courses are as good as classroom teaching, so that the next sentence can disagree with it.

feedback.why_key: A view you are about to argue with has to be on the page first, and it has to be somebody else's when it gets there.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the claim up so you can still walk away from it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the first three sentences of your online courses paragraph: the popular view reported without a named source, one qualification, and your own position stated plainly. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: The structure only earns its place if the paragraph eventually comes off the fence, so the third sentence is the test.
feedback.feed_forward: End the three sentences with your own view, unhedged.

title: Using this shape in places where a verb cannot carry a time

pays_in.note: It states what has to happen without naming who has to do it.
pays_in.model: Older housing stock needs to be insulated before any of this is worth doing.

pays_in.note: It joins two stages of a process into one sentence.
pays_in.model: The sheets are stacked without being trimmed at this stage.

pays_in.note: Dense academic sentences are dense largely because of these forms.
pays_in.model: Having been abandoned twice, the site was finally cleared in the 1970s.

teach.can_do: I can use this shape after another verb, or after a preposition, where a full sentence will not fit.
teach.why_it_matters: It is what lets one sentence carry two events. Without it, learners write two short sentences and lose the connection between them.
teach.meaning: Not every verb in a sentence carries a time. After another verb, and after a preposition, English uses a form that has no time of its own and takes it from the sentence around it. This shape has those forms too, and they let you say that something has to be done, is about to be done, or happened without anybody noticing, all inside a sentence that has already started.

form.pattern: to be + past participle  ·  being + past participle  ·  having been + past participle
notes: after another verb: the roof needs to be replaced, the gate has to be locked
after a preposition: the lorry left without being weighed
for something finished first: having been signed off in the spring, the scheme went to tender
the time is carried by the first verb in the sentence, never by this part
form.negative: the report does not need to be rewritten
form.question: Does the report need to be rewritten?

rungs.text: The roof needs to be replaced.
The lorry left without being weighed.
Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.

worked_example.sentence: The old cabling has to be replaced before the building can be let again.
worked_example.why_this_form: Has to already carries the time, so the verb after it has none of its own, and the cabling is on the receiving end of the work.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The old cabling has to replace would say the cabling goes off and replaces something else, which is a sentence about very unusual wiring.

notice_set.sentence: The pumps need to be serviced before the wet season starts.
notice_set.question: Are the pumps doing the servicing or having it done?
notice_set.why: The small word before the last one is what puts the pumps on the receiving end.

notice_set.sentence: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
notice_set.question: Did anybody weigh the lorry?
notice_set.why: After a preposition the -ing form is the only one allowed, and this shape has its own version of it.

notice_set.sentence: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender in May.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: The opening phrase reports the earlier event, which is how one sentence can hold two dates without saying either of them twice.

notice_set.sentence: The old panels are due to be removed next month.
notice_set.question: Have the panels gone yet?
notice_set.why: Due carries the time and points forward, so the whole sentence sits ahead of now.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.
notice_set.question: Who is doing the telling in this sentence?
notice_set.why: The teller is left out, exactly as in a full sentence of this kind, and the shape survives inside another verb.

teach.rule_line: Keep be in the sentence even when it cannot carry a time.
teach.false_rule: That the small word can go because the sentence is long already. It is the only thing putting the subject on the receiving end, and without it the sentence reverses.

errors.wrong: The roof needs to replaced before the winter.
errors.right: The roof needs to be replaced before the winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has to hold three verbs at once and the smallest of the three drops out. It carries no meaning of its own, so nothing warns them.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: be.

errors.wrong: The lorry left the yard without be weighed.
errors.right: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule that a preposition takes the -ing form is known, but it is applied to the last verb rather than to the first one, which is where it belongs.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: be becomes being.

errors.wrong: Having been approve in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.right: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.why_it_happens: Three words have already been produced correctly and attention has run out by the fourth, which is where the meaning actually lives.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one ending: approve becomes approved.

used_in.quote: A solutions paragraph is a list of things that need to be done, which is this structure repeated.

payload.sentence: The filters need to be changed before the dry season starts.
payload.question: Are the filters cleaning something else?
options: No, something is being done to them

feedback.why_key: Two small words in the middle turn the filters from the worker into the thing worked on.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for be before the last word of the pair.

payload.context: From a note about weighbridge procedure at a depot.
payload.sentence: No lorry may leave the yard without be weighed.
reasons: the word after without is in the wrong shape
may cannot be used here
the yard cannot be left
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: After a preposition English allows one shape only, and it is the first of the two verbs that has to take it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the -ing on the first verb after a preposition.

payload.context: From a surveyor's report on an empty flat.
payload.stem: The wiring needs ___ (replace) before the flat can be let again.

expected: to be replaced

feedback.why_key: Need carries the time, so all three of the words after it are fixed and none of them can be spared.
feedback.feed_forward: Write all three words after need, every time.

payload.context: From a note on a fault in a sorting line.
payload.stem: Several boxes went through without ___ (scan) at all.

expected: being scanned

feedback.why_key: Without takes the -ing shape, and the boxes are what somebody failed to scan, so both parts are needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Combine the -ing with the participle after a preposition.

payload.given: The plan was approved in March. It went out to tender in May.
payload.instruction: Join the two into one sentence that opens with the earlier event.

expected: been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may
having been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may

feedback.why_key: One sentence now carries both events and their order, which is what a reader was working out for themselves before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the earlier event, then give the main clause.

payload.context: One line from a maintenance schedule.

expected: the old panels are due to be removed next month
next month the old panels are due to be removed

feedback.why_key: Five words run in one fixed order in the middle, and the only thing that can move is the time phrase.
feedback.feed_forward: Lock the middle, then place the time phrase.

payload.audio_text: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.

expected: nobody likes being told what to do at short notice

feedback.why_key: Being runs into the word after it and the pair sounds like one word, which is how it disappears from writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Split what you heard into two words before you write it.

payload.sentence: The roof needs to replaced before the winter, and the gutters need clearing.

expected: needs to be replaced

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence is fine, which is what makes the first half easy to read past.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the short words in the middle before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Offices with long sitting hours are unhealthy. Write one sentence saying what has to change, without naming who should change it.

feedback.why_key: A solution stated this way commits to what must happen and leaves the argument about who out of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what must happen; leave out who must do it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of your sedentary working day answer. At least two sentences must say what needs to happen without naming an actor. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: A whole paragraph of solutions is where the shape either becomes automatic or keeps losing its small words.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the small words in each sentence before you stop.

title: Saying which person or thing I mean by hanging a clause on it

teach.can_do: I can add a clause after a noun to say exactly which person or thing I mean.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complex sentence in English and the safest one to risk. Two short sentences become one, and the reader stops asking which one you meant.
teach.meaning: This kind of clause does one job: it narrows a noun down until only the right thing is left. Say the driver and your listener has a whole depot to choose from. Say the driver who took the Ashfield run and there is one. The clause is not decoration you could lift out. Take it away and the sentence stops identifying anything, which is why nothing is allowed to separate it from its noun.

form.pattern: noun + who / which / that + the rest of the clause
notes: who for people, which for things, and that for either of them in this kind of clause
the relative word stands in for the noun inside the clause, so the noun is never said twice
the verb inside the clause agrees with the noun outside it, however far back that noun is
form.negative: The inside of the clause goes negative in the ordinary way: the driver who does not take the Ashfield run.
form.question: Ask which one? about the noun. Turn the answer into who took it or which arrived late, and hang it straight on the noun.

left.text: the driver

right.role: the clause that narrows it to one
right.text: who took the Ashfield run

spec.caption: Nothing comes between the two boxes. No comma, no pause, no breath.

worked_example.sentence: The engineer who checked the Ashfield line has written the report.
worked_example.why_this_form: On its own, the engineer could be any of nine people on that team. The clause cuts nine down to one, and then the sentence can get on with its news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would still be true, but they make the reader hold a person in mind and wait to find out which one was meant.

notice_set.sentence: The drivers who finished the safety course start on the new route in April.
notice_set.question: Do all the drivers start on the new route in April?
notice_set.why: Only the drivers picked out by the extra words start. The others are outside what the sentence is talking about.

notice_set.sentence: The lift that serves the north platform is out of order.
notice_set.question: Can you use a different lift?
notice_set.why: One lift has been picked out. Whether the station has any others is simply left open.

notice_set.sentence: The road that runs along the Verdon floods twice a winter.
notice_set.question: Does the road beside the river flood?
notice_set.why: The added words are how you know which road is meant, and that road is the one beside the river.

notice_set.sentence: Passengers who booked online can board first.
notice_set.question: Can a passenger who paid at the desk board first?
notice_set.why: The permission is attached to one group only, and paying at the desk puts you outside it.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic treats patients who live inside the county.
notice_set.question: Would the clinic treat someone from three counties away?
notice_set.why: Living inside the county is what makes someone one of the patients the sentence means.

teach.rule_line: If taking the words out leaves the reader asking which one, weld them on.
teach.false_rule: That who is for people and that is only for things. That works for people too here, and speakers use it constantly.

errors.wrong: The engineer who I trained him last year has taken over the depot.
errors.right: The engineer who I trained last year has taken over the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Plenty of languages keep the pronoun inside the clause. The learner builds a complete clause and then adds the relative word in front of it, and nothing feels missing, because nothing is.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: him.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Arabic, Persian and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The inspector which signed the report has retired.
errors.right: The inspector who signed the report has retired.
errors.why_it_happens: Which arrives first because it is the word learners meet most in written English. The check for whether the noun is a person happens later, once the sentence is already moving.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: which becomes who.

errors.wrong: The reports that covers the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.right: The reports that cover the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb inside the clause has to agree with a noun that is now several words behind, and the last thing the learner heard in their head was a singular word.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on covers.

errors.wrong: The scheme which the council approved in March. It has already run over budget.
errors.right: The scheme which the council approved in March has already run over budget.
errors.why_it_happens: The added clause makes the first group of words long enough to feel like a whole sentence, so a full stop goes in and the real news is left stranded in a new one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and let the sentence carry on.

pays_in.note: Every sentence in a body paragraph that defines who you are talking about.
pays_in.model: The households that struggle most with fuel bills are the ones least able to pay for insulation.

pays_in.note: It is how you identify a person or a place inside a long turn.
pays_in.model: The teacher who taught me to swim was the one everybody at the pool was frightened of.

pays_in.note: Passages define their key terms this way, and the questions test the definition.
pays_in.model: The technique that the survey team adopted had been abandoned almost everywhere else.

used_in.quote: You cannot argue about which services a small town should keep without a sentence that says which services you mean.
The passage introduces its central term and then narrows it with a clause, which is exactly what the first question turns on.

payload.sentence: The trains that stop at Brackenfield are always the slow ones.
payload.question: Is every train on this line slow?

feedback.why_key: Only one group of trains has been picked out, and it is the group that stops at Brackenfield.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the added words as a filter on the noun, not as extra news.

payload.sentence: Staff who work nights are offered a free eye test each year.
payload.question: Does a day-shift nurse get the free eye test?

title: Leaving out who, which or that when the clause already has a subject

teach.can_do: I can drop who, which or that when someone else is already doing the verb in the clause.
teach.why_it_matters: It makes your English sound like English rather than like a grammar drill, and it is the shape most people are actually listening for.
teach.meaning: The relative word has a job inside its own clause. Sometimes it is the one doing the verb, and then it cannot leave, because the clause would have nobody in it. Sometimes another subject is already there, doing the verb, and the relative word is only the thing the verb happens to. Then it is carrying no weight, and English quietly drops it. The meaning does not change at all. Only the number of words does.

form.pattern: noun + (who / which / that) + subject + verb ...
notes: keep the word when nothing follows it but a verb: the tutor who marked my essay
drop it when a new subject follows: the essay the tutor marked
a preposition left at the end of the clause is normal and stays where it is: the flat we looked at
form.negative: Nothing changes when the clause is negative: the essay the tutor did not mark.
form.question: Put your finger on the word straight after who, which or that. Is it a verb, or is it somebody new?

ends: nobody else in the clause, so the word has to stay
somebody else is already doing the verb, so the word can go

marks.label: the tutor who marked my essay
the bus that goes past the school
the essay that the tutor marked
the essay the tutor marked

worked_example.sentence: The form I filled in on Tuesday has gone missing.
worked_example.why_this_form: I is already doing the filling in, so the relative word has nothing left to do in the clause, and English lets it disappear without a trace.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting that back in front of I changes nothing about the meaning. It only slows the sentence down by a syllable and makes it a shade more careful.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer the depot hired last month starts on Monday.

notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: Nobody else appears before the verb, so the engineer is the one doing it.

notice_set.sentence: The report the council rejected ran to ninety pages.
notice_set.question: Who rejected it?
notice_set.why: The council has slipped straight in after the noun, and that is your signal about who acted.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor I emailed twice has finally replied.
notice_set.question: Who sent the emails?
notice_set.why: I is doing the emailing. The tutor is only on the receiving end of it.

notice_set.sentence: The parcel that arrived this morning is still on the desk.
notice_set.question: Did something arrive this morning?
notice_set.why: Nothing stands between that and arrived, so the parcel itself is what arrived.

teach.rule_line: Look at the word after the relative word. If it is a new subject, you can drop it.
teach.false_rule: That leaving it out is lazy or too informal for an essay. Careful written English drops it exactly as readily as conversation does.

errors.wrong: The bus goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.right: The bus that goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored the rule as the word is optional and applies it everywhere. Nothing in that stored version mentions who is doing the verb, so nothing fires to stop it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: that.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked at it on Saturday has already gone.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday has already gone.
errors.why_it_happens: With the relative word gone, the clause looks unfinished, so the learner puts an object back in to repair it. The repair is what creates the error.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The route the drivers complain about most. It has three level crossings.
errors.right: The route the drivers complain about most has three level crossings.
errors.why_it_happens: With no relative word to signal that the sentence has not finished, the run of words feels complete, a full stop goes in, and the actual news is stranded in the next sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and run the two halves together.

payload.context: A tenant writing to a landlord. Put in the missing word only if the sentence needs one.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a recipe in your family.

payload.audio_text: The shift I'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday.

payload.context: Two lines from a court report.
sentences: The officers the magistrate criticised have been moved to other duties.

The officers did the criticising and the magistrate was on the receiving end.

title: Deciding whether a clause picks something out or just adds news about it

teach.can_do: I can use commas to show whether a clause is telling my reader which one, or telling them something new about it.
teach.why_it_matters: A pair of commas changes how many people you are talking about. Your reader sees what you wrote, not what you meant.
teach.meaning: Both kinds of clause hang on a noun, and there the resemblance ends. One narrows the noun down until the right thing is left. The other assumes you already have the right thing and hands you a fact about it. Commas are the switch between those two jobs, and they are not decoration. Leave them out and you have quietly told your reader that other candidates exist. Put them in and you have said there are none.

form.pattern: noun , + who / which / whose + clause , + the rest of the sentence
notes: that is refused inside the commas; use who for people and which for things
the relative word can never be dropped here, however long the clause is
when the clause runs to the end of the sentence, one comma is enough: we walked to the depot, which shuts at six
form.negative: The inside goes negative as usual: the bridge, which does not carry lorries, reopened in April.
form.question: Before the comma goes in, ask whether your reader could already pick the thing out.

left.role: no commas: the clause says which one
left.text: the drivers who live in Marlow

right.role: commas: you already knew which, so this is news
right.text: the drivers, who live in Marlow,

spec.caption: Same seven words, two different head counts. The punctuation does all of it.

worked_example.sentence: The Sandmouth ferry, which stops running in November, carries about forty cars a trip.
worked_example.why_this_form: There is one ferry at Sandmouth and the reader already has it. The November detail is news about that ferry, not a way of telling it apart from another one.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the commas out and the sentence starts sorting Sandmouth's ferries into ones that stop in November and ones that do not, then picks the first kind.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery detail is set apart, so it is not being used to tell one aunt from another. There is nobody to tell her apart from.

notice_set.sentence: My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
notice_set.question: How many aunts does the speaker have?
notice_set.why: The bakery is doing the work of picking one aunt out, and picking out only makes sense when there is a choice.

notice_set.sentence: The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
notice_set.question: How many lifts does the building have?
notice_set.why: Nothing is being narrowed down, so the two named at the start are all there are.

notice_set.sentence: The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: Setting the detail apart means the whole group is meant, so the telling reached every one of them.

notice_set.sentence: The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
notice_set.question: Were all the staff told on Friday?
notice_set.why: One part of the staff is being talked about. What happened to the rest is simply left outside the sentence.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below says something different about how many there are. Work out what is doing that.
pairs: My aunt, who runs the bakery in Marlow, is retiring in June.
My aunt who runs the bakery in Marlow is retiring in June.
The staff, who were told on Friday, have already found other jobs.
The staff who were told on Friday have already found other jobs.
The two lifts, which were put in during 2019, keep breaking down.
The two lifts that were put in during 2019 keep breaking down.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the group is already settled and the clause adds news; on the right the clause is what settles the group.
Commas go in when the noun is a person's relative or a named place.
Use which after a comma and that when there is no comma.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether the reader already knows which one. If they do, the clause takes commas.
teach.false_rule: That the commas are a style choice, or that they mark where you would pause. They mark how many things you are talking about.

contrast.question: Does my reader already know which one I mean?

fork.answer: No, and this clause is how they will find out: no commas
fork.selects: a clause welded straight onto the noun

fork.answer: Yes, it is already settled, and this is news about it: commas both sides
fork.selects: a clause fenced off by commas

a.text: The drivers who live in Marlow have been given parking permits.
a.means: Some drivers live in Marlow and those are the ones with permits. The others got nothing.

b.text: The drivers, who live in Marlow, have been given parking permits.
b.means: Every driver has a permit, and all of them happen to live in Marlow.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You fenced the clause off with commas. That tells your reader that every driver got a permit and that Marlow is a footnote. If only some of them got one, the commas have just handed over the wrong number.

edge_case.text: In speech there are no commas to see. The difference is carried by a small pause and a drop in the voice, and plenty of fluent speakers do not bother with either. Write them; do not lose sleep over hearing them.

contrast.stronger_test: Put your thumb over the clause. If what is left still names one particular thing, the clause is news and takes commas. If what is left names nothing in particular, the commas would be a lie.

worked_pairs.a: The tenants who complained about the damp have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.b: The tenants, who complained about the damp, have been rehoused.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says a subset of the tenants moved. The second says all of them did, and mentions the damp on the way past.

worked_pairs.a: The two routes that lose money are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.b: The two routes, which lose money, are being withdrawn.
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first, losing money is how you know which routes are meant. In the second you already knew, and losing money is the reason being offered.

worked_pairs.a: My cousin who trained as a nurse has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.b: My cousin, who trained as a nurse, has moved to Sandmouth.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first quietly tells you the speaker has several cousins. The second tells you there is one worth mentioning.

errors.wrong: Students, who fail the January test, must retake the module.
errors.right: Students who fail the January test must retake the module.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that this kind of clause is extra information, so commas go round every one of them. The commas then quietly claim that the whole year group failed.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: Her sister who works at the clinic has offered to drive us.
errors.right: Her sister, who works at the clinic, has offered to drive us.
errors.why_it_happens: Nobody has ever told the learner that leaving the commas out makes a claim about how many sisters exist. The clause looks like ordinary detail, so it goes in bare.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one pair of commas.

errors.wrong: The Verdon bridge, that reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.right: The Verdon bridge, which reopened in April, is still single-lane.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the workhorse relative word and it goes in everywhere by default. Nothing in the way it is usually taught mentions that it will not sit inside a pair of commas.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: My uncle, lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.right: My uncle, who lives in Ashfield, has offered us the flat.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the relative word can sometimes be dropped and carries that habit across. Inside commas there is nothing else holding the clause to its noun, so the sentence comes apart.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: who.

pays_in.note: It lets you name a thing and comment on it inside one sentence.

which runs hourly on Sundays

feedback.why_key: There is one number 14, so the commas are doing the right job. It is the word between them that has to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Change that to which the moment the clause is fenced off.

payload.prompt_text: Your town has one railway station and it was rebuilt three years ago. Write one sentence that mentions the rebuilding as news, not as a way of picking the station out.

feedback.why_key: One station means there is nothing to distinguish it from, and that is exactly the situation the fenced-off clause exists for.
feedback.feed_forward: Fence the clause with a comma at each end, not just the first.

payload.prompt_text: Open your body paragraph on people living alone. Find the term you introduced first and rewrite that sentence so the definition sits inside a pair of commas. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Defining a term once and then commenting on it is how an essay stops repeating itself, and it costs one sentence rather than two.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the clause you fenced off is true of every case.

title: Putting the small word in the right place when a clause needs one

teach.can_do: I can keep the small word that a verb needs when the noun it belongs to has moved to the front.
teach.why_it_matters: The preposition carries the meaning here. Drop it and the sentence stops being English; move it wrongly and a spoken answer starts sounding like a legal document.
teach.meaning: Some verbs cannot stand alone: you depend on something, you complain to somebody, you look at a flat. When the thing they need becomes the noun that a clause hangs on, the verb still needs its small word. English gives you two places to put it. It can stay at the end of the clause, where the verb left it, or it can move to the front and take the relative word with it. The choice does not change the meaning at all. It changes how formal the sentence sounds.

form.pattern: noun + (that / who) + subject + verb ... + preposition    |    noun + preposition + which / whom + subject + verb
notes: the everyday shape leaves the preposition at the end: the supplier we ordered from
the formal shape moves it to the front, and then only which and whom will follow it: the supplier from whom we ordered
you cannot move it to the front and also leave it at the end, and you cannot delete it in either shape
form.negative: Negatives change nothing: the supplier we did not order from, the supplier from whom we did not order.
form.question: Say the clause as a plain sentence first. He ordered from them tells you the small word is from.

rungs.text: the team I worked with
the team that I worked with
the team with which I worked
the colleagues with whom I worked

spec.top_label: a report, a formal letter, an academic passage

worked_example.sentence: The supplier we ordered the parts from has gone into administration.
worked_example.why_this_form: The preposition stays where the verb dropped it, at the end of its own clause. That is ordinary written and spoken English and it costs nothing.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: From whom we ordered the parts says exactly the same thing in a colder voice. It suits a formal report and sounds strange in an interview answer.

notice_set.sentence: The colleague I share an office with is on leave until May.
notice_set.question: How many people use that office?
notice_set.why: Sharing takes two, and the small word at the very end is the thing that tells you the office is shared.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme we campaigned against went ahead anyway.
notice_set.question: Did the speakers want the scheme?
notice_set.why: Against is doing the whole job. Everything else in the sentence would be identical either way.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme we campaigned for went ahead anyway.
notice_set.question: Did the speakers want the scheme?
notice_set.why: One word has changed and it has reversed which side the speakers were on.

notice_set.sentence: The estate agent I complained to never replied.
notice_set.question: Who made the complaint?
notice_set.why: To points the complaint away from the speaker and towards the agent, so the speaker is the one who sent it.

notice_set.sentence: The bank from which the loan came has since closed its branch here.
notice_set.question: Where did the money come from?
notice_set.why: From has moved to the front, but it is still pointing at the bank as the source.

teach.rule_line: Leave the small word at the end unless you are writing something formal.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence must never end with a preposition. That rule was borrowed from Latin and English has never once obeyed it.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked on Saturday had already been let.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday had already been let.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner moves the noun to the front and the verb sounds finished without its small word, because the ear is listening for the end of the clause rather than for the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: at.

errors.wrong: The colleague I shared an office to has left the firm.
errors.right: The colleague I shared an office with has left the firm.
errors.why_it_happens: The small word is picked from what the sentence means rather than from what the verb demands, and share happens to demand with in every context, however the sentence is arranged.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to becomes with.
errors.l1_note: Learners often carry across whichever preposition their first language uses with the same verb.

errors.wrong: The supplier to that we sent the order has gone quiet.
errors.right: The supplier to whom we sent the order has gone quiet.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word, so it survives the move to the front. Nothing warns the learner that it is the one word which refuses to stand after a preposition.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes whom.

errors.wrong: That's the department in which I work, and the people with whom I deal are mostly in Marlow.
errors.right: That's the department I work in, and the people I deal with are mostly in Marlow.
errors.why_it_happens: The fronted shape has been learned as the correct one and the end-of-clause shape as a slip. In a spoken answer the effect is a candidate who sounds like a document being read out.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: in goes to the end of the clause.

pays_in.note: Answers about your job and your home run on these constantly.
pays_in.model: The team I work with is spread across two floors, so we mostly talk online.

pays_in.note: The fronted shape gives a formal register without any extra risk.
pays_in.model: The conditions under which the scheme was approved were never made public.

pays_in.note: Academic passages front the preposition, which hides where the clause starts.
pays_in.model: The period during which the readings were taken covered two unusually dry summers.

used_in.quote: Almost every follow-up on this card produces a sentence about the people you work with or the building you study in.

payload.sentence: The manager I report to has been off since March.
payload.question: Who is more senior?

feedback.why_key: Reporting to somebody points upwards, and the small word at the end is the whole of that direction.
