feedback.feed_forward: Read the last word of the clause before you decide who does what.

payload.sentence: The fund from which the grants are paid was set up in the 1970s.
payload.question: Where does the grant money come from?

feedback.why_key: From has moved to the front of the clause but it is still pointing back at the fund as the source.
feedback.feed_forward: Track the small word to whichever noun it is pointing at.

payload.context: From a first draft about staff shortages.
payload.sentence: Most of the training we relied has now been cut.
reasons: the verb has lost the small word it needs
the wrong relative word has been chosen
the clause belongs to a different noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Rely never stands alone. With the training moved to the front, on has nowhere to go except the end of the clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause as a plain sentence and see which word disappeared.

payload.context: From a note about a delayed order at the Marlow depot.
payload.stem: The supplier we ordered the axles ___ has stopped answering the phone.

expected: from

feedback.why_key: Turn it back into a plain sentence and you get we ordered the axles from them, which puts from at the end when the noun moves.
feedback.feed_forward: Rebuild the plain sentence to find the missing word.

payload.context: Somebody describing a flat they nearly took.
payload.stem: The place I told you ___ turned out to have no heating at all.

expected: about

feedback.why_key: You tell somebody about something, so when the something moves to the front, about is left standing at the end of the clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check what the verb demands, not what the meaning suggests.

payload.given: The readings were taken during a period. That period covered two dry summers.
payload.instruction: Write one formal sentence with the small word at the front of the clause.

expected: during which the readings were taken covered two dry summers
during which the readings were taken covered two dry summers.

feedback.why_key: Once during moves to the front, only which can follow it, and the sentence takes on the flat formality that a methods paragraph wants.
feedback.feed_forward: Front the small word first, then put which straight after it.

payload.context: Build a formal sentence about a grant.

expected: the conditions under which the grant was made were never published

feedback.why_key: Under and which travel to the front as a pair, and the sentence does not reach its own verb until the whole clause has gone by.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the small word and which side by side when you front them.

payload.audio_text: The firm we'd been dealing with pulled out in the end.

expected: the firm we'd been dealing with pulled out in the end
the firm we had been dealing with pulled out in the end
the firm wed been dealing with pulled out in the end

feedback.why_key: With is unstressed and sits next to another unstressed word, so it is exactly the kind of thing a listener writes straight past.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen right to the end of the clause, not to the main verb.

payload.sentence: Nobody has ever explained the standards we are judged in this department.

expected: the standards we are judged by
the standards by which we are judged

feedback.why_key: Judged demands by. Without it the sentence reads as though the standards themselves are being judged somewhere in the department.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the missing word at the end, or front it with which.

items.decision_cue: with whom I speak most often

payload.context: An examiner has asked who the candidate talks to most during the week.
payload.sentence: The person with whom I speak most often is my sister.
reasons: the small word has been left out
the wrong relative word follows the preposition
it is correct, but it sounds like a written document in a conversation
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The sentence is simply dressed for a report, and a spoken answer wants the person I speak to most.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the small word at the end when you are speaking.

payload.prompt_text: Say one sentence about a person you work or study with regularly. Keep the small word at the end where a speaker would put it.

feedback.why_key: The end-of-clause shape is what a listener expects, and it leaves you nothing extra to get wrong while you are still thinking.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the clause with the small word and then stop.

payload.prompt_text: In your four-day-week paragraph, find a sentence about the conditions or the people involved and rewrite it once with the small word fronted. Two minutes, then read both versions back.

feedback.why_key: Fronting the preposition is one of the few ways to raise the register of a sentence without adding anything new that could break.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the fronted shape once per paragraph, never twice.

title: Saying how much of a group you mean without starting a new sentence

point_json.grammar_name: Relative clauses after a quantifier: most of which, several of whom

teach.can_do: I can give a total and then say what happened to part of it, inside one sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the structure that turns the commonest punctuation error in academic writing into a complex sentence. One word is the whole difference.
teach.meaning: You often need to say two things about the same group: how many there were, and what happened to some of them. Written English lets you do both in one sentence by hanging the second fact on the first with a quantifier and a relative word. The clause is always news rather than a way of picking the group out, so it is always fenced off by a comma, and the relative word can never be dropped.

form.pattern: noun phrase , + quantifier + of + which / whom + verb ...
notes: which for things, whom for people, and after of there is no third option: that and who are both refused
any quantifier fits in the slot: most, some, several, three, half, none, all, the last of
the same shape works with a noun instead of a quantifier: the cost of which, the results of which
form.negative: None of which and neither of whom carry the negative on their own: the panel heard six witnesses, none of whom were named.
form.question: Ask how many out of how many. The answer is the phrase that goes in front of of.

left.role: two sentences taped together with a comma
left.text: ..., most of them came from one street.

right.text: ..., most of which came from one street.

spec.caption: One word turns a punctuation error into a complex sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
worked_example.why_this_form: The total and the exception arrive together, so the reader never has to hold two separate facts side by side and work out how they connect.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three of them had to be discarded is a second sentence wearing a comma. It says the same thing while telling the reader you cannot hear a sentence boundary.

notice_set.sentence: The department interviewed forty applicants, most of whom had never worked in a laboratory.
notice_set.question: How many of the applicants had laboratory experience?
notice_set.why: Most is counting the ones without experience, which leaves the smaller share on the other side.

notice_set.sentence: The survey used six instruments, two of which failed in the first week.
notice_set.question: How many instruments were still working after that week?
notice_set.why: Six minus the two that failed. The second half of the sentence is arithmetic on the first half.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme, the cost of which has never been published, is now in its fifth year.
notice_set.question: Do we know what the scheme cost?
notice_set.why: The whole point of the fenced-off clause is that the figure has been withheld.

notice_set.sentence: The team submitted three reports, none of which reached the minister.
notice_set.question: Did the minister see any of the reports?
notice_set.why: None covers all three, so nothing at all arrived on that desk.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic wrote to nine families, all of whom replied within a week.
notice_set.question: How many families did not reply?
notice_set.why: All of them replied, so the number left over is zero.

teach.rule_line: After of, use which for things and whom for people. Nothing else fits there.
teach.false_rule: That whom is old-fashioned and who will always do instead. After of, who is not available at all.

errors.wrong: The council received two hundred objections, most of them came from one street.
errors.right: The council received two hundred objections, most of which came from one street.
errors.why_it_happens: The second fact clearly belongs with the first, so a full stop feels too heavy and a comma goes in instead. A comma cannot hold two sentences together, and the writer has no other tool to hand.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: them becomes which.

errors.wrong: The panel heard six witnesses, two of who were never named.
errors.right: The panel heard six witnesses, two of whom were never named.
errors.why_it_happens: Who is the familiar word and whom feels like decoration, so it gets quietly dropped. After of, English offers no choice at all, whatever the writer thinks of the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the m on the end of who.

errors.wrong: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of that had to be discarded.
errors.right: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word everywhere else, so it survives into a slot where it has never been allowed. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to the writer's own ear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: The clinic wrote to nine families, much of whom replied at once.
errors.right: The clinic wrote to nine families, most of whom replied at once.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is stored as the general word for a large amount, and nobody checks whether the group it points back at can be counted. Families can be counted, so much has nothing to measure.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes most.

pays_in.note: A total and a striking part of it belong in one sentence, not two.
pays_in.model: Eleven countries were included, four of which accounted for almost the whole rise.

pays_in.note: It concedes a point and keeps the sentence moving at the same time.
pays_in.model: Several remedies have been proposed, none of which addresses why the shortage began.

pays_in.note: Passages hide their exceptions in this clause, and the questions live there.
pays_in.model: The programme trained sixty inspectors, half of whom left within two years.

used_in.quote: Describing four lines on one chart invites exactly this sentence: four sources, two of which rose steadily throughout.

payload.sentence: The laboratory ran twelve tests, five of which produced no reading at all.
payload.question: How many tests produced a reading?

feedback.why_key: The clause counts the failures, so what is left over is the number that worked.
feedback.feed_forward: Subtract the number in the clause from the total in front of it.

payload.sentence: We had about thirty on the course, half of whom dropped out by Christmas.
payload.question: Roughly how many finished the autumn term?

feedback.why_key: Half the group left, so half of the original thirty is what remained by the end of term.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the quantifier as a share of the group in front of it.

items.decision_cue: most of them closed within a year

payload.context: From a paragraph about new businesses in a small town.
payload.sentence: Nineteen shops opened on that street, most of them closed within a year.
reasons: a comma has been asked to hold two complete sentences together
the wrong quantifier has been chosen
the share has been hung on the wrong noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Most of them closed within a year could stand on its own, which is precisely why a comma cannot be the thing joining it on.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn them into which and the join becomes legal.

payload.context: From the methods section of a field report.
payload.stem: The team deployed eight sensors, three of ___ stopped transmitting within a fortnight.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Sensors are things, and after of only which is available, however natural that may feel.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose which for things and whom for people after of.

payload.context: From a paragraph about community sentences.
payload.stem: The scheme supervised ninety offenders, none of ___ reoffended in the first year.

expected: whom

feedback.why_key: Offenders are people, and after of the only form English will take is the one ending in m.
feedback.feed_forward: Write whom whenever of points back at people.

payload.given: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon. About sixty of them did not survive the summer.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence.
payload.starter: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon, ___

expected: about sixty of which did not survive the summer
sixty of which did not survive the summer

feedback.why_key: The second fact is arithmetic on the first, so the two belong inside one sentence rather than side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace them with which to join the two facts.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a small grants fund.

expected: the fund backed twelve projects, half of which ran over budget

feedback.why_key: The quantifier, of and which travel as a block, and the verb of the clause comes after all three of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep half of which together as one unit when you build.

payload.audio_text: We visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut.

expected: we visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut
we visited nine clinics two of which had already shut

feedback.why_key: Of and which are both unstressed and run together in speech, which is why they get heard as one blurred syllable and written as of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for two small words between the number and the verb.

items.decision_cue: several of them were never occupied

payload.sentence: The district built two thousand flats in a decade, several of them were never occupied.
payload.error_span: several of them were never occupied

expected: several of which were never occupied
several of which have never been occupied

feedback.why_key: The words after the comma make a whole sentence, and a comma is not strong enough to hold two of those together.
feedback.feed_forward: Change them to which and the comma becomes legal.

payload.context: Two sentences from different summaries of the same programme.
sentences: The programme funded thirty studies, few of which were ever completed.
The programme funded thirty studies, a few of which were ever completed.
meanings: Almost none of them finished, and the writer thinks that is the story.
A small number did finish, and the writer is pointing at those ones.

feedback.why_key: Few counts what is missing; a few counts what is there. One small word swaps disappointment for a modest success.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are counting the gap or the survivors.

payload.prompt_text: A research group applied for eleven grants and was turned down for eight of them. Write one sentence carrying both facts.

feedback.why_key: Two numbers about one group belong in one sentence, and this is the join that makes it possible without a semicolon.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the total first and hang the share on it with of which.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your chart description of renewable electricity. Find a place where you gave a total and then a share, and rewrite the two sentences as one. Ninety seconds.

feedback.why_key: Chart answers are full of totals followed by shares, which is why this one structure lifts the whole paragraph rather than one sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Scan your draft for a comma followed by a number and them.

title: Commenting on the whole thing you just said, without starting again

point_json.grammar_name: Sentential which: a relative clause commenting on a whole clause

teach.can_do: I can add a comment about what I have just said, and make sure my reader knows what the comment is about.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a sentence that comments on your own point and a sentence that says something about a bridge you never meant to mention.
teach.meaning: Which does not always point at the noun in front of it. It can reach back and take the whole event you have just described, so that the clause comments on what happened rather than on any single thing inside it. Your reader decides which by asking what could plausibly have done what the clause says. When both answers are plausible, the sentence has two meanings, and you will never find out which one your reader took away.

form.pattern: a complete clause , + which + verb ...
notes: the comment clause always comes last; it cannot be lifted into the middle of the sentence
the comma is compulsory, because without it which fastens straight onto the nearest noun
that is refused here, and so is what, however natural what may feel
form.negative: The comment goes negative like any clause: ..., which did not surprise anybody who works there.
form.question: Ask which noun could plausibly have done it. If two candidates could, name the one you mean.

ends: which lands on the nearest noun
which lands on the whole event

marks.label: the deadline, which had been extended twice
the memo, which the lawyers had advised against
the deadline, which surprised everybody

worked_example.sentence: The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota for October.
worked_example.why_this_form: A depot cannot leave anybody without a rota. Only the early closing can, so the reader carries which back over the whole event without noticing they did it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Had the clause said which had been rebuilt in 2019, nothing but the depot could fit, and the comment would have stopped dead at the noun.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
notice_set.question: What had been advertised?
notice_set.why: Only a job can be advertised, so the words after the comma can belong to nothing else in the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
notice_set.question: What did the office fail to understand?
notice_set.why: People fail to understand actions rather than job titles, so the comment reaches back over the whole thing he did.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
notice_set.question: What was cheaper to heat?
notice_set.why: Buildings are heated and moves are not, so there is only one candidate here.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
notice_set.question: What saved the four jobs?
notice_set.why: A building does not save jobs. The decision to move into it does, so the comment travels back over the whole event.

notice_set.sentence: The board approved the merger, which the unions had opposed for months.
notice_set.question: What had the unions been opposing?
notice_set.why: Both readings work here and nothing in the sentence chooses between them. That is the trap this whole point is about.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below ends differently. Work out what decides where the comment lands.
pairs: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
The depot closed six weeks early, which had been rebuilt in 2019.
The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota.

candidate_rules.text: What comes after the comma decides it: the comment lands on whatever could plausibly have done that.
The comment lands on the whole event whenever the clause is about how people reacted.
A comma in front of which always sends the comment back to the whole sentence.

teach.rule_line: Ask what could have done it. If two things could, name the one you mean.
teach.false_rule: That a comma in front of which always throws it back to the whole sentence. The comma only frees it; the verb decides where it lands.

contrast.question: Does the comment fit the nearest noun, or only the whole event?

fork.answer: It fits the nearest noun, and only that noun: leave it where it lands
fork.selects: a clause commenting on the noun

fork.answer: It only makes sense about the whole event: put it at the very end after a comma
fork.selects: a clause commenting on everything before it

fork.answer: Both work, so your reader cannot tell: replace which with a noun that names it
fork.selects: a summary noun such as a decision, a move, a refusal

a.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which had already been extended twice.
a.means: The deadline had been extended twice. The comment stops at the noun in front of it.

b.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which surprised everybody in the office.
b.means: Missing it is what surprised people. The comment reaches back over the whole event.

minimal_pair.only_difference: had already been extended twice / surprised everybody in the office

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You left which where it lands on the nearest noun. A reader takes it there first and only comes back if that reading collapses. If it does not collapse, they never come back, and they have read something you did not write.

edge_case.text: You will find a sentence-final which frowned on in a few style guides and used constantly by good writers. It is standard English. What is not standard is a which whose target the reader has to guess at.

contrast.stronger_test: Read only the words after the comma and ask what could have done that. If exactly one thing in your sentence could, you are safe. If two could, name it with a noun instead.

worked_pairs.a: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
worked_pairs.b: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved the trust four jobs.
worked_pairs.gloss: A building can be cheaper to heat; only a move can save jobs. The words after the comma say what was grabbed.

worked_pairs.a: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
worked_pairs.b: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
worked_pairs.gloss: The post was advertised. The refusal was the thing nobody could follow. Same eight opening words, two different targets.

worked_pairs.a: The paper printed the leaked memo, which ran to forty pages.
worked_pairs.b: The paper printed the leaked memo, a decision that cost the editor her job.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: a decision that cost the editor her job
worked_pairs.gloss: In the second sentence both readings were live, so the writer named the thing outright and the ambiguity vanished.

errors.wrong: The board approved the merger, which the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.right: The board approved the merger, a decision the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows perfectly well which idea they meant, so the sentence reads cleanly to them. The reader has two candidates, takes the nearer one, and nothing later in the sentence corrects them.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for a naming noun: which becomes a decision.

errors.wrong: Half the staff resigned in one week, what nobody had expected.
errors.right: Half the staff resigned in one week, which nobody had expected.
errors.why_it_happens: A great many languages use their question word for exactly this job, and what is the closest English match to it. English keeps what for a different job and will not lend it out.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes which.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Romance, Slavic and Germanic languages.

errors.wrong: They closed the ticket office which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.right: They closed the ticket office, which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.why_it_happens: Without the comma there is nothing to free which from the noun beside it, so the clause fastens onto the office and the reader is briefly told that an office meant something. The writer hears their own intended meaning and never sees the other one.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one comma in front of which.

pays_in.note: It comments on your own example without spending a whole new sentence.
pays_in.model: Fares rose twice in a single year, which pushed a good many regular passengers back into their cars.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers comment on what you have just said, and this is the join.
pays_in.model: A lot of people work from home now, which has emptied the town centre at lunchtime.

pays_in.note: Writers bury their own view in this clause, and questions go looking for it.
pays_in.model: The scheme was extended for a further decade, which few of its early critics had predicted.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt need a sentence that reports what happened and then says what the writer makes of it.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which had run since the 1970s.
payload.question: What had run since the 1970s?

feedback.why_key: A programme can run for fifty years. A single decision cannot, so the comment can only belong to the bulletin.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what could have done the thing the clause describes.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which upset a lot of older viewers.
payload.question: What upset the viewers?

feedback.why_key: The programme was the thing they liked, so it cannot be what upset them. Losing it is the only candidate left.
feedback.feed_forward: Test each candidate against the verb before you settle on one.

payload.context: From a first draft about a fare increase.
payload.sentence: Ticket sales fell sharply after the rise, what surprised nobody.
reasons: the wrong word is being used to point back at the whole event
the comma should not be there
the comment has been put in the wrong position
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: English gives this job to which and never lends it to what, however close the two feel in other languages.
feedback.feed_forward: Change what to which whenever it follows a comma.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a bridge closure.
payload.stem: The bridge stayed shut all winter, ___ cost the town a fortune in diversions.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: A bridge does not cost a town money in diversions; staying shut for a season does, so the comment takes the whole event.
feedback.feed_forward: Write which after the comma, never what and never that.

payload.given: The company moved its warehouse to Ashfield. That move added an hour to everybody's journey.
payload.instruction: Join these so the second fact is a comment on the move.
payload.starter: The company moved its warehouse to Ashfield, ___

expected: which added an hour to everybody's journey
which added an hour to everybodys journey
which added an hour to everyone's journey
which added an hour to everyones journey
a move which added an hour to everybody's journey
a move which added an hour to everybodys journey

feedback.why_key: A warehouse cannot add an hour to a journey. The relocating can, so the comment safely takes the whole event.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that no noun in the sentence could have done it.

payload.context: Build one sentence that ends with a comment on what the court did.

expected: the court released the figures late, which helped nobody

feedback.why_key: The comment can only sit at the end, after the sentence it is commenting on has finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the main sentence, then add the comma and the comment.

payload.audio_text: They've scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about.

expected: they've scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about
they have scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about
theyve scrapped the evening service which nobody was told about

feedback.why_key: In speech the comma is only a small dip in the voice, and which is unstressed, so the join is nearly inaudible until you know it is there.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a drop in the voice before an unstressed which.

items.decision_cue: the two firms should never combine

payload.context: The unions had said for months that the two firms should never combine.
payload.stem: The board approved the merger, ___ the unions had opposed from the start.

options.why_this_means: That the unions were against the merger itself, whoever approved it.
That the unions were against the board's approving of it, not against the merger.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Their objection was to the two firms joining, and the merger is sitting right there for which to land on.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave which bare when the nearest noun is what you mean.

items.decision_cue: wanted the vote held over until the pay talks ended

payload.context: The unions had accepted the merger but wanted the vote held over until the pay talks ended.
payload.stem: The board approved the merger, ___ the unions had opposed from the start.

options.why_this_means: That the unions were against the merger itself, whoever approved it.
That the unions were against the board's approving of it, not against the merger.

expected: a decision which

feedback.why_key: They were content with the merger and unhappy about the timing of the vote, so the objection has to be pinned to the decision by name.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the event with a noun when both readings are alive.

items.decision_cue: the crew often ran it empty

payload.context: Hardly anybody used the last train out of Marlow and the crew often ran it empty.
payload.stem: They scrapped the late train ___ was completely unnecessary.

options.why_this_means: That the train itself was unnecessary, so scrapping it was a sensible piece of housekeeping.
That scrapping it was the unnecessary act, whatever anybody thought of the train.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: An empty train every night is the thing nobody needed, so the comment belongs to the train and the comma would send it to the wrong place.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the comma out when the noun is what you are describing.

items.decision_cue: passengers are furious about losing it

payload.context: The last train out of Marlow was busy every Friday and passengers are furious about losing it.
payload.stem: They scrapped the late train ___ was completely unnecessary.

options.why_this_means: That the train itself was unnecessary, so scrapping it was a sensible piece of housekeeping.
That scrapping it was the unnecessary act, whatever anybody thought of the train.

expected: , which

feedback.why_key: A busy train is not the thing nobody needed. The comma frees the comment so it can land on the scrapping instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the comma when your complaint is about the action.

items.decision_cue: dropped its evening course after two years

payload.context: A note about a college that dropped its evening course after two years.
payload.stem: The college dropped the evening course, which ___

options.why_this_means: That the course was the thing that never filled, so the comment is about the course.

options.text: left forty students without a class
options.why_this_means: That dropping it is what stranded the students, so the comment is about the decision.

follow_up.question: Which ending comments on the college's decision rather than on the course?

feedback.why_key: Both endings are correct English and both are useful. They send the comment to different places, and the verb is what does the sending.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose your ending by deciding what you want to comment on.

items.decision_cue: which had broken down twice a month

payload.context: Two sentences from different reports on the same hospital.
sentences: The trust replaced the old scanner, which had broken down twice a month.
The trust replaced the old scanner, which took eleven months to arrange.
meanings: The reason it went is that it kept failing.
Arranging the replacement is what dragged on for the best part of a year.

feedback.why_key: A scanner can break down and a scanner cannot take eleven months to arrange, so each ending sends the comment to the only place it fits.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending first and work backwards to its owner.

items.decision_cue: which the lawyers had advised against

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a newspaper and a set of private letters.
payload.sentence: The editor published the letters, which the lawyers had advised against.
reasons: a reader cannot tell whether the lawyers were against the letters or against publishing them
the comma should not be there
the comment sits too far from what it describes
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Lawyers can advise against a document and against an act, so both readings survive and the sentence quietly holds two meanings.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace which with a naming noun whenever two readings survive.

payload.sentence: Half the shops on the high street have closed, what has left the council with no easy answer.

expected: which has left the council
a collapse which has left the council

feedback.why_key: Shops closing is the thing that has left the council stuck, and English hands that job to which alone.
feedback.feed_forward: Change what to which and check the comma is there.

payload.prompt_text: A local paper has started charging for its website. Write one sentence that reports this and then comments on what doing it has caused.

feedback.why_key: The comment has to be something a paper could not do and a decision could, or the reader will attach it to the wrong thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that no noun in your sentence could have done the commenting verb.

payload.prompt_text: In your paragraph on the privacy of public figures, find your strongest example and add one comment clause to it. Then check whether any noun in the sentence could have done what your comment says. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An example followed by your own comment on it is one of the few moves that answers a prompt and shows range in the same sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the comment, then reread it against every noun before it.

title: Shrinking a whole clause down to one word and hanging it on the subject

teach.can_do: I can cut a clause down to a single verb form and attach it to the subject of my sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shortest complex structure in written English and it carries one hidden condition. Get the condition wrong and the sentence says something absurd.
teach.meaning: A participle clause is a clause with the subject and the auxiliary taken out. Living beside the river is a whole clause that has been reduced to two words, and it works because the sentence supplies the missing subject from its own. That is the deal: the clause borrows a subject and the sentence lends it. The -ing shape means the subject is doing it; the -ed shape means the subject is having it done to them.

form.pattern: -ing / -ed clause , + subject + main verb ...    |    noun + -ing / -ed clause + main verb
notes: -ing when the borrowed subject does the action: families living beside the river
-ed when the borrowed subject receives it: samples collected in June
having + past participle when the first action clearly finished before the second: having lost the contract, the firm cut fifteen jobs
when the clause opens the sentence it takes a comma; when it sits behind a noun it takes none
form.negative: Not goes in front: not having heard from the council, the residents wrote again.
form.question: Ask who or what is doing the shortened verb. That answer has to be the subject of the sentence.

left.role: a clause with no subject of its own
left.text: Having finished the survey,

right.text: the team packed up and left.

spec.caption: The clause has no subject. It takes whichever one comes next, whether you meant it to or not.

worked_example.sentence: Built on flood plain, the estate has been under water twice since 2015.
worked_example.why_this_form: The estate is the thing that was built and the thing that floods, so one subject serves both halves and the sentence saves six words without losing anything.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Building on flood plain would hand the building to the estate itself, turning a housing scheme into a construction firm.

notice_set.sentence: Left unlocked overnight, the depot lost two vans.
notice_set.question: What was unlocked?
notice_set.why: The shortened opening borrows its subject from the sentence, and that subject is the depot.

notice_set.sentence: Living beside the river, the Norland families keep sandbags in the shed.
notice_set.question: Who lives beside the river?
notice_set.why: The opening has no subject of its own, so it takes the one that arrives after the comma.

notice_set.sentence: Delayed by the storm, the survey team lost two days of work.
notice_set.question: What was held up?
notice_set.why: The -ed shape means the borrowed subject is on the receiving end, and the storm is the thing doing the holding up.

notice_set.sentence: Having lost the contract, the firm cut fifteen jobs.
notice_set.question: Who lost the contract?
notice_set.why: Having borrows the subject exactly like the plain -ing shape does, and the subject here is the firm.

notice_set.sentence: The samples collected in June were the only usable ones.
notice_set.question: Who did the collecting?
options: somebody the sentence does not name
notice_set.why: The -ed shape puts the samples on the receiving end and leaves the collector out altogether.

teach.rule_line: Whoever is doing the shortened verb must be the subject of the sentence that follows.
teach.false_rule: That an -ing opening can be bolted onto any sentence to make it sound academic. It only fits a sentence whose subject is doing the -ing.

errors.wrong: Walking along the Verdon path, the smell from the mill was overpowering.
errors.right: Walking along the Verdon path, we found the smell from the mill overpowering.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows perfectly well who was walking, so the sentence reads correctly inside their own head. English hands the opening clause to whatever subject turns up next, and here that is a smell.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: the smell becomes we.

errors.wrong: Built in 1890, the council has never repaired the mill properly.
errors.right: Built in 1890, the mill has never been properly repaired.
errors.why_it_happens: The date belongs to the mill and the writer is thinking about the mill, but the sentence has put the council in the subject slot, so the council is what got built in 1890.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: the council becomes the mill.

errors.wrong: The figures publishing last week show a small rise in rainfall.
errors.right: The figures published last week show a small rise in rainfall.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing shape is the one learners meet first and it comes to stand for both directions. Nothing in it says who is acting, so the sentence sounds fine while claiming that figures publish themselves.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one ending: publishing becomes published.

errors.wrong: Having read the report twice. She still could not see the argument.
errors.right: Having read the report twice, she still could not see the argument.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening clause is long enough to feel like a sentence, and nothing inside it announces that it is unfinished. A full stop goes in and the borrowed subject never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one full stop into a comma.

pays_in.note: It attaches a date or a source to a figure in two words.
pays_in.model: Rainfall recorded at the Verdon gauge fell in every year after 2016.

pays_in.note: It packs a reason into the front of a sentence without a linker.
pays_in.model: Faced with a shrinking budget, most councils cut the services fewest people notice.

pays_in.note: Academic passages hide whole clauses in these, which makes them hard to unpack.
pays_in.model: Species introduced during the last century now outnumber those recorded in the original survey.

used_in.quote: The problem half of this answer is a list of things done to a river, which is exactly where the -ed shape earns its place.
The passage uses reduced clauses to attach dates and methods to its nouns, and a matching question turns on unpacking one.

payload.sentence: The trees planted along the embankment have all survived the winter.
payload.question: Who did the planting?
options: somebody the sentence does not name

feedback.why_key: The -ed shape puts the trees on the receiving end, and it says nothing at all about who held the spade.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the -ed shape as something done to the noun.

payload.sentence: Living on the top floor, we hear every one of those pipes.
payload.question: Who lives on the top floor?

feedback.why_key: Nothing in the opening says who did it, so the reader hands the job to whoever turns up first after the comma.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the comma to find who is doing the opening verb.

payload.context: From a first draft about water quality at Sandmouth.
payload.sentence: Swimming in the estuary, the bacteria levels are a real worry.
reasons: the sentence has the bacteria doing the swimming
the wrong verb ending has been used
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The opening borrows the next subject, and the next subject is bacteria levels, which is not what anyone meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the swimmer as the subject straight after the comma.

payload.context: From the methods paragraph of a survey write-up.
payload.stem: The readings ___ (take) before dawn were the steadiest of the week.

expected: taken

feedback.why_key: Readings do not take anything. Somebody takes them, so the shape has to be the one that puts the noun on the receiving end.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the noun acts or is acted on, then choose the ending.

payload.context: From a passage about a reserve at Norland.
payload.stem: Birds ___ (nest) on the shingle are disturbed by dogs every weekend.

expected: nesting

feedback.why_key: The birds are doing the nesting themselves, so the shape that shows the noun acting is the one that fits.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the -ing shape when the noun is the one doing it.

payload.given: The samples which were collected in June were the only usable ones.
payload.instruction: Cut the clause down to a single verb form.

expected: collected in june were the only usable ones
collected in June were the only usable ones

feedback.why_key: Which and were are carrying no meaning of their own here, so both can go and the sentence keeps everything it was saying.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the relative word and the auxiliary, and keep the ending.

payload.given: The council had already lost two appeals. It settled the third case out of court.
payload.instruction: Open the sentence with a shortened clause that shows the first event finished first.

expected: already lost two appeals, the council settled the third case out of court
lost two appeals already, the council settled the third case out of court
lost two appeals, the council settled the third case out of court

feedback.why_key: The council does both things, so it can lend its subject to the opening and keep it for the main clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that one subject can honestly do both verbs.

payload.context: Build one sentence that opens with the reason.

expected: faced with a smaller budget, the council cut two routes

feedback.why_key: The council is the thing facing the budget and the thing cutting the routes, which is what allows the opening to have no subject of its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the borrowing subject immediately after the comma.

payload.audio_text: The land drained in the 1950s is flooding again every winter.

expected: the land drained in the 1950s is flooding again every winter

feedback.why_key: Two endings in one short sentence point in opposite directions, and the -ed one is unstressed and easy to write straight past.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the ending on the word right after the noun.

items.decision_cue: the queue was already round the block

payload.sentence: Arriving at nine in the morning, the queue was already round the block.
payload.error_span: the queue was already round the block

expected: we found the queue already round the block
we found that the queue was already round the block
visitors found the queue already round the block

feedback.why_key: As written, the queue is the thing that arrived at nine. Naming the people who arrived fixes it without touching the opening.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the person who did the opening verb straight after the comma.

payload.context: From the opening of a research summary.
payload.sentence: Measured over ten years, the decline is smaller than the headline figures suggest.
reasons: the decline cannot be measured
the wrong verb ending has been used
the comma should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A decline is exactly the sort of thing that gets measured, so the borrowed subject fits and the sentence holds together.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the opening when the next subject can really receive that verb.

parts: The reserve was drained for farmland in the 1950s.
It is being deliberately flooded again.
Wading birds have returned to it within four years.
model_combinations: Drained for farmland in the 1950s and now deliberately flooded again, the reserve has drawn wading birds back within four years.
The reserve, drained for farmland in the 1950s, is being flooded again, and wading birds have returned within four years.
Having been drained for farmland in the 1950s, the reserve is now being flooded again, with wading birds back within four years.

feedback.why_key: All three facts are about one place, so one subject can carry every verb and the three sentences collapse into one.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the shared subject first, then hang the shortened clauses on it.

payload.prompt_text: A town has lost most of its shops to an out-of-town retail park. Write one sentence that opens with a shortened clause giving the reason.

feedback.why_key: The reason and the result share a subject here, which is the only condition under which the opening is safe.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the opening aloud and check who is doing it.

payload.prompt_text: Open your river pollution paragraph. Find two short sentences about the same thing and fold one into the other as a shortened clause. Then check who the opening belongs to. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is where the structure earns its keep and where it goes wrong: under time pressure the borrowed subject is the first thing to slip.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread your opening against the subject that follows it.

title: Putting a question inside a sentence without it behaving like a question

point_json.grammar_name: Embedded questions and other noun clauses

teach.can_do: I can drop a question into the middle of a sentence and keep the word order straight.
teach.why_it_matters: It is one of the most visible errors a listener notices, it happens in almost every polite request, and the repair is a single move.
teach.meaning: A clause can do the job of a noun. Instead of naming a thing, it names a piece of information: where the office is, whether the funding will continue, what the council intends. When a question goes into that slot it stops being a question and becomes a thing your sentence is talking about, so it loses the swapped word order that questions carry. The question word stays. The swap goes.

form.pattern: verb / adjective + question word or whether + subject + verb ...
notes: no swapping: where the office is, not where is the office
no do, does or did inside the clause: how much it cost, not how much did it cost
when there is no question word, use whether or if: I am not sure whether it is worth it
the clause can also be the subject of the sentence: what the council intends is anybody's guess
form.negative: The negative sits on the outer sentence or inside the clause, not on both: I do not know why they left.
form.question: Ask what the sentence is about. If the answer is a piece of information, that information is behaving like a noun.

left.text: Where is the ticket office?

right.role: the same question sitting inside a sentence
right.text: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?

spec.caption: Once the question is inside another sentence, it stops behaving like a question.

worked_example.sentence: Nobody can tell me how long the repairs will take.
worked_example.why_this_form: The question has become the thing the sentence is about, so it sits where a noun would sit and takes ordinary subject-before-verb order.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: How long will the repairs take is a question being asked out loud. Inside this sentence it leaves the reader waiting for a question mark that never comes.

notice_set.sentence: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for directions?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is a request, even though the part about the office has stopped looking like a question.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me whether the office was open on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Did she already know the answer?
notice_set.why: Asking is what you do when the information is missing, and whether marks the gap as a yes-or-no one.

notice_set.sentence: I can't remember how much the repairs cost.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know the figure?
notice_set.why: The missing piece of information is the amount, and the sentence is a statement about not having it.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody has explained why the meeting was moved.
notice_set.question: Was the meeting moved?
notice_set.why: The clause takes the move for granted. What is missing is only the reason for it.

notice_set.sentence: It is not clear whether the funding will continue.
notice_set.question: Has a decision been announced?
notice_set.why: Whether marks an open question, so nothing has been settled either way.

teach.rule_line: Once a question sits inside a sentence, put the subject before the verb.
teach.false_rule: That a question word always brings question order along with it. The question word stays; the swapped order is left behind.

errors.wrong: Could you tell me where is the ticket office?
errors.right: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is asking a question, so the question shape fires automatically. The shape belongs to the outer sentence, which already has it, and the inner clause never needed it.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: is goes to the end.

errors.wrong: Nobody knows how much did it cost.
errors.right: Nobody knows how much it cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Did is stored as part of the question, not as a signal of question order, so it travels inside with the question word and nothing flags it as redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: did.

errors.wrong: She asked me if would I be free on Thursday.
errors.right: She asked me if I would be free on Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: If already feels like the start of a question, so the swap comes with it. The learner is repeating the shape of the original question rather than reporting its content.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: would goes after I.

errors.wrong: I explained her where the office was.
errors.right: I explained to her where the office was.
errors.why_it_happens: Explain looks like tell and behaves like say, and nothing about its meaning warns the learner that it refuses a person straight after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

pays_in.note: Hedged answers about your own life are built out of these clauses.
pays_in.model: I'm not really sure why my parents chose that school, to be honest.

pays_in.note: It states a question the essay will answer without asking one.
pays_in.model: What is less clear is whether stricter rules would change anybody's behaviour.

pays_in.note: Requests and enquiries in a booking dialogue are almost all of this shape.
pays_in.model: Could you let me know whether the afternoon session still has places?

used_in.quote: Answers on this card keep reaching for it is hard to say whether and nobody really knows why.

payload.sentence: Do you know whether the library takes cards?
payload.question: Is the speaker asking a question?

feedback.why_key: The outer sentence is the question. The part about cards has become a piece of information the speaker is short of.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the outer sentence to see who is asking what.

payload.sentence: The report does not say how many staff were consulted.
payload.question: Were any staff consulted?

feedback.why_key: What is missing is the number. Whether anyone at all was asked is left entirely open by the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the clause for what is missing, not for what is claimed.

items.decision_cue: when does the last bus leave

payload.context: At the enquiry desk in Sandmouth.
payload.sentence: Could you tell me when does the last bus leave?
reasons: the inner clause has kept the shape of a question
the wrong question word has been chosen
the outer sentence is not a question at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Could you tell me is already doing the asking, so the second half only has to deliver the information in ordinary order.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete does and put the subject in front of the verb.

payload.context: Ask somebody at the station.

expected: do you know where the night bus stops

feedback.why_key: The swap happens once, at the front, in do you know. Everything after where runs in plain order.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap the outer sentence only, never the inner one.

payload.context: Build the last line of a formal letter.

expected: i should be grateful if you could confirm whether the post is still open

feedback.why_key: Whether opens a yes-or-no gap, and the clause after it runs in the same plain order as any statement.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow whether with a subject, then a verb.

payload.given: How much does the evening course cost?
payload.instruction: Turn this into a polite request inside one sentence.

expected: how much the evening course costs
how much the evening course costs?

feedback.why_key: Does disappears and its ending moves back onto the main verb, which is exactly what happens whenever a question goes inside.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the auxiliary and put its ending back on the verb.

payload.given: Will the landlord replace the boiler?
payload.instruction: Say that you have no information about this.

expected: whether the landlord will replace the boiler
if the landlord will replace the boiler

feedback.why_key: There is no question word here, so whether or if has to open the gap, and the subject then comes before the verb as usual.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for whether when the missing answer is yes or no.

payload.audio_text: I'm not sure where they've put the spare keys.

expected: i'm not sure where they've put the spare keys
i am not sure where they have put the spare keys
im not sure where theyve put the spare keys

feedback.why_key: The subject and its squashed auxiliary come straight after where, and that order is the whole difference between a statement and a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the subject arriving directly after the question word.

items.decision_cue: why do so many new teachers leave

payload.sentence: The study does not explain why do so many new teachers leave within five years.
payload.error_span: why do so many new teachers leave

expected: why so many new teachers leave

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a statement about a gap in the study, so nothing inside it needs the shape of a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the auxiliary whenever the clause is reporting, not asking.

payload.context: From a draft about newspapers and their audiences.
payload.sentence: The editorial explained readers why the paper had changed its position.
reasons: explain will not take a person immediately after it
the question inside has kept its swapped order
the wrong question word has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The clause after why is built correctly. The trouble is one word earlier, where explain needs to before the person.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert to before the person after explain, describe and suggest.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody has asked you whether people will still write letters in twenty years. Answer in one sentence that admits you do not know.

feedback.why_key: Admitting uncertainty is a real answer, and this clause is what lets you do it without sounding as though you have nothing to say.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with it is hard to say, then keep plain order.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 3 card about advice and experts. Give a forty-second answer that uses two of these clauses to hedge, and keep the order plain in both. Record it and listen back for a stray auxiliary.

feedback.why_key: Under speaking pressure the question shape comes back first, because it is the older and stronger habit. Hearing it in your own recording is what breaks it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and mark every place an auxiliary slipped in.

title: Splitting a sentence in two so one part cannot be missed

point_json.grammar_name: Cleft sentences: it is X that ... and what ... is

teach.can_do: I can split a sentence so that the part I care about cannot be read past.
teach.why_it_matters: English has almost no way of underlining a word in speech or in an essay. This structure is the way, and it does the job of a raised voice.
teach.meaning: A cleft takes one ordinary sentence and breaks it into two pieces so that one piece stands alone in the light and the rest is pushed into a clause behind it. Nothing new is being said. What changes is which part your reader treats as the news and which part they treat as already agreed. That makes it the tool for correcting an assumption, for setting two things against each other, and for holding the important word back until the end.

form.pattern: It + is / was + the part you want heard + that / who + the rest    |    What + clause + is / was + the part you want heard
notes: the it shape puts the spotlight early: it is the running costs that worry people
the what shape holds it back to the end: what worries people is the running costs
that works for people and things in the it shape; who is available for people
the verb after that agrees with the spotlit part, not with the it at the front
form.negative: The negative usually sits in the spotlight itself: it is not the rent that people object to.
form.question: Ask which single part of your sentence your reader might otherwise skim past. That part goes in the light.

left.text: The timing worries people.

right.role: one part moved into the light
right.text: It is the timing that worries people.

spec.caption: Nothing new has been said. One piece has been moved into the light and everything else into the shade.

worked_example.sentence: It is the running costs, not the building work, that will decide whether the scheme survives.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reader arrives expecting an argument about construction, so the sentence has to put the running costs where they cannot be skimmed and shove everything else back.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The running costs will decide whether the scheme survives reports the same fact and quietly lets the reader go on assuming the building work matters too.

notice_set.sentence: It was the noise that made them move, not the rent.
notice_set.question: Why did they move?
notice_set.why: The noise has been put in the light and the rent has been ruled out by name.

notice_set.sentence: What the council has not explained is where the money went.
notice_set.question: Has the council explained where the money went?
notice_set.why: The gap is held back to the very end, which is what makes it land.

notice_set.sentence: It was in March that the depot closed.
notice_set.question: What is the speaker putting right?
notice_set.why: March is standing in the light, so the date is the part the speaker thinks somebody has wrong.

notice_set.sentence: What surprised everybody was how quickly the shops emptied.
notice_set.question: Were people expecting the shops to empty that fast?
notice_set.why: Surprise means the speed was not expected, and the speed is the part held back until last.

notice_set.sentence: It is small firms that carry most of the cost.
notice_set.question: Who carries most of the cost?
notice_set.why: Small firms have been lifted out and put in front, which is where a reader looks first.

teach.rule_line: Use it when one part has to be corrected, set against something, or held back.
teach.false_rule: That this structure makes writing sound advanced. It sounds argumentative, and where nothing is in dispute it simply reads as odd.

errors.wrong: It is the timing what worries people, not the cost.
errors.right: It is the timing that worries people, not the cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages use their question word to open this second half, and what is the closest English match, so the writer's ear raises no objection at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes that.
errors.l1_note: Frequent where the learner's first language uses its question word here.

errors.wrong: It is the delays that worries commuters most.
errors.right: It is the delays that worry commuters most.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb has to agree with the spotlit part, but the writer's ear is still holding the singular it is from three words earlier, and that is what the ending copies.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on worries.

errors.wrong: What most people object to. The way the charge was brought in.
errors.right: What most people object to is the way the charge was brought in.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening feels heavy enough to stand alone and the second part feels like the answer to it, so a full stop goes between them and the sentence never gets a main verb at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one full stop into the word is.

errors.wrong: It is my brother who taught me to cook.
errors.right: My brother taught me to cook.
errors.why_it_happens: The frame has been learned as a way of sounding impressive rather than as a way of singling one thing out against a rival. With nothing in dispute it adds four words and makes an ordinary sentence sound like a correction of somebody.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: It is ... who.

pays_in.note: It corrects an assumption the prompt has planted in the reader's head.
pays_in.model: It is the shortage of small flats, not the price of large ones, that keeps young people at home.

pays_in.note: It marks which half of a long answer you actually want heard.
pays_in.model: What really changed things was the new bus route, not the car park.

pays_in.note: A writer's real claim often sits in the clause after that.
pays_in.model: It was the delay in publishing the figures that provoked most of the complaints.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt rest on saying which factor really does the work, which is what this structure is for.

payload.sentence: It is the smallest firms that lose most when a payment is late.
payload.question: Who is worst affected?

feedback.why_key: The smallest firms have been lifted to the front and stood in the light, which is where the reader's eye goes first.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the part before that as the writer's real claim.

payload.sentence: What puts people off is the deposit, not the monthly rent.
payload.question: Which of the two is the bigger obstacle?

feedback.why_key: The deposit is held back to the end and the rent is ruled out by name, so the sentence is choosing between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Wait for the end of a what sentence before deciding.

payload.context: From a paragraph about town centre shops.
payload.sentence: It is the empty units what people notice first when they walk down the street.
reasons: the second half has been opened with the wrong word
the verb does not agree with the units
a comma belongs in front of the second half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half of this structure opens with that or who. What has its own job elsewhere and English will not lend it out here.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the second half with that after it is.

payload.context: From a paragraph about household budgets.
payload.stem: It is the fixed bills that ___ (make) a small income impossible to plan around.

expected: make

feedback.why_key: The verb agrees with the fixed bills, which is the part in the light, and not with the it at the front of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the spotlit part, not to it is.

payload.given: Late payment closes small firms. Your reader assumes it is low demand.
payload.instruction: Put late payment where it cannot be missed.

expected: late payment that closes small firms
late payment, not low demand, that closes small firms

feedback.why_key: The reader has arrived with the wrong culprit in mind, and the only way to shift it is to stand the right one in front of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the corrected part straight after it is.

payload.given: Councils cannot find enough builders. That is the real obstacle to new housing.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that holds the obstacle back until the end.

expected: holds up new housing is the shortage of builders
stops councils building is the shortage of builders
councils cannot find is enough builders

feedback.why_key: Holding the answer back keeps the reader with you to the last word, which is the whole advantage of the what shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the two halves with is, never with a full stop.

payload.context: Build a sentence that keeps the answer until the end.

expected: what worries shoppers is the price of basics

feedback.why_key: Is is the hinge between the two halves, and without it the sentence is two pieces lying side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Place is between the two halves before anything else.

payload.audio_text: It's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent.

expected: it's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
it is the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
its the deposit that stops most people not the rent

feedback.why_key: Both hinges are unstressed in speech, so the whole frame can vanish and leave the listener with a list of two nouns.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small unstressed that in the middle.

payload.sentence: It is the entry costs that keeps them out of the market altogether.

expected: that keep them out

feedback.why_key: Costs is the part in the light and the verb belongs to it, however far away the singular it is now looks.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the spotlit noun, not to it.

items.decision_cue: It was my sister who suggested

payload.context: The examiner has simply asked how the candidate chose their job. Nobody has disagreed with anything.
payload.sentence: It was my sister who suggested it, and it was the hours that appealed to me.
reasons: the second half opens with the wrong word
the verb does not agree
it is correct, but nothing is in dispute, so the sentence sounds like an argument
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The structure exists to correct somebody, and there is nobody to correct, so the answer sounds defensive.
feedback.feed_forward: Save this structure for a point somebody might dispute.

payload.prompt_text: Most people blame online shopping for empty high streets. You think business rates matter more. Write one sentence that puts the reader right.

feedback.why_key: A correction is exactly the situation this structure was built for, and a plain sentence would let the reader keep their original culprit.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing you are ruling out as well as the one you are choosing.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on very high salaries. Find the one sentence where you disagree with the other side and rewrite it as a split sentence. Use it once in the paragraph and no more. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in a paragraph marks your real claim. Two of them cancel each other out, because everything cannot be the important part.
feedback.feed_forward: Use it once, at the point of disagreement, then stop.

title: Telling someone what another person said, in your own words

teach.can_do: I can tell someone what another person said, in my own words, without quoting them.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost every story you tell carries somebody else's words. Anchor them wrongly and your listener cannot work out who did what to whom.
teach.meaning: When you report what somebody said, you stop standing where they were standing and start standing where you are. Three things in their sentence were anchored to them: the person words, the time words and the place words. All three are re-anchored to you. The verb often steps back as well, because you are reporting from a later moment. None of this is decoration. Each shift tells your listener whose sentence they are currently inside.

form.pattern: reporting verb + (that) + a clause with ordinary statement word order
notes: that can be dropped in speech and in a friendly message; keep it in an essay
tell needs a listener straight after it (told me); say never takes one without to
the verb usually steps one place further back, and the person, time and place words move with it
here becomes there, tomorrow becomes the next day, this becomes that
form.negative: She said she had not seen the notice on the door.
form.question: Did she say the depot was closing, or did she only say it might?

left.role: what they said, anchored to where they were standing
left.text: "I am moving to Sandmouth in the spring."

right.role: what you say, anchored to where you are standing
right.text: She said she was moving to Sandmouth in the spring.

spec.caption: Nothing has been added and nothing has been lost. Everything that pointed at her now points from you.

worked_example.sentence: The site manager told us the scaffolding was coming down that week.
worked_example.why_this_form: Told takes a listener straight after it, and was coming steps back from is coming because you are passing this on from outside her week.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Keeping is coming and this week would put you back inside her week, as if you were relaying the message the same afternoon.

notice_set.sentence: The receptionist said the lift was out of order.
notice_set.question: Are these the receptionist's exact words?
options: No, her meaning in someone else's words
notice_set.why: There are no quotation marks and the pronouns have moved, so this is a report rather than a recording.

notice_set.sentence: Mina told her tutor she had finished the second reading.
notice_set.question: Which happened first, the reading or the telling?
notice_set.why: Had finished puts the reading behind the telling, which is the only job that form is doing here.

notice_set.sentence: Ravi said he was working in Sandmouth at the time.
notice_set.question: Is Ravi necessarily working in Sandmouth now?
options: No, the sentence only covers the stretch he spoke about
No, it says he has left
notice_set.why: The report is anchored to the moment he spoke, so it makes no claim at all about today.

notice_set.sentence: She said she would send the file the following day.
notice_set.question: The following day is counted from when?
options: from the day the file was needed
notice_set.why: Time words inside a report are measured from the reported moment, which is why tomorrow could not stay.

notice_set.sentence: Anya said she had been living there for a year.
notice_set.question: Had she moved out by the time she spoke?
notice_set.why: The year runs up to the moment she spoke, so she was still there when she said it.

notice_set.sentence: The email said the deadline had moved to the Friday.
notice_set.question: Is the Friday necessarily this week's Friday?
options: No, it is the Friday in the reported situation
notice_set.why: The article the points back into the reported week, not out into the reader's calendar.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing twice. Work out everything that changes on the way from left to right.
pairs: "I am waiting outside."
He said he was waiting outside.
"We finished the survey yesterday."
They said they had finished the survey the day before.
"I will bring the forms here tomorrow."
She said she would bring the forms there the next day.

candidate_rules.text: Everything anchored to the original speaker — the person, the time, the place — is re-anchored to whoever is reporting.
The verb moves one step further into the past.
If the sentence contains said, every verb after it must be in a past form.

teach.rule_line: Re-anchor the report to where you are standing: the person, the time, the place.
teach.false_rule: That reporting is a fixed list of swaps you apply without reading. The swaps follow the meaning, and when the anchor has not moved, nothing moves.

errors.wrong: The tutor said me that the deadline had moved.
errors.right: The tutor told me that the deadline had moved.
errors.why_it_happens: Say and tell come out as one verb in many languages, so the learner takes whichever surfaces first and hangs the listener on it. Say will not carry a listener unless to is there.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: said becomes told.

errors.wrong: Ravi said that I had already paid the deposit, so I stopped worrying.
errors.right: Ravi said that he had already paid the deposit, so I stopped worrying.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner keeps the pronoun the original speaker used. Inside the report, I now points at the reporter, and the sentence quietly hands the deposit to the wrong person.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: I becomes he.

errors.wrong: She told us she will look at the figures on Monday, but Monday came and went.
errors.right: She told us she would look at the figures on Monday, but Monday came and went.
errors.why_it_happens: The words come across from her mouth unchanged. It passes in speech and reads as a jolt on the page, because the sentence around it has already moved into the past.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: will becomes would.

errors.wrong: She explained that the office was short-staffed and the phones ring all morning.
errors.right: She explained that the office was short-staffed and the phones rang all morning.
errors.why_it_happens: The first verb gets re-anchored and the second is forgotten. The report starts in one time frame and finishes in another, and the reader is left to guess which was meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: ring becomes rang.

pays_in.note: Half of a two-minute talk about a person is what that person said.
pays_in.model: She told me the course was harder than she had expected, and she turned out to be right.

pays_in.note: It is how a second voice gets into an essay at all.
pays_in.model: Supporters of the scheme said it would pay for itself within a decade.

pays_in.note: Two students relaying a tutor's words is a standard section-three shape.
pays_in.model: He said the reading list had been shortened to four titles.

used_in.quote: Answers on this card are almost entirely about what other people say and how it lands, which is this point running for two minutes.
The prompt is about what gets passed on and how, so the essay reports claims in almost every body sentence.

payload.sentence: Kemi told me she had left the parcel with the neighbours.
payload.question: Who left the parcel?

feedback.why_key: She points back at Kemi, because inside a report every pronoun is measured from the person doing the reporting.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace each pronoun back to a name before you read on.

payload.sentence: The department said the fee had been waived for the second year.
payload.question: Where does the waiving sit?
options: at the moment the department spoke

feedback.why_key: Had been waived is the report's way of saying this was already done when the sentence was spoken.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the reported event against the moment of speaking, not against today.

payload.context: A new starter is telling a friend how the first shift went.
payload.sentence: The supervisor said me the rota was going up on Thursday.
reasons: say cannot take a listener without to
the rota is not going up on Thursday
the verb form of going is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Tell hands the words to a named listener; say only reports them. Said me tries to make one verb do the other's job.
feedback.feed_forward: If a listener is named, use told.

payload.context: Reporting a conversation that finished last week. Original: "I will confirm the room on Monday."
payload.stem: The office said they ___ (confirm) the room on Monday.

expected: would confirm
'd confirm
d confirm

feedback.why_key: Will belongs to the moment they spoke. From where you are standing that moment is behind you, so will steps back to would.
feedback.feed_forward: Step will back to would when the speaking is over.

payload.context: Two passengers on the platform. Original: "The Ashfield train has already left."
payload.stem: The guard told us the Ashfield train ___ (already leave).

expected: had already left
'd already left
d already left

feedback.why_key: The leaving was finished before he spoke, and the report keeps that order visible by putting the verb one place further back.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the earlier of two past events one step further back.

payload.given: Dev said: "I am training two new drivers here this month."
payload.instruction: Report what Dev said. You are writing about it later, somewhere else.

expected: he was training two new drivers there that month
that he was training two new drivers there that month

feedback.why_key: Three anchors move together: the person, the place and the month. Leave one behind and the sentence points in two directions at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the person, the place and the time in one pass.

payload.given: The letting agent to me: "Your deposit has gone back to your bank."
payload.instruction: Report it to a friend, naming yourself as the listener.

expected: me my deposit had gone back to my bank
me that my deposit had gone back to my bank

feedback.why_key: Told takes the listener bare and straight away, and your becomes my because the deposit is now being described from your side.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the listener immediately after told, with no to.

payload.context: Original: "The recording has been cut for time." Build the report.

expected: the presenter said the recording had been cut for time
