feedback.why_key: Has steps back to had and nothing else in the clause moves, because statement word order was already there.
feedback.feed_forward: Change only the auxiliary; leave the word order alone.

payload.audio_text: She said she'd sent the photos to the group already.

expected: she said she'd sent the photos to the group already
she said she had sent the photos to the group already
she said shed sent the photos to the group already

feedback.why_key: The whole report hangs on one unstressed syllable. She'd sent and she sent are a week apart in meaning and almost nothing apart in sound.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the 'd before the main verb, not for the main verb.

payload.sentence: The editor said that I had already approved the caption, so I stopped chasing it.

expected: she had already approved
he had already approved
they had already approved

feedback.why_key: Two people cannot both be I in one sentence. The approving belongs to the editor, so the pronoun has to point back at her.
feedback.feed_forward: Change every I inside the report to the reported speaker.

items.decision_cue: and the vans arrive before seven

payload.context: Someone is describing a conversation that happened last winter.
payload.sentence: The depot manager said the yard was too small and the vans arrive before seven.
reasons: the second half of the report was never re-anchored
the yard is not too small
the vans do not arrive before seven
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The report starts last winter and ends this morning. A listener has to pick one and cannot tell which was meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Re-anchor every clause in the report, not just the first.

payload.context: Two sentences from different paragraphs of the same report on an admissions scheme.
sentences: The registrar said that fewer students had applied.
The registrar said that fewer students were applying.
meanings: The applications were counted and the count was already in before she spoke.
The falling off was going on around her as she spoke, with no total yet.

feedback.why_key: One report hands you a finished number; the other hands you a trend still running at the moment of speaking.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the reported event was finished or still running.

payload.prompt_text: A local reporter interviewed you last month about how you get your news. Write one sentence reporting something you told her, from where you are standing today.

feedback.why_key: You are now the person being reported, so every anchor in your own sentence has to move across to the reporter's side.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the pronouns last; they are the ones that slip.

payload.prompt_text: Take one body paragraph from your last Task 2 answer on this prompt and add two sentences reporting what somebody on the other side of the argument said. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: A paragraph that reports nobody is a paragraph with one voice in it, and one voice is the hardest thing to argue with or from.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the two new sentences alone and check every anchor.

title: Deciding whether to move a reported verb back, instead of doing it automatically

teach.can_do: I can decide whether a reported verb should step back, instead of stepping it back every time.
teach.why_it_matters: The step back is a claim about whether the thing is still true. Applied automatically it puts live facts quietly into the past.
teach.meaning: Moving the verb back is not a tax you pay for having written said. It is a small piece of distancing, and your reader feels it. The step back says: I am reporting this from outside the moment it was spoken, and I am not standing behind it as I write. Leaving the verb where it is says the opposite — the situation has not moved, and this is a statement that is still live. English offers you both, and whichever you take, the reader takes something from it.

form.pattern: said / told + (that) + [verb stepped back]  OR  said / told + (that) + [verb left alone]
notes: after a present-tense reporting verb — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all
a past reporting verb makes the step available, never compulsory
will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might; must and should do not move
an event that finished before the speaking still steps back, because the order has to stay visible
form.negative: He said he did not think the figures were reliable. / He said he does not think the figures are reliable.
form.question: Before you write said, ask: is this still true as I write?

ends: still true as I write, and I will say so
sealed inside the moment it was spoken

marks.label: She said the fee is forty pounds — I am passing on a live fact
She said the fee was forty pounds — I take no position on today
She said the fee was forty pounds, though it has gone up since

worked_example.sentence: The tutor said the library opens at eight, so there is no rush.
worked_example.why_this_form: The opening time has not changed between her saying it and you passing it on, and the second half of your sentence is leaning on that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opened would seal the hours inside her sentence, and a reader would wonder whether they had since changed — which the rest of your sentence denies.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
notice_set.question: What has the person reporting committed themselves to?
options: that the water is safe as they write
that the water was safe only when Kemi spoke
notice_set.why: Leaving the verb alone hands the claim on as live, and the reporter has signed it on the way past.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
notice_set.question: Does this version say the water is unsafe today?
options: No, it simply declines to say
notice_set.why: The step back is a refusal to take a position, not a denial. It hands you Kemi's words and stops.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift was out of order, but it seems fine to me.
notice_set.question: Why does the second half sit comfortably here?
options: because the report was sealed at the moment he spoke
notice_set.why: The step back left room for an update, and the second clause walks straight into it.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift is out of order, so take the stairs.
notice_set.question: Is the lift broken as the speaker says this?
notice_set.why: The verb was left alone, so the report is a live instruction rather than a piece of history.

notice_set.sentence: The survey found that older houses lose more heat through the roof than through the walls.
notice_set.question: Is this claim tied to the moment of the survey?
options: No, it is offered as generally true
notice_set.why: Nothing about the claim has an end date, so there is nothing for the step back to mark.

notice_set.sentence: She said she was living in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Is she living in Marlow now?
notice_set.why: The stepped-back verb covers the moment she spoke and makes no offer about anything later.

discovery.prompt: Each pair reports exactly the same words. Work out what the right-hand version is refusing to claim.
pairs: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
The porter said the lift is out of order.
The porter said the lift was out of order.
The letter said the deposit is refundable.
The letter said the deposit was refundable.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand version keeps the claim live as the writer writes; the right-hand version seals it inside the moment it was spoken.
The left-hand version is for facts and the right-hand version is for opinions.
A past reporting verb such as said forces every verb after it into a past form.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether it is still true as you write. If it is, you may leave the verb alone.
teach.false_rule: That said pushes every following verb one step back. It offers the step; it does not demand it, and taking it always tells your reader something.

contrast.question: Is what they said still true as I write this?

fork.answer: Still true, and I am content to stand behind it: leave the verb where it is
Over, changed, or not something I want to vouch for: step the verb back

a.text: The agent said the flat is available from the first of the month.
a.means: It is available as I write. I am passing on a fact I expect to hold.

b.text: The agent said the flat was available from the first of the month.
b.means: That is what he told me at the time. Whether it has since gone, I am not saying.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote was. A reader takes that as a deliberate step back: you are reporting what the agent said then and declining to say whether it holds now. If you meant the flat is there today, was has quietly withdrawn the only useful part of your sentence.

edge_case.text: After a reporting verb in the present — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all, because there is no distance to mark and no choice to make. That is the single context where the question does not arise. Everything else you have read about compulsory shifts, leave it there.

contrast.stronger_test: Read the reported clause aloud on its own, as a statement of your own. If you would say it that way today, leave the verb alone. If saying it that way would make you a liar, step it back.

worked_pairs.a: The council said the footbridge is closed until the spring.
worked_pairs.b: The council said the footbridge was closed for most of last winter.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first closure is still running as you write. The second finished before you started, so there is nothing live left to keep.

worked_pairs.a: The letter said the deposit is refundable, so I have not paid the extra.
worked_pairs.b: The letter said the deposit was refundable, though the terms changed in April.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so I have not paid the extra
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: though the terms changed in April
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first you are acting on the claim today, so you keep it live. In the second you already know it has expired.

worked_pairs.a: Dr Anand argues that rural bus funding is the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.b: Dr Anand argued that rural bus funding was the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.gloss: A present reporting verb leaves nothing to decide. Once the reporting verb itself goes back, the choice opens and you have to make it on purpose.

errors.wrong: My landlord said the boiler was fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.right: My landlord said the boiler is fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that said pushes the next verb back, and applies it without reading on. The step back then withdraws the very claim the second half of the sentence is relying on.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: was becomes is.

errors.wrong: A guest on the programme said vaccines cause more harm than good.
errors.right: A guest on the programme said vaccines caused more harm than good.
errors.why_it_happens: Learners are told the unshifted form is for general truths and apply it to anything phrased like one. Leaving the verb alone reads as the writer signing a claim they never meant to sign.

title: Reporting a question without turning it back into a question

teach.can_do: I can report a question without turning it back into a question.
teach.why_it_matters: The word order slips back under pressure and it is the most audible error in this whole area. A listener hears it every single time.
teach.meaning: A reported question is not a question. Nobody in the room is being asked anything: you are telling someone what was once asked, and the sentence you produce is an ordinary statement. That is the whole idea, and every difference follows from it. The subject goes back in front of the verb where it lives in statements. The do, does or did that was holding the question together disappears, because the tense goes back onto the main verb. And the sentence ends with a full stop.

form.pattern: asked (+ person) + wh-word / if / whether + SUBJECT + VERB
notes: no do, does or did: where did she go becomes where she had gone
yes-no questions need if or whether, because there is no wh-word to hold the slot open
the sentence ends with a full stop, never a question mark
asked takes a person straight after it; wanted to know does not take one at all
form.negative: He asked why we had not signed the form.
form.question: The report is never a question. Turn it round to check: where does the bus leave from becomes he asked where the bus left from.

left.role: a question: the verb jumps in front of the subject
left.text: Where is the depot?

right.role: reported: the subject goes back in front
right.text: She asked where the depot was.

spec.caption: One move, and it is always the same move. The subject climbs back in front of the verb.

worked_example.sentence: The receptionist asked whether we had booked a slot.
worked_example.why_this_form: There was no wh-word in the original, so whether holds the slot open, and we sits in front of had exactly as it would in any statement.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Asked had we booked a slot sounds as though she is asking you now, in the middle of your own sentence, and the reader has to stop and start again.

notice_set.sentence: Ravi asked where the forms were kept.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking you a question?
options: No, they are telling you what Ravi asked
notice_set.why: The sentence is a statement about a question. Nobody in the conversation is being asked anything.

notice_set.sentence: She asked if I had finished the second draft.
notice_set.question: Was the original a yes-no question?
options: No, it started with a wh-word
notice_set.why: If is only ever there because there was no wh-word to hold the place open.

notice_set.sentence: He wanted to know how much the repair would cost.
notice_set.question: Who wants the information?
notice_set.why: Wanted to know is a reporting phrase like asked, and the person doing the wanting is the one who asked.

notice_set.sentence: The inspector asked what time the shift had started.
notice_set.question: Which happened first, the shift starting or the asking?
notice_set.why: Had started puts the shift behind the asking, which is why the verb sits one place further back.

notice_set.sentence: They asked whether the coast road was open.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you whether the road was open?
notice_set.why: A reported question reports the asking and nothing else. The answer is simply not in the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me why I had changed courses.
notice_set.question: Who changed courses?
notice_set.why: I inside the report points at whoever is reporting, so the change of course belongs to the speaker.

discovery.prompt: Each question on the left has been reported on the right. Two things have gone missing on the way across. Find both.
pairs: "Where does the ferry leave from?"
He asked where the ferry left from.
"Have you signed the form?"
She asked whether I had signed the form.
"Why did the class finish early?"
They asked why the class had finished early.

candidate_rules.text: The subject goes back in front of the verb and the do, does or did drops out, because the sentence is no longer a question.
The question mark is removed.
Any sentence containing asked keeps question word order after the wh-word.

teach.rule_line: Once a question sits inside a bigger sentence, it takes statement word order.
teach.false_rule: That a reported question is still a question and keeps question word order. Nobody is being asked anything; the sentence is a statement about an asking.

errors.wrong: She asked me where was the nearest chemist.
errors.right: She asked me where the nearest chemist was.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner hears where and the question word order fires by itself, because that is the only pattern they have ever produced after a wh-word. It outlives the rule by years, since it is a habit and not a belief.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: was goes to the end.

errors.wrong: He asked what time did the coach leave.
errors.right: He asked what time the coach left.
errors.why_it_happens: Did is carried across from the original, where it was doing real work. Inside the report the tense has already moved onto the main verb, so did has nothing left to do but duplicate it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: did, and put the tense on leave.

errors.wrong: She asked that I had brought my passport.
errors.right: She asked whether I had brought my passport.
errors.why_it_happens: A yes-no question has no wh-word, so the learner reaches for the that-frame they already own from reported statements. That introduces a statement; a question needs if or whether.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: that becomes whether.

errors.wrong: The clerk asked how long I am staying, and I said until Friday.
errors.right: The clerk asked how long I was staying, and I said until Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner replays the question as it was heard. The rest of the sentence has already moved into the past, so the unshifted verb reads as a jump out of the story and back into the room.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: am becomes was.

pays_in.note: Section three turns questions into reports constantly, and the word order says who asked.

payload.given: The interviewer asked: "Why did you leave your last position?"

feedback.feed_forward: Drop did first, then set the word order.

payload.given: My manager asked: "Are you free on Thursday morning?"

expected: if i was free on thursday morning
whether i was free on thursday morning

feedback.feed_forward: Open a yes-no report with if or whether.

payload.audio_text: She asked me what I'd said to the landlord.

expected: she asked me what i'd said to the landlord
she asked me what i had said to the landlord
she asked me what id said to the landlord

feedback.why_key: In speech the subject and the 'd run together into one sound, and that sound is the whole difference between a report and a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the subject squeezed in after the wh-word.

payload.sentence: The producer asked how many people did watch the repeat, and nobody could tell her.

expected: how many people had watched
how many people watched

feedback.why_key: Did is left over from the question it used to be. Once the clause is inside a statement, the tense belongs on watch and did has no work.

items.decision_cue: when would the results be ready

payload.sentence: Everyone wanted to know when would the results be ready, so I asked at the desk.

the samples were not logged before lunch

title: Reporting an order, a request or a piece of advice

teach.can_do: I can report an instruction, a request or a piece of advice without turning it into a statement.
teach.why_it_matters: An instruction has no statement inside it, so there is nothing for that to introduce. Forcing one in is where the whole pattern collapses.
teach.meaning: An order, a request and a piece of advice are not statements about the world. They are attempts to move somebody, and English reports them with a shape that keeps the movement visible: a person, then to, then the thing they were being moved towards. The verb you choose in front of it records how hard the push was — advised is a suggestion you could ignore, asked is a request, told is an instruction, warned means something bad was waiting. The negative goes in front of to, never inside it.

form.pattern: told / asked / advised / warned / reminded + PERSON + to + verb
notes: the person is compulsory: you cannot say she told to wait
the negative goes in front of to: he told us not to wait
asked is a request, told is an instruction, advised is advice, reminded means you already knew, warned means danger
there is no that-clause here: not she told me that I wait
form.negative: The steward told us not to block the aisle.
form.question: Did she ask you to sign it, or did she tell you to sign it?

rungs.text: "You could sit here." → suggested sitting there
"You should sit down." → advised me to sit down
"Could you sit down?" → asked me to sit down
"Sit down." → told me to sit down
"Don't sit there." → warned me not to sit there

worked_example.sentence: The site manager asked us to keep the gate shut after six.
worked_example.why_this_form: It was a request rather than an order, so asked; the person comes straight after it, and the instruction itself sits inside the to-infinitive.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Told us to keep the gate shut reports the same words as an instruction and makes the manager sound as though refusing was never on offer.

notice_set.sentence: The nurse told him to stop taking the tablets.
notice_set.question: Was this a suggestion or an instruction?
notice_set.why: Told records a push he was not really invited to refuse.

notice_set.sentence: The nurse advised him to stop taking the tablets.
notice_set.question: Was this a suggestion or an instruction?
notice_set.why: Same shape, softer verb. Advised leaves the decision with him.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me not to mention the figures.
notice_set.question: What am I supposed to do?
notice_set.why: Not sits in front of to, so it covers the whole instruction rather than one word of it.

notice_set.sentence: The steward reminded us to keep our passes visible.
notice_set.question: Had we been told this before?
notice_set.why: Reminded only makes sense if the instruction was already somewhere in our heads.

notice_set.sentence: He warned the drivers not to use the coast road.
notice_set.question: What does warned add that told would not?
notice_set.why: Warn carries the reason for the instruction inside the verb: something bad was waiting.

notice_set.sentence: They asked us to send the receipts by Friday.
notice_set.question: Who sends the receipts?
notice_set.why: The person named after asked is the one who does the thing in the to-infinitive.

discovery.prompt: Each instruction on the left has been reported on the right. Work out where the instruction itself ends up.
pairs: "Wear the harness."
The supervisor told us to wear the harness.
"Could you send the receipts?"
They asked us to send the receipts.
"Don't lean on the doors."
The guard told us not to lean on the doors.

candidate_rules.text: The person being moved comes first, and the instruction goes into a to-infinitive after them.
The imperative verb keeps its own form and a to is added in front of it.
Any sentence with told needs a that-clause after the person.

teach.rule_line: Report an instruction with a person and a to-infinitive, and put any not in front of to.
teach.false_rule: That every report needs that. That introduces a statement, and an instruction has no statement in it for that to introduce.

errors.wrong: The supervisor told to us to wear the harness.
errors.right: The supervisor told us to wear the harness.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has said something to somebody a thousand times, and the to leaks forward onto the listener. Tell takes its listener bare; only say needs to in front of one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the first to.

errors.wrong: The guard told us to don't lean on the doors.
errors.right: The guard told us not to lean on the doors.
errors.why_it_happens: Don't is how the original was spoken, so it travels across in one piece. Inside the report the negative belongs in front of to, where it can cover the whole instruction.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: to don't lean becomes not to lean.

errors.wrong: She asked me that I should send the file again.
errors.right: She asked me to send the file again.
errors.why_it_happens: The that-clause is the only reporting frame the learner has practised, so a request gets forced into it and then needs should to carry the push. The infinitive does that job in three words fewer.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: that I should send becomes to send.

errors.wrong: The officer warned us against to park on the verge.
errors.right: The officer warned us against parking on the verge.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other verb in this family took a to-infinitive, so the learner reaches for one again. Warn against is a fixed pair, and after a preposition English takes only the -ing form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to park becomes parking.

pays_in.note: Talks about advice, teachers and first jobs are made of this shape.
pays_in.model: My first supervisor told me to write everything down, which I still do.

pays_in.note: A letter about repairs or a course reports what you were instructed to do.
pays_in.model: Your office asked me to send the meter reading before the end of the month.

pays_in.note: Instruction-heavy passages report requirements this way rather than as rules.
pays_in.model: Residents are reminded not to leave bicycles in the stairwell.

used_in.quote: The card is about advice and who gives it, so almost every answer reports somebody telling somebody else to do something.
The letter has to report what the landlord asked the writer to do before it can complain about what happened next.

payload.sentence: The physiotherapist told me to walk on it every day.
payload.question: Who does the walking?

feedback.why_key: The person named after told is the one who carries out whatever comes after to.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the named person as the doer of the to-verb.

payload.sentence: The office asked staff not to park in the loading bay.
payload.question: What are staff supposed to do?
options: keep out of the loading bay

feedback.why_key: Not sits in front of to, so it cancels the whole instruction rather than one word inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read not before to as covering everything after it.

payload.context: Someone describing being stopped at a level crossing.
payload.sentence: The signaller told to us to wait behind the barrier.
reasons: tell takes its listener with no to in front
the barrier was already up
wait is the wrong verb form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The listener belongs immediately after told. The extra to has come across from say, which is a different verb with a different habit.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the listener straight after told, with nothing between.

payload.context: Original: "Please send the timesheets by Friday."
payload.stem: The payroll office asked us ___ (send) the timesheets by Friday.

expected: to send

feedback.why_key: The instruction goes inside the to-infinitive, which is where English keeps the thing somebody is being moved towards.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the instruction in a to-infinitive after the person.

payload.context: Original: "Don't lift anything heavy for a fortnight."
payload.stem: The doctor told me ___ (lift) anything heavy for a fortnight.

expected: not to lift

feedback.why_key: The negative goes in front of to so that it covers the whole instruction, not just the lifting.
feedback.feed_forward: Put not in front of to, never after it.

payload.given: The inspector to the driver: "Take the diversion at the roundabout."
payload.instruction: Report the instruction as an instruction, not as a request.

expected: the driver to take the diversion at the roundabout
him to take the diversion at the roundabout

feedback.why_key: Told records that the driver was not being offered a choice, which is exactly what a bare imperative does.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the reporting verb to how hard the push was.

payload.given: My neighbour to me: "You should get the gutters cleared before the autumn."
payload.instruction: Report it as advice you were free to ignore.

expected: me to get the gutters cleared before the autumn
me to clear the gutters before the autumn

feedback.why_key: Advised keeps the decision with you, which is what should was doing in the original.
feedback.feed_forward: Use advised when the original left the choice open.

payload.context: Original: "Don't leave the bay unlocked." Build the report.

expected: the supervisor told us not to leave the bay unlocked

feedback.why_key: Four things in a fixed order: verb, person, not, to. Move any of them and the sentence stops working.
feedback.feed_forward: Build it in that order every time: verb, person, not, to.

payload.audio_text: They've asked us not to book anything before the audit.

expected: they've asked us not to book anything before the audit
they have asked us not to book anything before the audit
theyve asked us not to book anything before the audit

feedback.why_key: Us not to runs together into one unstressed lump in speech, and it is the lump that carries the whole instruction.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the person and the not squeezed in before to.

payload.sentence: The conductor told passengers to don't board until the platform staff had finished.

expected: not to board

feedback.why_key: Don't belongs to the words as they were spoken. Inside the report the negative moves in front of to, where it covers the whole instruction.
feedback.feed_forward: Convert don't into not in front of to.

payload.context: From a clinic leaflet.
payload.sentence: The trust warned patients against to take the two tablets together.
reasons: against is a preposition, so it needs an -ing form after it
the two tablets can be taken together
warned cannot take an object
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Warn against is a fixed pair, and no preposition in English is ever followed by a to-infinitive.
feedback.feed_forward: After any preposition, use the -ing form.

payload.prompt_text: Your building manager gave everyone an instruction about the bins last month and nobody followed it. Write one sentence reporting the instruction, including what people were told not to do.

feedback.why_key: A negative instruction is where this pattern earns its keep, because that is where the shape most often falls apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that not is in front of to before you stop.

payload.prompt_text: Write the second paragraph of this letter. It must report at least two things you were asked or told to do, and one thing you were advised not to do. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: A complaint only works if the reader can see what you were told to do and what you then did, in that order and in that shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Read back only the reporting verbs and check each has a person after it.

title: Choosing a reporting verb that says what you think of the claim

teach.can_do: I can choose a reporting verb that shows what I think of a claim, and get its pattern right.
teach.why_it_matters: Said is neutral and free. Claimed, argued, admitted and pointed out each add a judgement, and the judgement lands whether you meant it or not.
teach.meaning: Every reporting verb does two jobs in one word. It reports, and it rates. Argue says the person is building a case. Claim says they have asserted something you are not signing. Admit says the statement cost them something. Point out says it was a fact already lying there. Concede says they gave ground under pressure. The second job is why this is essay grammar and not vocabulary. Each verb also carries its own pattern, which cannot be worked out from the meaning and has to be stored with the word.

form.pattern: verb + that-clause | verb + -ing | verb + object + to-infinitive | verb + preposition + -ing
notes: that-clause: argue, claim, point out, insist, deny, admit, concede, warn, suggest
-ing form: admit, deny, suggest — she denied seeing the email
object + to-infinitive: urge, advise, warn, remind — they urged the council to reopen it
preposition + -ing: accuse someone of, warn against, insist on, object to
suggest never takes an object with to: not suggest us to wait
form.negative: He denied that the figures had been changed. / He denied changing the figures.
form.question: Which verb says what I actually think of this claim?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this?

steps.gloss: it is a fact and I am with them
they demonstrated it and I accept it
they are making a case; I am neutral
they float it, and so do I
they assert it; I am not signing
they assert it and I have doubts

worked_example.sentence: Supporters of the charge point out that the money is ring-fenced for buses.
worked_example.why_this_form: Point out treats the ring-fencing as a fact already sitting there, so the writer has quietly agreed with it before the argument even starts.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Claim would hold the same words at arm's length: the money may or may not be ring-fenced, and the writer is not vouching for it.

notice_set.sentence: The company admitted that the data had been stored abroad.
notice_set.question: Was this comfortable for the company?
notice_set.why: Admit is only used when the statement costs the person making it something.

notice_set.sentence: The company claimed that the data had been stored securely.
notice_set.question: Is the writer standing behind this?
options: No, the writer is only reporting it
The writer says it is false
notice_set.why: Claim reports an assertion and declines to endorse it. It does not say the assertion is false.

notice_set.sentence: Ms Oduya pointed out that the two figures had been measured differently.
notice_set.question: Is this presented as something already true?
notice_set.why: Point out treats the difference as a fact lying in plain sight that somebody has drawn attention to.

notice_set.sentence: The panel conceded that the first estimate had been too low.
notice_set.question: Whose estimate was it?
notice_set.why: Concede means giving ground, and you can only give ground on your own position.

notice_set.sentence: The union urged the trust to reopen the ward.
notice_set.question: Who would reopen the ward?
notice_set.why: Urge takes an object and a to-infinitive, and the object is the one who would act.

notice_set.sentence: The developer denied cutting the number of affordable flats.
notice_set.question: What does the developer say happened?
notice_set.why: Deny takes an -ing form and reverses it: the developer's position is that no cut took place.

discovery.prompt: The same report is written two ways. Work out what the second verb in each pair is doing besides reporting.
pairs: The minister said the scheme would pay for itself.
The minister claimed the scheme would pay for itself.
Researchers said the effect was small.
Researchers found the effect was small.
The council said the consultation had been rushed.
The council admitted the consultation had been rushed.

candidate_rules.text: The second verb adds the writer's rating of the claim on top of the report.
The second verb in each pair is simply more formal than said.
Any reporting verb can replace said as long as a that-clause follows it.

teach.rule_line: Pick the verb that says what you think of the claim, then check its pattern.
teach.false_rule: That these verbs are synonyms of said that make writing look academic. Swapping one in without meaning its judgement is how an essay accidentally takes a side.

contrast.question: Am I signing this claim, staying neutral, or holding it away from me?

fork.answer: Signing it — it is a checkable fact and I am with them
Neutral — they are making a case and I am reporting it
At arm's length — they assert it and I am not vouching for it

a.text: The developer pointed out that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
a.means: The brownfield land is a fact, and the writer has accepted it on the way past.

b.text: The developer claimed that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
b.means: That is the developer's assertion, and the writer is not standing behind it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote claimed. In one word you have told your reader you do not believe the developer, and the rest of your paragraph now has to earn that. If you had no reason to doubt them, claimed has picked a fight you did not intend to pick.

edge_case.text: Suggest is the trap of the set. It takes a that-clause or an -ing form and never an object with to, so suggest us to wait is wrong however natural it feels next to advise us to wait. Store suggest that and suggest doing as two fixed chunks and stop reasoning about it.

contrast.stronger_test: Read your sentence back as if you were the person being reported. If they would object to the verb you chose, you have taken a position. Decide whether you meant to take it.

worked_pairs.a: Campaigners point out that both consultations closed in August, which the council's own diary confirms.
worked_pairs.b: Campaigners claim that both consultations were deliberately timed to be missed.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: which the council's own diary confirms
worked_pairs.gloss: A date anybody can check invites point out. A statement about somebody's intentions is exactly what claim is for.

worked_pairs.a: The trust admitted that it had missed the target for a third year.
worked_pairs.b: The trust insisted that it had missed the target only because of the strike.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: it had missed the target for a third year
worked_pairs.gloss: Admit is for something that costs the speaker. Insist is for a defence they are holding on to while somebody pushes.

worked_pairs.a: Drawing on three small trials, the report suggests that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.b: Drawing on a decade of hospital records, the report shows that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.gloss: The strength of the evidence picks the verb. Suggest is honest about thin evidence; show over-claims on it.

errors.wrong: The committee suggested us to postpone the vote.
errors.right: The committee suggested postponing the vote.
errors.why_it_happens: Suggest sits in the same meaning space as advise and urge, and both of those take an object with to. The pattern cannot be worked out from the meaning, so it has to be stored with the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: us to postpone becomes postponing.

errors.wrong: The report accused the operator to cut corners on maintenance.
errors.right: The report accused the operator of cutting corners on maintenance.
errors.why_it_happens: Accuse looks like a verb that should take to, because so many verbs in this family do. Its preposition is of, and after of English takes only an -ing form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: to cut becomes of cutting.

errors.wrong: She denied to send the message from the shared account.
errors.right: She denied sending the message from the shared account.
errors.why_it_happens: Deny is stored as a refusal verb and refuse takes to. Deny takes an -ing form or a that-clause and never an infinitive, which is a fact about the word rather than about refusing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to send becomes sending.

errors.wrong: The survey proves that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.right: The survey suggests that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.why_it_happens: Proves feels like the strongest available word and therefore the most persuasive. The reader hears a promise the evidence cannot keep, and the whole paragraph loses credit for it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: proves becomes suggests.

pays_in.note: It is how an essay gets other voices in without agreeing with all of them.
pays_in.model: Critics argue that the levy is regressive; the review concedes that its early years were poorly targeted.

pays_in.note: Paraphrase questions turn on whether the writer signed the claim or only reported it.
pays_in.model: The author notes that the two surveys used different age bands.

pays_in.note: Referring to what people argue lifts an answer off your own opinion.
pays_in.model: A lot of people argue that streaming has killed the album, though the sales figures suggest otherwise.

used_in.quote: A discussion essay on funding has to report two sides fairly, and the verb chosen for each side is where fairness is won or lost.
The card asks who gets believed and why, so answers report claims the speaker rates very differently.
The passage reports several researchers with different verbs, and one question depends on noticing which one the author endorses.

payload.sentence: The broadcaster conceded that the interview had been edited before transmission.
payload.question: Was this something the broadcaster wanted to say?

feedback.why_key: Concede reports a position given up under pressure, which is information about the situation and not just about the words.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the reporting verb as information about the speaker.

payload.sentence: The team leader urged the depot to keep two vans on standby.
payload.question: Who would keep the vans on standby?

feedback.why_key: Urge puts the person being pushed straight after it, and that person is the one who would act.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the object after urge; that is the doer.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph resting on a single pilot study.
payload.sentence: The pilot study proves that shorter lessons improve retention.
reasons: the verb claims more than one pilot study can support
shorter lessons do not improve retention
proves is the wrong form of the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The verb writes a cheque the evidence cannot cash, and a reader who notices stops trusting the rest of the paragraph.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb's strength to the evidence you have.

payload.context: Original: "We did not release anything into the river."
payload.stem: The plant denied ___ (release) anything into the river.

expected: releasing
having released

feedback.why_key: Deny takes an -ing form, which is a fact about the word and not something the meaning can tell you.
feedback.feed_forward: Store deny with an -ing form attached.

payload.context: Original: "The channel has been burying corrections."
payload.stem: The regulator accused the channel ___ burying corrections.

expected: of

feedback.why_key: Accuse comes with of welded to it, and the -ing form after it is there because of arrived first.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn accuse of as one unit, never as two words.

payload.given: The panel said: "Screening should start five years earlier."
payload.instruction: Report it with suggest, using the pattern suggest takes.

expected: that screening should start five years earlier
screening should start five years earlier
starting screening five years earlier

feedback.why_key: Suggest takes a that-clause or an -ing form. It never takes an object with to, however much it feels like advise.
feedback.feed_forward: After suggest, write that or an -ing form.

payload.audio_text: They've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately.

expected: they've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately
they have admitted deleting the footage, but they have denied doing it deliberately
theyve admitted deleting the footage, but theyve denied doing it deliberately

feedback.why_key: Two verbs, two -ing forms, and two completely different admissions. Miss one and the sentence says the opposite of what was said.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the -ing form that follows each reporting verb.

items.decision_cue: figures the council has published itself

payload.context: The writer is using figures the council has published itself and is not disputing them.
payload.stem: Residents' groups ___ that the estate has lost two of its four bus routes.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact on the record and the writer accepts it.
That this is the groups' assertion and the writer is not vouching for it.

expected: point out

feedback.why_key: The figures are the council's own, so there is nothing to hold at arm's length and holding it there would look evasive.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the claim is checkable before you pick the verb.

items.decision_cue: a figure nobody has been able to check

payload.context: The writer is repeating a figure nobody has been able to check and intends to query it later.
payload.stem: Residents' groups ___ that the estate has lost two of its four bus routes.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact on the record and the writer accepts it.
That this is the groups' assertion and the writer is not vouching for it.

expected: claim

feedback.why_key: You are about to query the figure, so signing it in the sentence before would leave you arguing against yourself.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold a claim at arm's length if you plan to query it.

payload.context: The study followed twelve volunteers over one week.
payload.stem: The authors ___ that daylight lamps improve winter concentration.

options.why_this_means: That the finding leans one way and the evidence is thin.
That the finding is established and the writer is treating it as settled.

expected: suggest

feedback.why_key: Twelve people over one week will support a lean, not a settlement, and the verb has to say which of those you have.
feedback.feed_forward: Size the verb to the study before you write it.

items.decision_cue: eleven thousand workers across four winters

payload.context: The study followed eleven thousand workers across four winters and has been repeated twice.
payload.stem: The authors ___ that daylight lamps improve winter concentration.

options.why_this_means: That the finding leans one way and the evidence is thin.
That the finding is established and the writer is treating it as settled.

expected: show

feedback.why_key: Hedging evidence this strong is its own kind of inaccuracy: the reader is told to doubt something the writer has no reason to doubt.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not hedge a finding the evidence fully supports.

items.decision_cue: which had been their own policy for years

payload.context: The board was defending a pay freeze which had been their own policy for years.
payload.stem: The board ___ that the freeze had held wages below inflation.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

expected: admitted

feedback.why_key: The point damages their own policy, and a verb that damages the speaker is exactly what admit is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whose case the claim hurts, then choose.

items.decision_cue: against three hours of questions from the floor

payload.context: The board held the same line against three hours of questions from the floor.
payload.stem: The board ___ that the freeze had protected jobs at the plant.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

expected: insisted

feedback.why_key: The claim helps their case and they repeated it under pressure, which is the situation insist exists to report.
feedback.feed_forward: Use insisted for a position defended under pressure.

items.decision_cue: a long piece about local newspapers

payload.context: From a long piece about local newspapers, where the writer has not yet declared a position.
payload.stem: The editor ___ that free distribution had kept the paper alive.

options.why_this_means: That she was making a case, and the writer is reporting it without judging it.
That she has held this view for a long time and has been challenged on it.

follow_up.question: Which version implies somebody has been arguing back?

feedback.why_key: Both are neutral and both are correct. They differ in whether the reader is told there is an opposing view in the room.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose on what the reader needs to know about the argument.

payload.context: Two sentences from different sections of the same review of a clinic.
sentences: The trust acknowledged that waiting times had risen.
The trust alleged that waiting times had been recorded incorrectly.
meanings: The trust accepted a point that did not help it, and the writer treats it as settled.
The trust made an accusation, and the writer is keeping well clear of it.

feedback.why_key: One verb records something conceded, the other records something asserted against somebody else. The writer's distance is different in each.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who each claim damages before you read on.

payload.sentence: The waste review suggested residents to sort food waste separately, which most of them already did.

expected: suggested that residents sort
suggested that residents should sort
suggested sorting

feedback.why_key: Suggest will not take an object with to. The pattern has come across from advise, which means something similar and behaves differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the object and to with a that-clause after suggest.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about a change in how people get their news. In the first, report a view you accept. In the second, report a view you do not accept. Do not use said in either.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences of the same shape with two different verbs is the fastest way to feel how much of your position lives in the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each verb against what you actually think.

payload.prompt_text: Write one body paragraph for this prompt that reports both sides. Use three different reporting verbs, none of them said, and make sure each one shows where you stand. Eight minutes.

feedback.why_key: A discussion paragraph that reports both sides with the same verb has not discussed anything. The verbs are where the discussion actually happens.
feedback.feed_forward: Read back the three verbs alone and check the pattern of each.

title: Attributing a view in an essay without saying 'some people say'

teach.can_do: I can attribute a view in an essay to a holder or a source instead of to nobody.
teach.why_it_matters: Some people say is the phrase that marks an essay as unattributed opinion. Three frames replace it, and each one buys you room to disagree.
teach.meaning: Academic attribution does two things at once. It puts a view on the page, and it puts a measured distance between that view and you. There are three frames and no more. Name the holder: Critics of the scheme argue that. Name nobody and let the passive carry it: It has been argued that. Name the source rather than the person: the 2019 review found that. Which frame you take decides how much of the claim lands on you, and it also decides whether your next sentence is able to push back against it.

form.pattern: HOLDER + reporting verb + that-clause  |  It + be + past participle + that-clause  |  SOURCE + verb + that-clause
notes: the holder frame: Critics argue that … / Supporters of the policy maintain that …
the passive frame: It has been argued that … / It is widely accepted that … — nobody is named, so there is nothing for an opponent to attack
the source frame: The review found that … / The data suggest that … — a source a reader could go and check
acknowledge and concede let you name the opposing view before you answer it: While it is widely acknowledged that …, …
that is not optional in these frames; it is the only thing holding the clause to the frame
form.negative: It has not been established that the charge reduces total traffic.
form.question: It might be asked whether the savings would ever materialise.

rungs.text: Loads of people reckon that…
Some people say that…
It is widely accepted that…
Critics of the scheme argue that…
The 2019 review found that…

spec.top_label: attributed to a source a reader could check

worked_example.sentence: It is widely accepted that congestion charging shifts journeys rather than removing them; what remains disputed is where they go.
worked_example.why_this_form: The passive frame puts an agreed point on the page without pretending the writer has counted anybody, and the second half moves straight to what is still open.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Some people say congestion charging shifts journeys hands the reader a vague crowd and an argument that can be waved away, because nothing has been agreed by anyone.

notice_set.sentence: It has been suggested that flexible hours reduce peak-time crowding.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you who suggested it?
notice_set.why: The passive frame deliberately leaves the holder out, which is both its use and its limit.

notice_set.sentence: Critics of the policy argue that the savings have been overstated.
notice_set.question: Does the writer agree with the critics?
notice_set.why: Argue reports a case being made and takes no position on it, which leaves the next sentence free to go either way.

notice_set.sentence: The 2019 review found that the two schemes had similar running costs.
notice_set.question: Where could a reader go to check this?
notice_set.why: Naming a source is what makes a claim checkable, and checkable is what academic writing means by supported.

notice_set.sentence: While it is widely acknowledged that fees deter some applicants, the measured effect is small.
notice_set.question: What is the writer about to do?
options: accept the point and then limit it
notice_set.why: Acknowledge concedes ground on purpose so that the limit arriving after the comma has something to push against.

notice_set.sentence: It is often assumed that longer opening hours increase visitor numbers.
notice_set.question: Is the writer likely to agree in the next sentence?
options: No — assumed usually sets up a challenge
notice_set.why: Assume marks a belief held without evidence, which is a place to attack rather than a place to agree.

notice_set.sentence: The data suggest that the drop began before the charge was introduced.
notice_set.question: How strong is the claim being made?
notice_set.why: Suggest reports a lean in the evidence, which is honest when the evidence leans rather than settles.

discovery.prompt: The same idea is put on the page twice. Work out what the right-hand version gives the reader that the left-hand one does not.
pairs: Some people say that fees put students off.
It is often argued that fees deter applicants from lower-income households.
Everyone knows that the buses are unreliable.
Passenger surveys consistently report low satisfaction with reliability.
I think the charge has worked.
The evidence collected since 2019 suggests that the charge has worked.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand versions attach the claim to a holder or a source, which is what lets a reader agree or disagree with something specific.
The right-hand versions are longer and use more formal words.
A sentence is academic if it starts with It is.

teach.rule_line: Name a holder, name a source, or use the passive frame — but name something.
teach.false_rule: That an essay becomes academic by adding some people say and according to many experts. Both attribute the claim to nobody, which is where it already was.

errors.wrong: Loads of people reckon that a four-day week would never work in hospitals.
errors.right: It is often argued that a four-day week would be unworkable in hospitals.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has the idea and reaches for the words they would use to say it out loud. The content is fine; the frame belongs to a conversation and arrives on the page unchanged.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: Loads of people reckon that becomes It is often argued that.

errors.wrong: It has often argued that public transport should be free at the point of use.
errors.right: It has often been argued that public transport should be free at the point of use.
errors.why_it_happens: The frame is stored as one lump and under time pressure the middle of the lump falls out. Has argued is perfectly grammatical, which is why nothing in the writer's ear objects to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: been.

errors.wrong: Research proves that homework has no effect on examination results.
errors.right: Research suggests that homework has little effect on examination results.
errors.why_it_happens: Proves and no effect both feel more forceful, and force feels like persuasion. A reader who knows the area hears an overclaim and discounts the rest of the paragraph on the strength of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: proves becomes suggests.

errors.wrong: It is widely accepted the charge has reduced traffic in the centre.
errors.right: It is widely accepted that the charge has reduced traffic in the centre.
errors.why_it_happens: That is droppable after said in speech and the habit crosses over. In this frame it is the only thing holding the clause on, and without it the sentence reads as two half sentences pushed together.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: that.

pays_in.note: It is the difference between an argued essay and a page of opinions.
pays_in.model: It is widely accepted that remote study widens access; what remains disputed is whether it improves outcomes.

pays_in.note: Which-view-matches-the-writer questions run entirely on attribution frames.
pays_in.model: It has been argued that the two measures were never comparable.

pays_in.note: Describing what a figure shows is attribution to a source.
pays_in.model: The chart shows that domestic demand fell in every year after 2014.

used_in.quote: A discussion prompt needs two attributed positions before the writer's own view can mean anything, and this is how they get attributed.
The passage separates what has been argued from what the author holds, and one question depends entirely on that separation.

payload.sentence: It has been argued that shorter degrees would suit older students better.
payload.question: Whose view is this?
options: somebody's, but the sentence does not say whose

feedback.why_key: The passive frame puts a real view on the page and deliberately declines to name who holds it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the passive frame as a view without an owner.

payload.sentence: While it is widely acknowledged that the scheme reduced traffic, the effect on air quality was smaller than expected.
payload.question: What is the writer doing with the first half?
options: giving ground so the second half can push back

feedback.why_key: Acknowledging a point on purpose is what gives the limitation after the comma something solid to be measured against.
feedback.feed_forward: Read While it is acknowledged as a set-up for a limit.

payload.context: The opening sentence of a Task 2 body paragraph.
payload.sentence: According to many experts, printed newspapers will disappear within a decade.
reasons: no expert is named, so the claim is attributed to nobody
printed newspapers will not disappear
will disappear is the wrong verb form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The phrase looks like a citation and functions as none. There is nobody a reader could go and check, so the claim is still just an opinion.
feedback.feed_forward: Name a source, or drop the crowd and use the passive frame.

payload.context: Opening an essay paragraph on funding for basic research.
payload.stem: It has long ___ (argue) that basic research pays for itself over decades rather than years.

expected: been argued

feedback.why_key: The frame is a passive, so been is doing the work of leaving the arguer out. Without it the sentence claims it did the arguing.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for been every time you write It has.

payload.context: The study is one survey of four hundred households, and the writer wants to be honest about that.
payload.stem: The survey ___ (suggest / prove) that households overestimate how much they recycle.

expected: suggests

feedback.why_key: One survey supports a lean. Proves would promise a settlement, and the reader would be entitled to ask where it came from.
feedback.feed_forward: Size the verb to the evidence you actually have.

payload.given: Some people say that class size does not matter much.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the claim is attributed to somebody, using the holder frame.

expected: critics of smaller classes argue that class size matters less than teaching quality
critics of the policy argue that class size does not matter much
critics of the reform argue that class size has little effect

feedback.why_key: Naming a holder gives your reader something to picture and gives your next sentence something to answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the crowd with a named group.

payload.given: Everyone knows that sitting all day is bad for you.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it as an attributed claim using the passive frame, and hedge it to match ordinary evidence.

expected: it is widely accepted that prolonged sitting carries health risks
it is generally accepted that prolonged sitting carries health risks
it is widely accepted that sitting for long periods carries health risks

feedback.why_key: Widely accepted claims agreement without claiming a headcount, which is exactly as much as the evidence will carry.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap everyone knows for widely accepted.

payload.context: Build the passive attribution frame around this claim.

expected: it has been suggested that shorter shifts reduce clinical errors

feedback.why_key: Four fixed words open the frame and that closes it. Everything you actually want to say sits after that.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the frame first, then hang the claim on that.

payload.audio_text: It's been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered.

expected: it's been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered
it has been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered
its been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered

feedback.why_key: In speech the whole frame reduces to about two syllables, which is why been is the first thing to go missing when it reaches the page.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for been between the auxiliary and the participle.

payload.sentence: It has frequently claimed that recycling targets are set without reference to what councils can collect.

expected: it has frequently been claimed

feedback.why_key: Without been, the sentence says that it did the claiming, and there is no it in the paragraph for that to point at.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert been after the auxiliary in every passive frame.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph resting on a single national dataset.
payload.sentence: The dataset proves beyond doubt that automation has cut entry-level hiring in every region.
reasons: the verb and the phrase after it claim far more than one dataset can carry
automation has not cut entry-level hiring
proves is the wrong tense
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Beyond doubt is a promise no single dataset can keep, and in every region rules out the exceptions a reader will immediately think of.
feedback.feed_forward: Cut the intensifier before you cut anything else.

payload.context: Two opening sentences from different paragraphs of the same article.
sentences: It is often assumed that longer opening hours raise visitor numbers.
It is widely accepted that longer opening hours raise staffing costs.
meanings: The writer is about to challenge this, because assume marks a belief held without evidence.
The writer is taking this as settled and will build on it rather than argue about it.

feedback.why_key: Both frames are passive and both name nobody. The participle inside them tells the reader which claim is about to be taken apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the participle to see where the paragraph is going.

payload.prompt_text: Write the opening sentence of a body paragraph arguing that online courses widen access to study. Attribute the claim to somebody or to something, and do not use said, some people or according to.

feedback.why_key: An opening sentence that attributes gives the paragraph somebody to answer, and a paragraph with nobody to answer has nowhere to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Name a holder or a source in the first eight words.

payload.prompt_text: Write the concession paragraph for this prompt. It must acknowledge the opposing view using a passive attribution frame, then limit it using a named source. Do not use some people say. Eight minutes.

feedback.why_key: The concession paragraph is where an essay proves it has read the other side, and attribution is the only thing that proves it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that every claim in the paragraph has an owner.

title: Pointing back at something so the reader lands on the right thing

teach.can_do: I can point back at something I have already said and be sure my reader lands on the right thing.
teach.why_it_matters: This is what cohesion actually is. Not linking words, but a chain of pointing that never leaves the reader holding two candidates at once.
teach.meaning: Words like it, they, this and such carry no meaning of their own. They borrow it from something already on the page, and your reader resolves them without noticing, by taking the nearest thing that fits. That is where the risk lives. If two things fit, the reader picks one and never registers that they chose, and you never find out which. A pointing word is only safe when exactly one thing can be at the other end of it.

form.pattern: it / they / this / that / these / such (+ a noun that names what you mean)
notes: it and they point back at a single noun and must match it for number
this and that can point back at a whole idea, which is exactly why they go wrong
the safe habit is this plus a noun that names the idea: this closure, this refusal, this shift
such plus a noun does the same job at a higher register: such measures, such an approach
form.negative: Neither of these worked and none of them was cheap: the negative sits on the pointing word itself.
form.question: Cover everything before the pointing word. Could a stranger say what it means? If not, name it.

left.text: ... and this has never been explained.

right.text: ... and this refusal has never been explained.

spec.caption: One noun after this turns a guess into a fact.

worked_example.sentence: The council shut two of the four recycling points. This closure has doubled the queues at the two left open.
worked_example.why_this_form: Closure names what the second sentence is pointing at, so the reader is never briefly holding two candidates, the council and the shutting.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: A bare this would leave the reader to guess, and a fair share of them would land on the recycling points rather than on the decision.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved into the old library. It has been shut for a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What has been shut?
notice_set.why: Two single things have just been named and nothing in the second sentence chooses between them.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved into the old library. The clinic has been shut for a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What has been shut?
notice_set.why: Repeating the noun costs two words and removes the guesswork entirely.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed told Emeka that his car had been towed.
notice_set.question: Whose car was towed?
notice_set.why: Both men have been named and both are equally available, so the sentence holds two readings at once.

notice_set.sentence: The council raised the charge and cut two routes. This has been widely criticised.
notice_set.question: What has been criticised?
notice_set.why: Three things are on offer here: the charge, the cuts, and both together. Nothing narrows it down.

notice_set.sentence: The council raised the charge and cut two routes. This second decision has been widely criticised.
notice_set.question: What has been criticised?
notice_set.why: Second decision counts along the sentence before it and lands squarely on the route cuts.

teach.rule_line: Every pointing word needs exactly one possible owner. Two owners is a broken sentence.
teach.false_rule: That repeating a noun is clumsy and a pronoun is always tidier. A repeated noun is clear; an unclear pronoun costs far more than the repetition.

errors.wrong: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before it had been approved.
errors.right: The supplier sent the invoice to the contractor before the invoice had been approved.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has one thing in mind and cannot see the other reading at all. The reader has two singular nouns to choose from and takes the nearer one, which is the contractor.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for its noun: it becomes the invoice.

errors.wrong: Schools cut music and drama while protecting sport. This is short-sighted.
errors.right: Schools cut music and drama while protecting sport. This choice of priorities is short-sighted.
errors.why_it_happens: A bare this feels like a summary because the writer has just finished summarising in their own head. On the page it points at three or four things at once and settles on none of them.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one noun after this.

errors.wrong: In the article, it says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.right: The article says that fewer teenagers are learning to drive.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught to open with a phrase and then needs a subject, so it arrives to fill the slot. It now points at nothing, because the only candidate has been shut inside the opening phrase.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two words: in and it.

errors.wrong: Councils tried three approaches. Second approach worked best.
errors.right: Councils tried three approaches. The second approach worked best.
errors.why_it_happens: The approaches have already been introduced, so they feel established to the writer. English marks an established thing with the, and without it the reader has nothing telling them to look back.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of languages with no article system.

pays_in.note: Every second sentence of a paragraph points back at the first one.
pays_in.model: Fares rose twice in a single year. This second increase pushed regular users back into their cars.

pays_in.note: Reference questions ask what a highlighted word is pointing at.
pays_in.model: Such measures rarely survive a change of administration.

pays_in.note: A long answer falls apart the moment this stops having an owner.
pays_in.model: People shop online and go out less, and that combination has emptied the high street.

used_in.quote: One question on this passage asks what a highlighted pronoun refers to, which is this point tested directly.

payload.sentence: The firm replaced the old system with a cloud service. It has cut costs by a third.
payload.question: What has cut the costs?

feedback.why_key: The old system was thrown out, so it cannot be saving anybody money. Only one candidate survives the sentence before it.
feedback.feed_forward: Test every candidate against the verb before you settle.

payload.sentence: Tamsin rang her sister after she got back from Sandmouth.
payload.question: Who came back from Sandmouth?

feedback.why_key: Two women have been named and both fit. The speaker knows which one; the listener is quietly guessing.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the person again when two of them are in play.

payload.context: From a draft about phones in classrooms.
payload.sentence: Schools ban phones, teachers confiscate them, and parents complain. This is worrying.
reasons: the pointing word has three different things it could mean
the wrong pointing word has been used
the sentence needs a linking word in front of it
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The banning, the confiscating and the complaining are all available, and a bare this settles on none of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a noun after this that names what you mean.

payload.context: A firm moved its records online and lost three days of work when the service went down.
payload.stem: This ___ persuaded the directors to keep paper copies after all.

expected: failure
outage
breakdown
collapse

feedback.why_key: The noun names the event the sentence is pointing at, so the reader never has to choose between the move and the crash.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow this with a noun that names the event.

payload.given: The paper printed the correction on page nineteen. This annoyed the readers who had complained.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so nobody has to guess what annoyed them.

expected: burial annoyed the readers who had complained
placement annoyed the readers who had complained
decision annoyed the readers who had complained

feedback.why_key: Naming the thing removes the choice between the correction itself and where the paper chose to put it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the action, not the object, when the action is your point.

payload.given: The trust opened two walk-in centres. Second centre closed within a year.
payload.instruction: Fix the second sentence so it points back properly.

expected: second centre closed within a year
second of these closed within a year

feedback.why_key: The centres are already on the page, and the is the word that tells your reader to look back rather than forward.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the in front of anything you have already introduced.

payload.context: The paragraph before this one described three separate hold-ups in the fieldwork.

expected: such delays are rarely reported in the summary

feedback.why_key: Such plus a noun gathers up several things already mentioned and hands them to the reader as one labelled bundle.
feedback.feed_forward: Use such plus a noun to sum up a list you have just given.

payload.audio_text: They've fixed the router, but that hasn't helped the signal.

expected: they've fixed the router, but that hasn't helped the signal
they have fixed the router but that has not helped the signal
theyve fixed the router but that hasnt helped the signal

feedback.why_key: That is unstressed and easily heard as the, which would turn a pointing word into an article and lose the link between the two halves.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the vowel in that when it points backwards.

payload.sentence: The developer bought the mill from the trust two years before it was demolished.

expected: before the mill was demolished
before the building was demolished

feedback.why_key: A trust can be wound up and a mill can be knocked down, so both nouns survive the verb and the reader has to pick one.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the pointing word with the noun when two candidates fit.

items.decision_cue: This shift has left small towns

payload.context: From the middle of a passage about where people now do their shopping.
payload.sentence: More households now buy their weekly food online. This shift has left small towns with empty units on the main street.
reasons: the pointing word has more than one owner
the noun after this does not match anything before it
the two sentences should be joined
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Shift names the change described in the sentence before, so there is exactly one thing at the far end of the pointing word.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the reference when one noun names one prior idea.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences. The first says that many services can now only be booked online. The second must begin with This and a noun, and say what that has done to older users.

feedback.why_key: The noun you choose after This is the thing that tells your reader which part of the first sentence you are building on.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the noun before you write the rest of the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on phones in schools. Circle every it, this and they, and for each one write down the single thing it points at. Rewrite any where you had to think. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: If you had to stop and think about your own sentence, a reader coming to it cold has no chance at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Rewrite any pointing word you had to pause over.

title: Not saying the same words twice, and leaving out what the reader can rebuild

point_json.grammar_name: Substitution and ellipsis: one, ones, do so, so, not

teach.can_do: I can avoid repeating myself by leaving a placeholder where the repeat would have been.
teach.why_it_matters: Repetition is the loudest sign of a writer with a small toolkit, and this is the cheapest way out of it. Nothing new has to be learned, only left out.
teach.meaning: English hates saying the same words twice in a row. Instead of repeating a noun it puts a placeholder there: one, ones, that one. Instead of repeating a verb and everything after it, it leaves only the auxiliary standing: does, did, has, will. Instead of repeating a whole clause it uses so or not. Every one of these is a promise to the reader that the missing words are recoverable from what came before, and the promise has to be kept.

form.pattern: one / ones for a noun · do, does, did, do so for a verb phrase · so / not for a whole clause
notes: one and ones need something to stand for: the small loaf, the fresh ones
the leftover auxiliary must match the kind of verb it replaces: cycle takes do, is takes is, has finished takes has
so and not follow think, hope, believe, expect and suppose: I hope so, I think not
after and, but, or and than, English deletes whatever is identical: Halima can drive and her brother cannot
form.negative: The negative lives on the leftover auxiliary: some cafés take cards and some do not.
form.question: Ask whether your reader can put the missing words back word for word. If not, put them back yourself.

left.text: I took the small loaf because the small loaf was fresher.

right.role: the repeat swapped for a placeholder
right.text: I took the small loaf because that one was fresher.

spec.caption: English does not repeat. It leaves a marker where the repeat would have gone.

worked_example.sentence: Some canteens still cook from scratch; most no longer do.
worked_example.why_this_form: Do stands in for cook from scratch, so the second half is four words long and the contrast between the two groups lands without anything in the way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Most no longer cook from scratch repeats three words the reader already holds and buries the contrast somewhere in the middle of them.

notice_set.sentence: Some of the cafés take cards; the older ones don't.
notice_set.question: Can you pay by card in the older cafés?
notice_set.why: Don't is standing in for don't take cards, and the words it replaces are only two clauses back.

notice_set.sentence: Halima said the market would be open, and I hope so.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether it is open?
notice_set.why: So stands in for the whole clause about the market, and hoping is what you do when you have no information.

notice_set.sentence: The big supermarkets deliver; the corner shop does too.
notice_set.question: Does the corner shop deliver?
notice_set.why: Does carries the whole of deliver across, and too adds the corner shop to the group.

notice_set.sentence: I asked for the brown loaf, but they'd sold the last one.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker get the brown loaf?
notice_set.why: One stands in for brown loaf, and the last one being sold means there was none left.

notice_set.sentence: Neither of the cafés opens before eight, and nor does the bakery.
notice_set.question: Can you buy bread at half past seven?
notice_set.why: Nor does carries the negative across to the bakery without repeating a single word of it.

teach.rule_line: Leave a word out only when your reader can rebuild it exactly.
teach.false_rule: That leaving words out looks careless and repeating them is the safe option. Repetition is what makes a paragraph read like a machine.

errors.wrong: There were two loaves left and I took the fresher.
errors.right: There were two loaves left and I took the fresher one.
