errors.why_it_happens: In a great many languages an adjective can stand on its own as a noun. English needs a placeholder in that slot and the learner has no reason to suspect it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: one.
errors.l1_note: Common for speakers of Spanish, Italian, French, German and Russian.

errors.wrong: Some people cook every night and some are not.
errors.right: Some people cook every night and some do not.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reaches for the auxiliary they use most rather than the one that matches the verb being replaced, and cook is not a be verb, so nothing can be borrowed from it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes do.

errors.wrong: She said she would bring the bread, and I hope it.
errors.right: She said she would bring the bread, and I hope so.
errors.why_it_happens: It is the all-purpose placeholder in most learners' English, so it turns up wherever something has to be stood in for. So is the one that carries a whole clause, and it is the only one that will.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: it becomes so.

errors.wrong: I don't think the rules will change, and neither my colleagues.
errors.right: I don't think the rules will change, and neither do my colleagues.
errors.why_it_happens: Neither feels like a complete link on its own, and in several languages it is. English wants an auxiliary after it and then the subject, in that order.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: do.

pays_in.note: It keeps a comparison short enough to finish inside one breath.
pays_in.model: Older shoppers still use the market; younger ones mostly don't.

pays_in.note: It removes the repetition that makes a body paragraph read like a list.
pays_in.model: Some countries tax sugary drinks heavily; others have declined to do so.

pays_in.note: A short answer is often nothing but an auxiliary, with the meaning further back.
pays_in.model: The morning session does, but the afternoon one doesn't.

used_in.quote: This prompt sets two groups of schools against each other, and the second half of every comparison is where the words drop out.

payload.sentence: The northern schools kept their kitchens; the southern ones did not.
payload.question: Do the southern schools have kitchens?

feedback.why_key: Did not is carrying keep their kitchens across the semicolon, so the southern schools gave theirs up.
feedback.feed_forward: Rebuild the missing words from the clause before.

payload.sentence: I wanted the seeded rolls but they only had the plain ones.
payload.question: What did the speaker end up with?

feedback.why_key: Ones stands in for rolls, so plain ones is the only thing the shop had, whatever the speaker wanted.
feedback.feed_forward: Read ones as the noun from earlier in the sentence.

payload.context: Two people talking about who cooks at home.
payload.sentence: I cook most evenings and my brother is too.
reasons: the leftover word does not match the verb it is standing in for
the placeholder should be a noun
too should be at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Cook has no be in it, so there is no is to leave behind. The verb that stands in for it is does.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the leftover auxiliary to the verb it replaces.

payload.context: From a paragraph comparing two kinds of school meal.
payload.stem: Both menus were cheap, but the cooked ___ was better balanced.

expected: one

feedback.why_key: Menus is already on the page, so English wants a placeholder rather than the noun again, and it will not accept the adjective on its own.
feedback.feed_forward: Put one after an adjective that is standing for a noun.

payload.context: Two colleagues comparing their weekends.
payload.stem: I swim on Saturdays and Marek ___ too, though he goes much earlier.

expected: does

feedback.why_key: Swim needs a do form to stand in for it, and Marek is one person, so the ending goes on.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the auxiliary from the verb, then fix the ending.

payload.given: Some councils have banned fast food outlets near schools. Most councils have not banned fast food outlets near schools.
payload.instruction: Write the second sentence again without repeating anything.

expected: have not
have not, however
councils have not

feedback.why_key: Everything after have is identical, so the reader can rebuild all of it and none of it needs writing out.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete everything the previous sentence already supplied.

payload.context: Talking about a childhood street.

expected: my parents grew vegetables and so did everyone on the street

feedback.why_key: So and the auxiliary come first and the subject follows them, which is the one place in a plain sentence where that order is required.
feedback.feed_forward: Put so, then the auxiliary, then the subject.

payload.audio_text: Some of them deliver and some of them don't, honestly.

expected: some of them deliver and some of them don't, honestly
some of them deliver and some of them do not honestly
some of them deliver and some of them dont honestly

feedback.why_key: The whole of the second half is carried by one contracted word, and if you miss it the sentence says the opposite.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a single stressed auxiliary at the end of a clause.

payload.sentence: The trust does not publish waiting times, and neither the private clinics.

expected: and neither do the private clinics
nor do the private clinics

feedback.why_key: Neither carries the negative but it cannot carry the verb as well. Do has to arrive before the subject to finish the job.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow neither and nor with an auxiliary, then the subject.

items.decision_cue: some have declined to do so

payload.context: From a passage about how governments respond to a rise in food prices.
payload.sentence: Several governments have capped the price of staples, though some have declined to do so.
reasons: do so has nothing to stand for
the wrong auxiliary has been chosen
the two halves should be separate sentences
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Do so is standing in for cap the price of staples, which is six words back and rebuildable exactly, so the promise is kept.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the shortening when the missing words are recoverable.

payload.prompt_text: Some schools teach children to cook and some have dropped it. Write one sentence comparing the two groups without repeating the verb.

feedback.why_key: The second half of a comparison is where repetition piles up, and it is also where it is easiest to remove.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first half fully, then delete every repeated word.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on cooking lessons in schools. Find any noun or verb you have written twice within three lines and remove the second one. Then read the paragraph aloud and check nothing has gone missing. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Reading it aloud is the test that matters: if a listener can rebuild the missing words, so can a reader.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the second copy, then read the paragraph aloud.

title: Choosing a linking word by what it means and by where it is allowed to stand

point_json.grammar_name: Connectors grouped by function and by grammatical class

teach.can_do: I can pick a linking word that says the right thing and put it where English allows it to stand.
teach.why_it_matters: Half of all linking-word errors are not about meaning at all. The writer picked the right relation and then put the word somewhere it is not allowed to go.
teach.meaning: A linking word does two separate jobs at once, and learners are usually only taught one of them. The first is the relation: does the next idea add, contrast, explain, follow from or qualify what came before? The second is grammatical: some of these words join two clauses inside one sentence, some open a fresh sentence and point back at the last one, and some take a noun and nothing else. Getting the relation right and the class wrong still breaks the sentence.

form.pattern: joins two clauses: because, although, while, whereas, so that · opens a sentence: however, therefore, in addition, even so · takes a noun: despite, because of, in spite of
notes: the joining kind can start the sentence or sit in the middle: although it rained, we went / we went although it rained
the sentence-opening kind needs a full stop or a semicolon in front of it, and usually a comma after
the noun kind will not accept a clause: despite the cost, never despite it cost
and, but, so and or join two clauses and stay between them
form.negative: The negative belongs inside a clause, not on the linking word: although the clinic did not close, hours were cut.
form.question: First ask what the relation is. Then ask what the word is standing next to: a clause, or a noun?

left.role: joins two clauses inside one sentence
left.text: although · because · while · whereas · so that

right.role: opens a new sentence and points back
right.text: however · therefore · in addition · even so

spec.caption: The relation is only half the choice. The other half is what the word is allowed to stand beside.

worked_example.sentence: The clinic opened a late surgery because so many of its patients work full time.
worked_example.why_this_form: Because joins the two clauses inside one sentence, so the reason and the decision arrive as a single idea rather than as two facts placed side by side.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Because of expects a noun and nothing else. Write because of so many patients work and the sentence falls over at the word work.

notice_set.sentence: The surgery stays open late because most of its patients work.
notice_set.question: Why does the surgery stay open late?
notice_set.why: Because always points backwards from the result to the reason, and the reason is the half that follows it.

notice_set.sentence: Most patients work; therefore the surgery stays open late.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Therefore points forwards, so the half before it is the cause and the half after it is what followed.

notice_set.sentence: Although the surgery stays open late, few patients come in after six.
notice_set.question: Do many people use the late hours?
notice_set.why: Although warns you that the second half will not be what the first half led you to expect.

notice_set.sentence: The surgery stays open late despite the cost.
notice_set.question: Is the late opening expensive?
notice_set.why: Despite concedes something real. The cost is a fact the sentence is pushing past, not a fact it doubts.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer patients now miss appointments. In addition, the waiting list has shortened.
notice_set.question: How many improvements are mentioned?
notice_set.why: In addition promises another item of the same kind, so the second sentence has to be a separate piece of good news.

teach.rule_line: Choose the relation first, then check what the word is allowed to stand next to.
teach.false_rule: That however, but and although are three ways of saying one thing. They mean the same and stand in three different places, which is why swapping them breaks sentences.

errors.wrong: Despite the clinic was full, nobody waited more than ten minutes.
errors.right: Although the clinic was full, nobody waited more than ten minutes.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although carry the same relation, so whichever comes to mind first gets used. Despite is only allowed in front of a noun, and a whole clause has just turned up behind it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.

errors.wrong: The waiting list has shortened, however the staff shortage is worse than ever.
errors.right: The waiting list has shortened; however, the staff shortage is worse than ever.
errors.why_it_happens: However does the same job as but, so it feels like a joining word. It is not one, and neither is the comma, which leaves two whole sentences with nothing holding them together.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into a semicolon.

errors.wrong: The trust closed two clinics. As a result, demand had been rising for years.
errors.right: Demand had been rising for years. As a result, the trust closed two clinics.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner can see that the two facts belong together and reaches for a connecting phrase without checking which way it points. As a result always runs from the cause to what followed it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one pair of sentences.

errors.wrong: Although the surgery stays open late, but few patients come in after six.
errors.right: Although the surgery stays open late, few patients come in after six.
errors.why_it_happens: Several languages mark both halves of a contrast, so leaving one half unmarked feels unfinished. English marks it once and reads the second marker as a stutter.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Chinese, Vietnamese and Turkish.

pays_in.note: Every body paragraph needs a reason and a contrast, correctly placed.
pays_in.model: Although the scheme cut traffic in the centre, it pushed the queues onto the ring road.

pays_in.note: The connector tells you whether the next sentence agrees or turns.
pays_in.model: The trial was halted early. Even so, the results were published in full.

pays_in.note: A lecture signals its shape with these, and the answers follow the signals.
pays_in.model: Now, having dealt with the causes, I want to turn to what can be done.

used_in.quote: A problem and solution answer is a chain of causes and consequences, so every join in it is one of these words.
The talk marks each new section with a connector, and two answers depend on hearing which one arrived.

payload.sentence: The pool closed for repairs. Consequently, the swimming club moved to Marlow.
payload.question: Why did the club move?

feedback.why_key: Consequently runs forwards from a cause, so whatever came before it is the reason for what comes after.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the connector as an arrow and check which way it points.

payload.sentence: Even though the gym is free for staff, hardly anybody uses it.
payload.question: Do many staff use the gym?

feedback.why_key: Even though warns you that the second half will go against what the first half sets up, so free does not lead to popular.
feedback.feed_forward: Expect the turn when a sentence opens with a concession.

payload.context: From a first draft about university costs.
payload.sentence: Despite the fees rose again in 2022, applications went up.
reasons: this word cannot have a whole clause after it
the relation between the two halves is the wrong way round
the two halves need a full stop between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The meaning is right and the class is wrong. Despite takes a noun, and the fees rose again is a clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap to although when a clause follows.

payload.context: From a paragraph about sitting all day at work.
payload.stem: ___ the health warnings, most office jobs still involve eight hours in a chair.

expected: despite
in spite of

feedback.why_key: The health warnings is a noun phrase with no verb in it, so only the noun-taking word will fit in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for a verb before you choose the word.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a river clean-up at Verdon.
payload.stem: Farm run-off has fallen sharply. ___, fish have returned to the upper river.

expected: as a result
consequently
therefore

feedback.why_key: The first sentence is the cause and the second is what followed, so the word between them has to point forwards.
feedback.feed_forward: Name which half is the cause before you choose.

payload.given: Despite the high cost, the trust kept the late surgery open.
payload.instruction: Say the same thing using a word that takes a whole clause.

expected: the cost was high, the trust kept the late surgery open
it was expensive, the trust kept the late surgery open
the cost was high the trust kept the late surgery open

feedback.why_key: Once the word takes clauses, the noun has to grow a verb, and the high cost becomes the cost was high.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the noun a verb when you switch to although.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a free sports club.

expected: although the club charges nothing, very few children join

feedback.why_key: One word marks the contrast and the second half carries no marker at all, which is what English expects.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the contrast once and leave the other half bare.

payload.audio_text: The clinic's moved, so we'll have to book earlier from now on.

expected: the clinic's moved, so we'll have to book earlier from now on
the clinic has moved so we will have to book earlier from now on
the clinics moved so well have to book earlier from now on

feedback.why_key: So is one unstressed syllable and it is carrying the entire relation between the two halves of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small word at the join of two clauses.

payload.sentence: The new flats filled within a month, however the rents rose again in the spring.

expected: ; however, the rents rose
. however, the rents rose
, but the rents rose

feedback.why_key: However points backwards but joins nothing, so the two halves need either a stronger mark or a word that really does join.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the comma to a semicolon, or swap however for but.

items.decision_cue: In spite of this, the shops that survived

payload.context: From a passage about a town centre after a retail park opened.
payload.sentence: Two thirds of the units on the main street stood empty by 2021. In spite of this, the shops that survived reported steady trade.
reasons: the relation between the two sentences is the wrong way round
this phrase cannot come at the start of a sentence
the two sentences should be joined with a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Empty units would normally predict weak trade, and the second sentence goes against that, which is exactly what the phrase promises.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the connector when the second half really does turn.

payload.prompt_text: Free exercise classes were offered at a local sports centre and hardly anybody came. Write one sentence about it, and pick a linking word that can sit in front of a subject and a verb.

feedback.why_key: The contrast is real and the only decision left is whether the word you chose can sit in front of a clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that a subject and a verb follow your linking word.

payload.prompt_text: Open your problem and solution answer on the sedentary working day. Underline every linking word and, for each one, write C if it joins two clauses, S if it opens a sentence and N if it needs a noun. Fix any that are in the wrong place. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Sorting your own linking words into three classes takes two minutes and finds errors that reading for meaning never will.
feedback.feed_forward: Label each linking word by class before you reread for sense.

title: Knowing when a linking word earns its place and when it costs you

point_json.grammar_name: Linker restraint: cohesion built into the sentence rather than bolted onto it

teach.can_do: I can tell when a linking word is doing real work and when it is only announcing that I know some linking words.
teach.why_it_matters: Stacking linkers is the single clearest sign of a memorised answer. It lowers the impression of your writing while feeling, as you do it, like an improvement.
teach.meaning: A linking word is a road sign. Its job is to stop a reader taking the wrong turning, and where there is only one turning it is clutter. Most connections between sentences are already carried by what the sentences say: a cause looks like a cause, a contrast looks like a contrast. Real cohesion comes from ordering ideas so each one grows out of the last, from pointing back with a noun, and from joining clauses. A sign nailed on afterwards is not the same thing.

form.pattern: add a marker only where a careful reader might otherwise join the ideas wrongly
notes: one signposted relation per two or three sentences is plenty in a short answer
never open more than one sentence in a paragraph with the same kind of marker
prefer the joins that live inside a sentence: although, because, which, and a noun that points back
if the sentence before already makes the relation obvious, the marker is only telling the reader what they know
form.negative: Not every contrast needs marking: two sentences that plainly disagree already disagree.
form.question: Cover the linking word. Does the paragraph still say the same thing? Then it was not doing anything.

spec.label: how much work is this linking word actually doing?

steps.gloss: three ways of saying keep reading; almost never needed
useful once in a long answer, ruinous once per sentence
earn their place when the turn would genuinely surprise a reader
the relation is built into the sentence, where nobody can skip it

worked_example.sentence: Rents in the capital doubled in a decade. Younger workers moved out to towns like Ashfield, where a flat still costs half as much.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second sentence follows from the first because of what it says. Nothing needs announcing when the content already points in one direction.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with therefore would tell the reader something they had already worked out, and would quietly suggest you did not trust them to do it.

notice_set.sentence: Wages have not risen since 2015. Rents over the same period have gone up by a third.
notice_set.question: Are people better or worse off than they were?
notice_set.why: Nothing announced the contrast and you found it anyway, because the two facts do that work between them.

notice_set.sentence: Firstly, wages have stalled. Secondly, rents have risen. Thirdly, transport costs more. Moreover, food is dearer.
notice_set.question: Would you have known these were four separate points without the numbering?
notice_set.why: Four full stops already told you there were four points. The numbering repeats what the punctuation had covered.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme cost forty million pounds. It cut journey times by nine minutes.
notice_set.question: Which two numbers is the writer inviting you to weigh against each other?
options: the cost against the time saved
notice_set.why: Setting a very large figure beside a very small one is an argument, and no word had to make it.

notice_set.sentence: Many governments have promised to cut emissions. Few have met the targets they set themselves.
notice_set.question: Have the promises been kept?
notice_set.why: The turn is inside what the second sentence says, and a reader takes it without needing to be warned.

notice_set.sentence: Visitor numbers have risen every year. However, visitor spending has risen too.
notice_set.question: Do the two sentences disagree with each other?
notice_set.why: The word promised a turn that never came, so the reader spends a second hunting for a disagreement that is not there.

teach.rule_line: Add a linking word only when a reader could take the wrong relation without it.
teach.false_rule: That more linking words show better organisation. They show that the ideas underneath were never organised.

errors.wrong: Firstly, tourism creates jobs. Secondly, it brings money in. Moreover, it funds restoration. Furthermore, it raises the town's profile.
errors.right: Tourism creates jobs and brings money into a town with little other income. Some of that money funds restoration, and the town's profile rises with it.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told that linking words show cohesion, so more of them ought to show more of it. What they show is four sentences that were never joined in any other way, and taking the markers out is what forces the joining to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete four words: Firstly, Secondly, Moreover and Furthermore.

errors.wrong: In conclusion, to sum up, it is clear that tourism brings both benefits and problems.
errors.right: On balance, tourism brings more to a small town than it takes away.
errors.why_it_happens: Two closing phrases were memorised separately as the way to finish, so both arrive. Together they announce the ending twice and say nothing at all about the argument.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: to sum up.

errors.wrong: Although tourism creates jobs, however most of them last only four months.
errors.right: Although tourism creates jobs, most of them last only four months.
errors.why_it_happens: The contrast has already been marked once at the front, but the second half feels unmarked to a writer whose first language marks both ends of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: however.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Chinese, Turkish and Vietnamese.

errors.wrong: Visitor numbers have risen every year. However, visitor spending has also risen.
errors.right: Visitor numbers have risen every year, and spending has risen with them.
errors.why_it_happens: However has been stored as the word that joins two sentences rather than as the word that warns of a turn. Here nothing turns, so the reader stops and looks for a disagreement.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: however becomes and.

pays_in.note: A stack of memorised openers is the loudest signal of a rehearsed answer.
pays_in.model: Cheap flights opened the coast to weekend visitors, and the town has been rebuilt around them.

pays_in.note: A long turn stacked with markers sounds rehearsed rather than fluent.
pays_in.model: The flat was tiny, so we spent most of our time out on the balcony.

pays_in.note: Good writing links by content, which is what makes summary questions hard.
pays_in.model: Rents doubled in a decade. Younger workers left for the towns along the line.

used_in.quote: An advantages and disadvantages answer invites a list, and a list invites four memorised openers in a row.

payload.sentence: Factories moved abroad through the 1990s. The town lost two thirds of its manufacturing jobs in fifteen years.
payload.question: Why did the town lose the jobs?

feedback.why_key: You read the cause straight off the content. No word had to point at it, and adding one would have told you what you already had.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the content has already made the relation plain.

payload.sentence: Firstly the hotel was lovely, and secondly the beach was quiet, and moreover the food was excellent.
payload.question: How does this speaker come across?
options: as though they are reading a list they prepared
as though they are describing something they remember
as though they disliked the holiday

feedback.why_key: Three markers in one breath announce that the answer was assembled beforehand, which is the opposite of what a long turn is meant to sound like.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the numbering and let one detail lead to the next.

items.decision_cue: Furthermore, teaching in English also attracts

payload.context: From a body paragraph about degrees taught in English.
payload.sentence: Teaching in English opens a course to students from anywhere. Furthermore, teaching in English also attracts staff from abroad.
reasons: the marker adds nothing that the second sentence was not already saying
the marker points the relation the wrong way
the two sentences should be joined by a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Also is already inside the sentence doing that job, so the opener is the second sign on the same road.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the opener when the sentence already signals addition.

payload.given: Firstly, container shipping made distance cheap. Secondly, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest.
payload.instruction: Write this as one sentence with the relation built into it.

expected: container shipping made distance cheap, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest
shipping made distance cheap, factories moved to wherever labour was cheapest

feedback.why_key: Once carries the whole relation inside the sentence, so neither number is needed and the two facts become one idea.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace two openers with one joining word inside the sentence.

payload.given: The town gets two million visitors a year. Moreover, it has only nine hundred residents.
payload.instruction: Rewrite this as one sentence and let the figures do the work.

expected: nine hundred residents takes two million visitors a year
nine hundred people takes two million visitors a year
nine hundred residents receives two million visitors a year

feedback.why_key: Putting the two numbers in one sentence makes the contrast unmissable, which is more than any opener could have done for it.
feedback.feed_forward: Let two figures sit side by side and delete the marker.

payload.context: The paragraph has already given three reasons why small exporters struggle. This is the last sentence of it.
payload.stem: ___ these pressures, a handful of firms in Brackenfield have doubled their overseas sales.

expected: despite
in spite of

feedback.why_key: This is a genuine turn after three sentences going the other way, which is exactly the situation in which a marker earns its place.
feedback.feed_forward: Save the marker for the sentence that actually turns.

payload.context: Build one sentence. Mark the contrast once and only once.

expected: while the festival draws crowds, few of them stay overnight

feedback.why_key: The contrast is marked at the front and the second half carries nothing, which is the shape English wants.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark a contrast at one end only and then stop.

payload.audio_text: It rained all week, so we've booked somewhere inland this time.

expected: it rained all week, so we've booked somewhere inland this time
it rained all week so we have booked somewhere inland this time
it rained all week so weve booked somewhere inland this time

feedback.why_key: One unstressed syllable does the whole job here, which is what natural cohesion sounds like when nobody is performing it.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how small the join is when the content already fits.

payload.sentence: Although foreign firms brought work to the district, but however these jobs paid less than the ones lost.

expected: these jobs

feedback.why_key: Although at the front has already marked the contrast. Two more markers behind it say the same thing twice and hold up the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete every marker after the first one.

items.decision_cue: Even so, the paper kept its Sunday edition

payload.context: The three sentences before this one all described falling print sales.
payload.sentence: Even so, the paper kept its Sunday edition and hired two more reporters.
reasons: the marker adds nothing the content did not already carry
the phrase sends the reader in the wrong direction
two markers are doing the same job
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Three sentences of decline set up an expectation, and this sentence breaks it, so the reader genuinely needs the warning.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the marker when the sentence goes against what came before.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why a small exporter might struggle to sell abroad. Use no sentence-opening linking word at all, and make each sentence grow out of the one before it.

feedback.why_key: Taking the signs away forces the ordering to do the work, and ordering is what cohesion actually is.
feedback.feed_forward: Begin each sentence with something the sentence before mentioned.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on English-medium degrees. Cross out every sentence-opening linking word, then read the paragraph. Put back only the ones whose absence made you stumble. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Most of them will not go back in, and the paragraph will read faster and sound less rehearsed for their absence.
feedback.feed_forward: Restore only the markers whose loss you actually noticed.

title: Starting a sentence with what the reader already has and ending with the news

teach.can_do: I can order a sentence so it begins with something my reader already holds and ends with the part they do not.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the reason some paragraphs read as one argument and others as a pile of true sentences. It is also the real reason the passive exists.
teach.meaning: A reader is always holding something from the sentence before. English expects the next sentence to start from that and to put the new part at the end, where the voice falls and the weight lands. When a sentence opens with a brand-new noun, the reader has to hold it up in the air until they find out what it has to do with anything. Do that four times in a paragraph and the paragraph stops joining up, whatever linking words you nail onto it.

form.pattern: old information + verb + new information
notes: a pronoun or the plus a known noun is the cheapest way to open from what is already there
the passive exists partly for this: it lets the known thing take the front and pushes the doer to the end
there is and there are exist to bring something in for the first time, which is why they cannot open with the
the last few words of a sentence are the loudest, so put there whatever you want remembered
form.negative: The rule survives the negative: what is known still comes first, and the denial lands at the end.
form.question: Look at the first four words of your sentence. Did your reader already have them?

ends: what the reader has not been told yet

marks.label: the subject slot: known things live here
the verb, carrying you across
the end of the sentence: the news lands here

worked_example.sentence: The council opened a new footbridge in March. It was paid for out of the parking surplus.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second sentence starts from something the first one handed over and ends with the part nobody knew, so the paragraph moves forward instead of starting again.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with the parking surplus puts a brand-new noun in the first four words and leaves the reader holding it until the sentence finally explains itself.

notice_set.sentence: The trust bought the old mill in 2019. It has stood empty ever since.
notice_set.question: What has stood empty?
notice_set.why: The second sentence opens from the thing the first one has just handed over, so there is nothing to work out.

notice_set.sentence: Rents doubled between 2013 and 2023. The sharpest rise came in the last two years.
notice_set.question: When did rents rise fastest?
notice_set.why: The news sits at the end of the sentence, which is where the weight falls and where a reader looks for it.

notice_set.sentence: There is a new bus shelter outside the surgery.
notice_set.question: Had the listener heard about the shelter before?
notice_set.why: There is exists to bring something into a conversation for the first time, so it announces that this is new.

notice_set.sentence: The shelter outside the surgery has been vandalised twice this year.
notice_set.question: Had the listener heard about the shelter before?
notice_set.why: Opening with the shelter treats it as shared property, which only works if the listener already has it.

notice_set.sentence: Two of the blocks are coming down. Asbestos in the stairwells is the reason.
notice_set.question: Which part of the second sentence is the news?
notice_set.why: The news has been put at the front, which is why the sentence reads slightly backwards even though nothing in it is wrong.

teach.rule_line: Start with what your reader already has. Finish with what they do not.
teach.false_rule: That the most important idea should come first so nobody misses it. English puts its weight at the end of a sentence, not at the beginning.

errors.wrong: The footbridge was opened by the council in March, and the parking surplus was used by them to pay for it.
errors.right: The council opened the footbridge in March and paid for it out of the parking surplus.
errors.why_it_happens: The passive has been learned as the formal option and goes in everywhere. Here the council is the thing the paragraph is already about, so pushing it to the end hides the one familiar noun in the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one verb: was opened becomes opened.

errors.wrong: The survey report on the stairwells was buried for two years.
errors.right: The housing department buried the survey report on the stairwells for two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The passive lets you leave the doer out, and a writer who has been told that formal English avoids naming people leaves everybody out. Here who did it is the entire point of the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one agent: by the housing department.

errors.wrong: Rents in Ashfield doubled in a decade. However, a two-bedroom flat now costs more than a house did in 2015.
errors.right: Rents in Ashfield doubled in a decade. A two-bedroom flat now costs more than a house did in 2015.
errors.why_it_happens: The flat price is new information arriving in a new sentence, and new information feels as though it needs announcing. It does not: it already grows out of the rent rise, and however tells the reader to brace for a disagreement that never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: however.

pays_in.note: A chart description that restarts every sentence is exhausting to read.
pays_in.model: Coal supplied a third of the total in 2000. By 2020 that share had fallen to a twentieth.

pays_in.note: It is why a paragraph reads as one argument rather than five true facts.
pays_in.model: Most new flats are built for sale. Those that are not go to housing associations.

pays_in.note: Matching-information questions turn on which idea a sentence starts from.
pays_in.model: The scheme was extended in 2019. Two years later it was quietly dropped.

used_in.quote: The answer moves from a problem to a cause to a remedy, and each step has to start from the step before it.

payload.sentence: The estate was finished in 1974. Half of it was sold to private landlords twenty years later.
payload.question: Which part of the second sentence is the news?
options: sold to private landlords twenty years later

feedback.why_key: The estate is already on the page, so the fresh information is everything after the verb, where English lets it land.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the news in the last few words of a sentence.

payload.sentence: There's a leak in the ceiling of the back bedroom.
payload.question: Had the listener been told about the leak before?

feedback.why_key: There's is how English opens the door for something the listener has not met yet, so it marks the leak as fresh news.
feedback.feed_forward: Read there is as a door opening on something new.

items.decision_cue: A shortage of small units is the underlying cause

payload.context: The sentence before this one said that young people in Ashfield are staying at home into their thirties.
payload.sentence: A shortage of small units is the underlying cause.
reasons: the sentence opens with a noun the reader has not met yet
the doer of the action has been left out
the two sentences need a linking word between them
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A shortage of small units is brand-new, and the only familiar words, the underlying cause, have been left to the end where the news should have been.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the cause word and close with the shortage.

payload.given: Two of the tower blocks are coming down. Asbestos in the stairwells is the reason.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so it opens from what the reader already has.

expected: is asbestos in the stairwells
is asbestos in the stairwells.

feedback.why_key: A reason has already been implied by the first sentence, so it belongs at the front, and the asbestos lands at the end where it hits hardest.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the known word to the front and the news to the end.

payload.given: The samples arrived in March. A laboratory in Norland analysed them.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so it keeps the samples at the front.

expected: were analysed by a laboratory in norland
were analysed by a laboratory in Norland
were then analysed by a laboratory in norland

feedback.why_key: This is the honest reason for the passive: it lets the known thing keep the front of the sentence and sends the new laboratory to the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for the passive when the doer is the news.

payload.context: The paragraph has been describing a single housing scheme in Brackenfield.
payload.stem: ___ was finally approved in 2021, eight years after the first application.

expected: it
the scheme

feedback.why_key: The scheme is what the paragraph has been discussing, so it takes the front and the eight-year wait lands at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the noun the paragraph is already about.

payload.context: The sentence before said that terraced housing made up half the stock in 1990.

expected: that share had fallen to a fifth by 2020

feedback.why_key: That share reaches back to the half from the previous sentence, so the reader starts on solid ground and the new figure arrives last.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with a pointing word that reaches back one sentence.

payload.audio_text: It's been empty since the trust bought it in 2019.

expected: it's been empty since the trust bought it in 2019
it has been empty since the trust bought it in 2019
its been empty since the trust bought it in 2019

feedback.why_key: The sentence opens with two squashed syllables carrying old information, which is exactly why they are unstressed and easy to miss.
feedback.feed_forward: Expect the opening words to be small and already known.

items.decision_cue: The grant was withdrawn in June

payload.context: The paragraph is arguing that a particular department cannot be trusted with the money.
payload.sentence: The grant was withdrawn in June with no explanation.
reasons: the sentence leaves out the one thing the paragraph is trying to prove
the sentence opens with a noun nobody has met
the news has been put at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is about who is responsible, and this sentence quietly removes them. The passive is hiding the only thing being argued for.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the doer whenever your point is about who acted.

items.decision_cue: A private management company was appointed by the trust

payload.sentence: The trust took over the estate in 2016. A private management company was appointed by the trust to run it.
payload.error_span: A private management company was appointed by the trust

expected: it appointed a private management company
the trust appointed a private management company
it then appointed a private management company

feedback.why_key: The trust is already known and the company is new, so the sentence currently has them the wrong way round and the passive is what put them there.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the known noun first and drop the by phrase.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why first-time buyers struggle in a small town. Every sentence after the first must open with something the sentence before it gave you.

feedback.why_key: Once each sentence opens from the one before, you will find you no longer need a marker between them at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Copy one word from the end of each sentence into the start of the next.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on first homes. Underline the first four words of every sentence in one body paragraph and mark each one old or new. Rewrite any sentence that starts on something new. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Marking your own openings old or new takes two minutes and finds the disjointed paragraph that reading for meaning never catches.
feedback.feed_forward: Rewrite any sentence whose first four words are new.

title: Building the first sentence of a paragraph so the rest of it has a job

point_json.grammar_name: The grammar of a topic sentence

teach.can_do: I can open a paragraph with a claim that is narrow enough for the next four sentences to prove.
teach.why_it_matters: The first sentence sets the size of the job. Make the claim too big and nothing you write underneath it will be enough.
teach.meaning: A paragraph opener is a claim about a class of things, and its grammar shows that. The subject names the class rather than one example of it, so it is usually plural and usually has no the in front. The verb is present simple, because the claim is meant to hold generally rather than to report one occasion. And it carries a word that says how far the claim reaches, because a claim with no limit on it is the easiest thing in the world to knock down.

form.pattern: general noun phrase + present simple verb + a limit on how far the claim reaches
notes: the subject names the class: short prison sentences, community schemes, first offenders
the verb stays in the present simple even when your evidence is about the past
tend to, most, generally and rarely narrow the claim without weakening the writing
keep the example out of this sentence; it belongs in the next one
form.negative: A negative claim needs the same limit: short sentences rarely reduce crime, not short sentences never reduce crime.
form.question: Ask whether four sentences could prove what you have just written. If not, narrow it.

spec.label: how much of this claim could you actually defend?

steps.gloss: a whole essay's worth of claim in three words, and nothing below it can carry that
still absolute; one contrary case sinks the paragraph

steps.text: Community sentences tend to reduce reoffending among first offenders.
steps.gloss: narrow enough that four sentences can hold it up

worked_example.sentence: Short prison sentences tend to make reoffending more likely rather than less.
worked_example.why_this_form: The subject names the class the paragraph is about, the verb is general because the claim is general, and tend to leaves room for the cases that go the other way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Short prison sentences made reoffending more likely would report one particular occasion, and a paragraph under it would have nothing left to prove.

notice_set.sentence: Community sentences tend to work better for first offenders.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is true in every case?
notice_set.why: Tend to admits the exceptions in advance, which is what stops one contrary case from sinking the paragraph.

notice_set.sentence: Community sentences work better for first offenders.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is true in every case?
notice_set.why: With no limit on it, the claim covers every first offender everywhere, and the writer has to defend all of them.

notice_set.sentence: Last year the Marlow scheme cut reoffending by a fifth.
notice_set.question: Is this about schemes in general or about one of them?
notice_set.why: A named scheme and a named year make this an example, and an example is what a paragraph offers second, not first.

notice_set.sentence: Most magistrates prefer to keep first offenders out of custody.
notice_set.question: Do all magistrates prefer this?
notice_set.why: Most says the majority and quietly concedes the rest, which is exactly the amount a paragraph can carry.

notice_set.sentence: Prison costs the taxpayer far more than supervision in the community.
notice_set.question: What will the rest of the paragraph be about?
options: the cost of the two options
notice_set.why: The claim names cost, so cost is the debt the paragraph now owes its reader.

teach.rule_line: Name the class, keep the verb general, and leave the example for the next sentence.
teach.false_rule: That an opening claim should be as strong as you can make it. A claim you cannot defend in four sentences costs more than it earns.

errors.wrong: Prison never reduces crime.
errors.right: Long prison sentences rarely reduce crime on their own.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told to state a clear position, and never feels clearer than usually does. It is also the one word a reader can disprove with a single case, after which the whole paragraph is defending the indefensible.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: never becomes rarely.

errors.wrong: Everybody agrees that community sentences are better for society.
errors.right: Community sentences have wide support among magistrates and probation staff.
errors.why_it_happens: Everybody agrees has been memorised as a confident opening. It makes a claim about the entire world, which one disagreeing voice destroys, and it says nothing about who actually holds the view.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: everybody agrees that.

errors.wrong: Firstly, the first advantage of community sentences is that they are cheaper.
errors.right: Community sentences cost the state far less than custody.
errors.why_it_happens: Two openers and a scaffolding phrase have each been memorised as the way to begin, so all three arrive, and the actual claim starts seven words into the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: the first advantage of.

errors.wrong: This is a serious problem in many countries.
errors.right: Overcrowding in prisons is a serious problem in many countries.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has the topic in their head from reading the prompt, so this feels anchored to them. On the page it is the first sentence of a paragraph and there is nothing behind it to point at.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for its noun: this becomes overcrowding.

pays_in.note: The first sentence of a paragraph decides what the rest has to do.
pays_in.model: Short custodial sentences tend to break up work and housing without reducing crime.

pays_in.note: Heading-matching questions are usually answered by one sentence per paragraph.
pays_in.model: Community supervision has expanded steadily since the 1990s.

pays_in.note: An answer that opens with a limited claim has somewhere to go next.
pays_in.model: On the whole, tougher sentences change what people are given rather than what they do.

used_in.quote: Each body paragraph on this prompt lives or dies on whether its first sentence is a claim or a stray fact.

feedback.feed_forward: Place the limiting word directly before the verb.

they are far more likely to reoffend within the first year
theyre far more likely to reoffend within the first year

feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the words that measure how far a claim goes.

payload.sentence: In 2019 the Ashfield club opened its pitches to two local primary schools.
reasons: it reports one occasion instead of making a claim about a class
the claim has no limit on it
the opening word points at nothing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A named club and a named year make this an example. An example is the second sentence of a paragraph, and it needs a claim above it to be an example of.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the example down and write the claim above it.

feedback.why_key: The size of this sentence is the size of the debt you take on, and a smaller debt is easier to pay off in four lines.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the claim, then ask what would disprove it.

feedback.why_key: Reading only your openers is the fastest structural check there is, and it takes less than a minute in a real timed answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your opening sentences in sequence and check they cohere.

title: Turning something that happened into a thing you can then talk about

teach.can_do: I can turn something that happened into a thing, so that my next sentence can measure it, explain it or argue about it.
teach.why_it_matters: It lets a paragraph refer back to a whole event in three words, and it is the commonest source of wrong word endings.
teach.meaning: Prices rose is an event: it happens, and then it is over. The rise in prices is a thing: it can be sharp or gradual, it can have a cause, it can be the subject of the next sentence, and it can be counted. English lets you convert one into the other, and the conversion is what makes it possible to talk about an event rather than merely report it. The price is weight. Every conversion makes a sentence heavier.

form.pattern: verb or adjective + an ending + a preposition + the rest
notes: common endings: -tion, -ment, -al, -ure, -ance, -ness, -th, and sometimes no change at all
each of these nouns keeps a preposition, and it is not always the one the verb used: a rise in, a solution to, an increase in, a fall in
the conversion nearly always needs the or a in front of it once it becomes a thing
when you convert, the person who did it disappears unless you put them back with by or a possessive
form.negative: The negative usually converts too: they did not comply becomes their failure to comply.
form.question: Ask whether the next sentence needs to say something about the event itself. If so, make it a thing.

left.role: an event, which happens and is over
left.text: Fuel prices rose sharply last winter.

right.role: a thing, which can be measured and argued about
right.text: the sharp rise in fuel prices

spec.caption: Once it is a thing, it can be the subject of your next sentence, or be counted, or be blamed.

worked_example.sentence: Fuel prices rose sharply last winter. That rise pushed a fifth of rural households into arrears.
worked_example.why_this_form: Making the event into a thing lets the second sentence open from something the reader already holds and puts the new figure at the end, where the weight lands.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Because fuel prices rose sharply, a fifth of rural households fell behind says the same thing but opens on a marker rather than on the reader's own ground.

notice_set.sentence: The closure of the two branches was announced in March.
notice_set.question: Did the branches shut?
notice_set.why: What happened in March was the announcement. Whether the shutting itself has happened yet is left completely open.

notice_set.sentence: The two branches closed in March.
notice_set.question: Did the branches shut?
notice_set.why: As an event it is simply reported, and there is no announcement standing in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: There has been a sharp fall in the number of small savers.
notice_set.question: Are there more or fewer small savers than before?
notice_set.why: Fall carries the direction, and sharp measures it, which is something you cannot do to a verb without an adverb.

notice_set.sentence: Repayment of the loan begins in April.
notice_set.question: Who pays?
notice_set.why: Packing the action into a thing lets the writer leave the person out altogether, which is sometimes useful and sometimes evasive.

notice_set.sentence: The council's refusal to publish the figures surprised nobody.
notice_set.question: Were the figures published?
notice_set.why: The refusal is a thing that happened, and the possessive in front of it puts the council back in as the one who did it.

teach.rule_line: Make the event a thing when your next sentence needs to say something about it.
teach.false_rule: That these nouns make writing academic. They make a sentence heavier, and three in a row make it unreadable.

errors.wrong: There has been a steady improve in air quality since the depot shut.
errors.right: There has been a steady improvement in air quality since the depot shut.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows exactly which word they want and reaches for the shape they have met most often, which is the verb. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to them because the meaning arrived intact.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one ending: improve becomes improvement.

errors.wrong: The analyse of the figures took three weeks longer than expected.
errors.right: The analysis of the figures took three weeks longer than expected.
errors.why_it_happens: This pair changes more than an ending, so the usual pattern of adding something to the verb does not produce the right word and the learner has nothing else to fall back on.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one ending: analyse becomes analysis.

errors.wrong: The increase of rents has slowed since the spring.
errors.right: The increase in rents has slowed since the spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the default for anything belonging to anything, so it arrives first. These nouns each keep their own preposition and it is rarely predictable from the verb they came from.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: of becomes in.

errors.wrong: Rise in fuel prices has hit rural households hardest.
errors.right: The rise in fuel prices has hit rural households hardest.
errors.why_it_happens: The event felt like a general fact when it was a verb, and turning it into a thing does not change how it feels. English marks a particular, identified thing with the, and this one is particular.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Very common where the first language has no articles at all.

pays_in.note: It names a trend so that the next sentence can compare it with another.
pays_in.model: The fall in coal use was steeper than the rise in wind generation over the same period.

pays_in.note: It lets a sentence open from the event described in the one before.
pays_in.model: The removal of the subsidy has been blamed for most of the increase.

pays_in.note: Passages compress whole clauses into these, which is what makes them dense.
pays_in.model: Widespread adoption of the technique followed its approval in 2016.

used_in.quote: Describing shares of a budget means naming rises and falls as things, then setting them against each other.

payload.sentence: The withdrawal of the free bus pass affected about nine thousand people.
payload.question: Was the pass taken away?

feedback.why_key: The event has been packed into a thing, but the thing still describes something that took place and the sentence treats it as done.
feedback.feed_forward: Unpack the heavy noun back into a verb to check what happened.

payload.sentence: There's been a big drop in the number of people paying cash.
payload.question: Are more or fewer people paying cash?

feedback.why_key: Drop carries the direction on its own, and big measures it, which is why the thing can be sized in a way the event could not.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the heavy noun for direction before anything else.

payload.context: From a draft about household borrowing.
payload.sentence: The reduction of interest rates in 2021 encouraged people to borrow more.
reasons: this noun keeps a different small word after it
the ending on the noun is wrong
the word the should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Reduction takes in when it is measuring a change in something. Of would be right if the rates themselves were being reduced in number.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn the small word as part of the noun, not separately.

payload.context: From a description of a chart on household spending.
payload.stem: The steady ___ (decline) in cash payments continued throughout the period.

feedback.why_key: This one converts without changing at all, which is exactly why learners add an ending it does not want.

payload.context: From a paragraph about regional employment.

feedback.feed_forward: Store the noun and its small word together as one item.

payload.context: Build one sentence comparing two lines on a chart.

feedback.feed_forward: Convert both sides before you try to compare them.

payload.audio_text: There's been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing.

expected: there's been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing
there has been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing
theres been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing

feedback.why_key: The small words around the heavy noun are all unstressed, and they are the ones that go missing when a listener writes down only the content words.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the small words around the heavy noun first.

payload.sentence: Local firms objected to the develop of the waterfront on cost grounds.

expected: the development of the waterfront
the redevelopment of the waterfront

feedback.why_key: The slot after the wants a thing, and the verb has been dropped into it unchanged because it carried the right meaning already.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the noun ending whenever the word follows the or a.

feedback.feed_forward: Turn at least one of them back into a verb.

feedback.why_key: Two events cannot be compared inside one clause. Two things can, and that is the only reason to make the conversion here.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the small word after each noun before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Open your description of the council budget chart. Find one place where you reported a change twice and rewrite it so the second mention is a thing you then measure. Then count the heavy nouns in the sentence and cut it back to two. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: The conversion earns its place once per sentence. Beyond that it stops compressing anything and simply removes the verbs.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep at most two heavy nouns in any one sentence.

title: Loading detail onto a noun instead of writing three short sentences

teach.can_do: I can load several pieces of information onto one noun so that a sentence makes a single point rather than three.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complexity in English. A long noun phrase raises the level of a sentence with almost nothing in it that can break.
teach.meaning: A noun can carry a great deal before it and a great deal after it. In front go the determiner and the describing words. Behind go the small phrases and the clauses: by the harbour, with twelve rooms, that the guidebooks recommend, opened last spring. All of it belongs to one noun, and that noun is still the subject of the sentence, however far the verb has been pushed back. Filling this space is how a writer packs three facts into one sentence without stacking clauses.

form.pattern: determiner + describing words + NOUN + small phrase + clause
notes: before the noun, English fixes the order and nobody has to be taught it: a lovely old stone cottage, never a stone lovely old cottage
after the noun you can stack a small phrase and then a clause: the path along the cliff that floods at high tide
the verb agrees with the head noun, which is the one everything else is hanging on, not the nearest word to it
keep the items in a list the same shape as each other, or the reader has to start again halfway through
form.negative: The negative goes on the verb, not inside the phrase: the hostel by the harbour has not reopened.
form.question: Find the one word everything else is describing. That is the word the verb has to agree with.

rungs.text: the hostel
the hostel by the harbour
the cheap hostel by the harbour
the cheap hostel by the harbour that the guidebooks all recommend

spec.top_label: as much as one noun can carry

worked_example.sentence: The steady rise in weekend visitors that followed the new rail link has emptied the car parks by nine in the morning.
worked_example.why_this_form: Everything the reader needs about the rise is packed in before the verb, so the sentence makes one point instead of three and never has to name the rise twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry the same facts and would make the reader hold the rise in mind while the other two arrived and joined on.

notice_set.sentence: The hostel by the harbour that the guidebooks recommend is shut all winter.
notice_set.question: Is every hostel in the town shut all winter?
notice_set.why: One hostel has been picked out with two pieces of detail. What the others do is outside the sentence altogether.

notice_set.sentence: The number of visitors staying more than two nights has fallen since 2019.
notice_set.question: What has fallen?
notice_set.why: Everything after number is describing it, so number is the word the verb belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: Cheap flights from the northern cities have filled the town every August.
notice_set.question: Where do the flights come from?
notice_set.why: The small phrase after flights says where they start, and the town is where they end up.

notice_set.sentence: The path along the cliff above the old lifeboat station floods at high tide.
notice_set.question: What floods?
notice_set.why: Two small phrases have stacked up behind path, but path is still the thing the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: A converted warehouse with twelve rooms and a shared kitchen opened last spring.
notice_set.question: How many rooms does it have?
notice_set.why: The rooms and the kitchen are both hanging off warehouse, so both belong to the same building.

teach.rule_line: Pack the detail behind the noun and keep the verb agreeing with the noun itself.
teach.false_rule: That range means long sentences. Long noun phrases show range; long sentences with three clauses show how many ways there are to break one.

errors.wrong: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August have doubled.
errors.right: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August has doubled.
errors.why_it_happens: Eight words separate the noun from its verb, and the last thing in the writer's ear was towns in August. The verb copies whatever plural was nearest.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: Increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.right: The increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause behind the noun has already identified exactly which increase is meant, so the phrase feels complete. English still wants the word at the front that says the reader can now find it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for learners whose first language marks no articles.

errors.wrong: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and it has a long beach.
errors.right: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and a long beach.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer runs out of the list shape halfway through and finishes the third item as a fresh sentence, because by then they are thinking about the beach rather than about the list.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: it has.

pays_in.note: It names a category exactly, in one phrase rather than a sentence.
pays_in.model: The share of households with no car rose in every district outside the centre.

pays_in.note: Complexity you can risk, because so little of it can go wrong.
pays_in.model: Towns dependent on a single summer season have the least room to absorb a bad year.

pays_in.note: A long subject hides the verb, which is often exactly what the question tests.
pays_in.model: The decision to close the two smallest sites was taken without any consultation.
