title: Keeping everything in a list the same shape as everything else

teach.can_do: I can build a list where every item has the same shape, so my reader can take them in at one go.
teach.why_it_matters: Readers read a list by its pattern. Break the pattern in the third item and they go back to the beginning, which costs you far more than the words saved.
teach.meaning: When you join things with and, or, but or than, English expects the joined parts to be built the same way. Three nouns, or three -ing forms, or three whole clauses, but not two nouns and a clause. The shape is what tells a reader where each item ends and the next begins. When one item changes shape halfway through, the reader loses the thread and has to reread, and they will blame the sentence rather than themselves.

form.pattern: item + , + item + and / or + item, all built the same way
notes: the commonest break is the last item, because by then the writer is thinking about content and not about shape
the paired joiners are stricter still: both ... and, either ... or, not only ... but also, whether ... or
with the paired joiners, whatever follows the first half must match whatever follows the second
than and as are joiners too: better at running than at swimming, not better at running than to swim
form.negative: A negative list matches as well: the scheme covers neither travel nor equipment.
form.question: Read the joining word, then read each item on its own with the opening of the sentence. Do all of them fit?

left.role: the pattern breaks on the last item
left.text: fitness, concentration and it helps them sleep

right.text: fitness, concentration and sleep

spec.caption: A reader takes a list in by its shape. Change the shape and they start it again.

worked_example.sentence: The scheme pays for coaching, equipment and travel to away matches.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three nouns in a row let the reader take all three in one movement, because the shape itself says where each item begins and ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Coaching, equipment and it pays for travel turns the third item into a fresh sentence, and the reader goes back to check whether they missed something.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and transport to matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: Three items of the same shape, so the counting happens without any effort at all.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and it will take children to away matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: The third item has changed shape, so it no longer reads as part of the same list and the count comes apart.

notice_set.sentence: Children who play twice a week sleep better than those who play once.
notice_set.question: Which group sleeps better?
notice_set.why: Both sides of than are built the same way, so the comparison lines up and the answer falls out of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council will either build a new pool or refurbish the old one.
notice_set.question: How many of these will the council do?
notice_set.why: Either and or offer a choice of one, and the two matching verbs make it clear these are the two options.

notice_set.sentence: Not only does the club train children, but it also runs a holiday scheme.
notice_set.question: How many activities does the club run?
notice_set.why: The paired joiner promises a second item and delivers exactly one, in the same shape as the first.

teach.rule_line: Everything joined by and, or or than has to be built the same way.
teach.false_rule: That variety is a virtue, so items in a list should look different from one another. Variety belongs between sentences, never inside one list.

errors.wrong: The programme improves fitness, concentration and helps children sleep.
errors.right: The programme improves fitness and concentration, and helps children sleep.
errors.why_it_happens: By the third item the writer is thinking about what to say rather than about the shape they set up two items ago, and the sentence quietly changes gear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into and.

errors.wrong: Children learn more by playing regularly than to sit through a lesson about it.
errors.right: Children learn more by playing regularly than by sitting through a lesson about it.
errors.why_it_happens: Than feels like a link between two ideas rather than between two matching shapes, so the second half is built from scratch in whatever form comes to mind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one form: to sit becomes by sitting.

errors.wrong: The club offers coaching, to hire equipment and free travel.
errors.right: The club offers coaching, equipment hire and free travel.
errors.why_it_happens: The middle item arrives as an action rather than as a thing, because that is how the writer thought of it, and nothing forces it back into the shape of its neighbours.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one item: to hire equipment becomes equipment hire.

errors.wrong: Not only the club trains children but also it runs a holiday scheme.
errors.right: The club not only trains children but also runs a holiday scheme.
errors.why_it_happens: Not only has been learned as a phrase that opens a sentence, so it goes to the front. From there it takes a whole clause on each side and the two halves stop matching.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: not only goes after the club.

pays_in.note: Any sentence listing reasons or benefits is a list, and lists break.
pays_in.model: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and behaviour in the afternoon.

pays_in.note: Chart answers list categories, and the categories have to match.
pays_in.model: Spending rose in housing, transport and education, and fell in everything else.

pays_in.note: A long turn is mostly lists, and a broken list is audible.
pays_in.model: It was cheap, easy to get to and open until quite late.

used_in.quote: The benefits paragraph on this prompt is one long list, which is exactly where a shape starts to slip.

payload.sentence: The centre runs classes in swimming, judo and climbing.
payload.question: How many activities does the centre run classes in?

feedback.why_key: Three items of the same shape count themselves, and the reader never has to stop and work anything out.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the items by their shape, not by the commas.

payload.sentence: She's better at running long distances than at sprinting.
payload.question: Which does she do better?

feedback.why_key: Both sides of than open with at and a verb form, so the two halves line up and the comparison is unmistakable.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both sides of than start the same way.

payload.context: From a draft on school sport.
payload.sentence: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and it also builds confidence.
reasons: the last item is built differently from the first two
there are too many items in the list
the verb does not agree with the subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two nouns set up a pattern and the third item arrives as a whole clause, so the reader loses the list and has to go back to the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Make the last item match the shape of the first.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a village sports club.
payload.stem: The club depends on volunteers for coaching, fundraising and ___ (maintain) the pitches.

expected: maintaining

feedback.why_key: The first two items are -ing forms, so the third has to be one as well or the list changes gear on its last word.
feedback.feed_forward: Copy the shape of the first item into the last.

payload.given: The scheme pays for coaching. It pays for equipment. It also pays for travel to away matches.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence with all three items in the same shape.

expected: coaching, equipment and travel to away matches
coaching, equipment and travel

feedback.why_key: One verb serves all three items once they are the same shape, and the sentence drops from fifteen words to nine.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the verb once and hang matching items off it.

payload.given: Not only the college teaches languages but also it runs evening courses.
payload.instruction: Rewrite this so both halves match after the paired joiner.

expected: teaches languages but also runs evening courses
teaches languages, but also runs evening courses

feedback.why_key: With the subject in front, each half of the pair is now just a verb and its object, and the two halves finally match.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the subject first, then the paired joiner.

payload.context: Build one sentence about cheap ways of staying active.

expected: walking, cycling and swimming are all free or nearly free

feedback.why_key: Three -ing forms make one subject, and because they match, the verb after them can be a single word.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the shape with the first item and hold it.

payload.audio_text: It's cheap, easy to reach and open until ten.

expected: it's cheap, easy to reach and open until ten
it is cheap easy to reach and open until ten
its cheap easy to reach and open until ten

feedback.why_key: Three describing items hang off one squashed opening, and the and is the only signal that the list is about to close.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for and to know the list is ending.

items.decision_cue: and to reduce the cost of equipment

payload.sentence: The plan involves opening the pitches at weekends, training more volunteers and to reduce the cost of equipment.
payload.error_span: and to reduce the cost of equipment

expected: and reducing the cost of equipment
and cutting the cost of equipment

feedback.why_key: Two -ing forms have set the shape, and the third item arrives in a different one, which is where the reader stumbles.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the odd item to match the two before it.

payload.context: From a paragraph about the four-day week.
payload.sentence: Most staff would rather work five ordinary days than working four longer ones.
reasons: the two sides of the comparison are built differently
the comparison word is wrong
the subject and the verb do not match
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Would rather work sets a plain verb on the first side, so the second side needs work rather than working.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb form on both sides of than.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence giving three reasons why a school might make daily exercise compulsory. All three reasons must be built the same way.

feedback.why_key: Three reasons in one shape read as one argument. Three reasons in three shapes read as a writer thinking aloud.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first item, then copy its shape twice.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on daily school exercise. Find every and and or in it, read the items on either side, and fix any pair that is not built the same way. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Hunting for the joining words rather than reading for sense is what finds these, because a broken list still means what you intended.
feedback.feed_forward: Search for the joining words, then check both sides.

title: Writing long sentences that hold together under time pressure

teach.can_do: I can write long sentences that stay in one piece, and I know which long sentences are worth the risk.
teach.why_it_matters: A higher score asks for more clean complex sentences, not for fewer mistakes. Writing short and safe is not the cautious option; it is a decision to score lower.
teach.meaning: Two things are being marked at once, and learners usually protect one at the expense of the other. Range means sentences that carry more than one idea and join them properly. Accuracy means those sentences arriving whole. The way to have both is not to write more carefully; it is to reach for structures that have very little in them to go wrong, use two of them per sentence at most, and check three specific things at the end. Long is not the risk. Uncontrolled is.

form.pattern: main clause + one or two supporting clauses, each doing exactly one job
notes: the low-risk workhorses are the relative clause, the because and although clause, the shortened clause and the loaded noun phrase
two supporting clauses in one sentence is plenty; a third rarely adds anything a reader notices
vary the length on purpose, because a short sentence after two long ones is the strongest thing on the page
the three end checks: does every sentence have a main verb, does each verb match its own subject, and did every clause you opened get closed
form.negative: A negative main clause changes nothing about the joins: because nobody else was free, my grandmother collected us.
form.question: Read your sentence back and find the main verb. If you cannot, the sentence has not finished.

spec.label: how much is there in this structure to get wrong?

steps.text: a relative clause, a because clause, an although clause
steps.gloss: one or two things to get right, so use them constantly

steps.text: a shortened clause, a loaded noun phrase
steps.gloss: two or three things, and safe once you have checked whose subject it borrowed

steps.text: an inverted opening, a mixed unreal sentence
steps.gloss: four things at once, under time pressure, for one sentence's worth of credit

worked_example.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, the person who actually raised me was my grandmother, who lived three streets away.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two supporting clauses, each doing one job, and both of the kinds that hardly ever break. The sentence is plainly long and has very little inside it that can fail.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry every one of those facts and would leave a reader with no evidence that the writer can join anything at all.

notice_set.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, my grandmother was the one who actually raised me.
notice_set.question: Who raised the speaker?
notice_set.why: The opening explains why, and the part after the comma is the sentence's real news.

notice_set.sentence: My grandmother moved in when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
notice_set.question: How many separate things is the speaker reporting?
notice_set.why: Nothing marks where the first report ends, so the reader has to hunt for the join and may find it in the wrong place.

notice_set.sentence: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
notice_set.question: What does the speaker end up telling you happened?
notice_set.why: Everything here is background. The part it was building towards never arrives, so the sentence makes no claim.

notice_set.sentence: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
notice_set.question: Does the family still eat together?
notice_set.why: The noun after the comma names the practice and the clause behind it reports that it has gone.

notice_set.sentence: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
notice_set.question: Who grew up in a house of six?
notice_set.why: Nobody is named in the first half, so the reader waits for the comma and gives the growing-up to whoever turns up next, which here is the speaker.

teach.rule_line: Two supporting clauses per sentence, and check every sentence still has a main verb.
teach.false_rule: That a higher score means making fewer mistakes. It means more clean complex sentences, so short safe writing scores lower rather than higher.

errors.wrong: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
errors.right: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine, and she stayed for eleven years.
errors.why_it_happens: One subordinate clause has already gone in, so the sentence feels complex enough and the second main idea gets attached with nothing joining it at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one joining word after nine.

errors.wrong: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.right: Although both my parents worked full time, my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses feel like enough for one sentence. Neither of them is the main one, because and pulled the second clause inside the although along with the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: and.

errors.wrong: We ate together every evening, that has completely disappeared now.
errors.right: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
errors.why_it_happens: The comment plainly belongs with the sentence in front of it, so a full stop feels too heavy. A comma cannot hold two sentences, and there is nothing else in the sentence doing the work.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one noun: a habit, in front of that.

errors.wrong: Having grown up in a house of six, sharing a room felt completely normal.
errors.right: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is thinking about their own childhood, so the opening is anchored inside their head. On the page it borrows the subject that follows, and that subject is an activity rather than a person.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: sharing a room becomes I.

pays_in.note: It is the difference between an answer that is correct and one that shows range.
pays_in.model: Because rents rose faster than wages, the young people who stayed had to live at home.

pays_in.note: Longer answers need joins that hold while you are still deciding what to say.
pays_in.model: The people who moved out were mostly the ones who had young children.

pays_in.note: Dense passages are two-clause sentences, and finding the main one is the skill.
pays_in.model: Although the scheme proved popular, the council that introduced it lost the following election.

used_in.quote: This prompt pulls answers towards long sentences about families, which is exactly where the joins start giving way.
A two-minute turn about a change in your life is where a candidate either joins their sentences or lists them.

payload.sentence: Because the flat was too small and my sister had just started school.
payload.question: What does this tell you actually happened?

feedback.why_key: Two pieces of background have arrived and the thing they were explaining never turns up, so no event has been reported at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the clause that is not explaining anything.

payload.sentence: Living so far from my parents, I only see them twice a year.
payload.question: Who lives far away?

feedback.why_key: The opening takes the subject that comes after the comma, and that subject is the speaker rather than the parents.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the opening's subject from the clause after the comma.

payload.context: From a first draft about growing up.
payload.sentence: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
reasons: two whole sentences have been run together with nothing joining them
the sentence has no main verb at all
the opening clause has borrowed the wrong subject

feedback.why_key: She stayed for eleven years could stand alone, which is exactly why it cannot simply be laid against the sentence in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a joining word wherever two whole sentences meet.

payload.given: My parents both worked shifts. My grandmother lived three streets away. She was the one who raised me.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence using no more than two supporting clauses.

my parents both worked shifts, i was raised by my grandmother, who lived three streets away
both my parents worked shifts, the person who raised me was my grandmother

feedback.why_key: One reason and one piece of description are enough. A third clause would add length without adding anything the reader notices.
feedback.feed_forward: Stop at two supporting clauses and find your main verb.

payload.given: Evening classes were free until 2019. That has completely changed.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence without using a full stop or a semicolon.

expected: a situation that has completely changed
an arrangement that has completely changed
which has completely changed

feedback.why_key: Either a naming noun or a relative word turns the second sentence into part of the first, and a bare comma does neither.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a noun or a relative word before the comma can hold.

payload.context: From a paragraph about older relatives living with a family.
payload.stem: The flat was already crowded, ___ nobody suggested that my aunt should move out.

expected: but
yet
and yet

feedback.why_key: Both halves are whole sentences, so a comma on its own cannot join them and the word after it has to do the work.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a joining word after the comma between two full clauses.

payload.context: Build one sentence with a concession and a relative clause.

expected: although the house was small, nobody who visited ever complained

feedback.why_key: Two supporting clauses and one main verb at the very end, which is what a long sentence looks like when it is under control.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish with the main verb so you can see it is there.

payload.audio_text: She'd moved in by the time I started school.

expected: she'd moved in by the time i started school
she had moved in by the time i started school
shed moved in by the time i started school

feedback.why_key: One contracted auxiliary sets the order of two events, and by the time is the join. Miss either and you have two loose facts.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the squashed auxiliary that orders the events.

, my brother was still at school

reasons: two whole sentences have been run together
the sentence has no main verb

parts: Older people in Brackenfield used to live with their children.
Most of them now live alone or in sheltered flats.
Housing built in the last twenty years has almost no room for a second household.
model_combinations: Older people in Brackenfield, who once lived with their children, now live alone or in sheltered flats, largely because housing built in the last twenty years has no room for a second household.
Because almost nothing built in the last twenty years has room for a second household, the older people of Brackenfield, who once lived with their children, now live alone.
Housing built in the last twenty years leaves no room for a second household, which is why older people in Brackenfield now live alone rather than with their children.

feedback.why_key: Three facts, one main verb, and two supporting clauses of the kinds that rarely break. Three ways of arranging it and all three are fine.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the main verb first and hang the rest around it.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about why fewer families now live with an older relative. Make the first one long, with two supporting clauses, and the second one short.

feedback.why_key: The short sentence is doing work here. After a long one it lands hard, and varying the length on purpose is part of what range means.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the main verb in the long sentence before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on residential care. Run the three end checks over one body paragraph: a main verb in every sentence, every verb matching its own subject, and every clause you opened closed again. Fix what fails. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: These three checks take under two minutes on a real answer and they catch almost everything that breaks a long sentence under time pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: Run the three checks in order, one pass each.
